If 'Light Years' was the album that put Kylie back on the pop landscape, then 'FEVER' is the album that solidified Kylie as disco's most loved and pretentious diva--Fever made Kylie a superstar (again). While this album may not be Kylie's best compared to the landmark 'Impossible Princess', 'Fever' is an electro-pop confection that will leave you wanting more as the last song ends. Fever is an all out dance record. Don't look or substance or depth--it's all about FUN FUN FUN!

Kylie, being the showgirl that she is mixes up a concoction of pulsating dance beats to heat up the dancefloor. 1st single 'Cant Get You Out Of My Head' is unarguably one of the best songs of the millenium, the catchiest and hypnotizing in a while. 'In Your Eyes' is a faux dance ditty that is dizzying, swirling full of bubbly synths and tight beats. 'Love At First Sight' is reminiscent of Daft Punk's 'One More Time', already an instant Kylie classic, you'll be dancing and singing along after a few listens. 'Fragile' and 'Come Into My World' offer a look into Kylie's mysterious and sexy persona as she seduces you and coos in the most purring and provocative ways amidst a mystic backdrop of filtered strings, crazy bleeps and throbbing drums. While 'Burning Up' starts with a lazy guitar progression then leads into a frenzied euphoria. However my favorite moment in the album is 'Your Love' a laid-down affair (but still danceable!) complete with Spanish Guitars which makes Kylie's unsynthesized voice as the centerpiece of the yearning piece. I recommend this album to pop, dance and euro-music lovers alike. I guarantee this will not disappoint.

reviewText:
As I understand it, Devon Allman is Greg's son, but Greg was not at all involved in his son's life for most of Devon's life. Greg was not there, so there were no occasions for Devon to be hanging around with any of the Allman Brothers' members, or jam sessions, or practices or recordings, knew little or nothing about his legendary uncle, Duane, and generally was not directly exposed to his rich musical heritage. I guess genes win out in the end and here is Devon with a band called "Honeytribe," showing extraordinary chops. His voice sounds so much older and wiser than any man could at his young age. A Gift of the genes, no doubt.
I only just became aware of this album recently, having bought Devon's 2nd solo release, "Ragged & Dirty". That album just shocked me with its power and grace, grit and honesty.
My conclusion is that he had those qualities since he realized that he, like his father, just had that talent in him. This is not a return to Southern Rock. This is the son of a Southern Rocker, finding his way without his famous father. The songs and production are polished, no rough edges or signs of limitations of budget. Every song is a gem.
I had one moment while reading the song list before listening to the album, and that was the choice of "No Woman No Cry". It just didn't seem to fit the genre the album was purported to belong. I was wrong. It is a standout track, done his (their) way.
The album opens with the blistering (excuse me) "Torch." It makes it clear that this is going to be a "take no prisoners" effort. And it is.
I won't go track by track, since the album has been around so long. I will say that if you are a fan of Devon Allman, or of "The Royal Southern Brotherhood," then you will love this album. If you are just a fan of good soulful, bluesy rock music played by superb musicians, and sung by a voice that will be known as legendary, then get this and then follow Devon's catalogue. You'll be glad you did. Highest recommendation.

reviewText: At this point still reeling from the mildly unexpected blockbuster success of their previous album Break Out The Pointer Sisters and Richard Perry come at this album utilizing somewhat similar flavors to that album. At the same time there is a difference here. The production on this album is a tad less slick and quite considerably less glossy. The new wave elements and synthesizers are still very much in attendance but rather come right out at you often in quick bursts. "Twist My Arm","Pound,Pound,Pound" and "Burn Down The Night" all showcase this quality as channeled through a very similar new-wave/soul combination that was made famous on Jump (For My Love) a year earlier. Anyone who loved that song will find music to their liking on this song. Other tunes here focus more on songwriting and a more organic style of music,showing a funkier influence. One of the places that happens is on the Rush Pointer sung "Hey You",a message song from the point of view of someone confused about why it's necessary for all the poverty around them to exist when there seems to be ample ways to supply everyone. "Back In My Arms" and the sassy "Dare Me" have a somewhat similar musical effect armed with the same catchy pop hooks and funk rhythms. Taken together these three tunes are some of the strongest on the entire album. The title song showcases the stop and start synth/drum machine grooves of the Minneapolis sound at the time and,again with Ruth's husky gospel/soul vocal style scaling up and down the song has enormous amounts of impact and power. The album rounds out with two very different kinds of songs. The very very organic 80's gospel/R&B/soul of "Bodies And Souls" and the elongated closing song "Freedom";now this tune is not only again hugely gospelish in it's construction but has some uniquely chorded,very jazzy vocal harmonies that are a potent reminder of the individual spirit of these sisters and how their voices,together and apart serves as a potent reminder of the history of soul vocalizing,from it's source to it's then current sound. There's a lot more here musically than a lot of great pop/R&B songs with great vocals. It's an album showing,if nothing else the Pointer's had something else (and pretty creative) to say after their commercial peak in the decade.

Of the  tenors I have heard over six decades (probably all of the greats except Bjoerling and Bergonzi), the three that gave me the most pleasure were Luciano Pavarotti, Jon Vickers and Richard Tucker.  I saw Mr. Tucker in concert and as Alfredo, Cavaradossi, Samson, and Turridu.  He had a large but flexible voice that was never forced and had a golden timbre with ringing high notes. When he avoided the sobs and vocal gestures that were not uncommon in that era (and thankfully are not frequent on these recordings), he sang with elegance.  He was perhaps not the most insightful of actors in contrast to Vickers, nor did he have Pavarotti's natural exuberance with the audience, but he  always provided his best to the audience and  appeared fond of the audience.  In the modern recording era, his is probably the voice that most closely resembles that of Caruso.

These recordings are very welcome.  The sound is a bit overly reverberant at times but adequately capture the size, timbre, and clarity of Mr. Tucker's voice.  The recordings document his progression from a lyric to a spinto tenor.  While the size and weight of his voice grew, he maintained the clarity and flexibility.  The only drawback to these recordings are that some arias are repeated, but at this price point, it is hard to complain.

I suspect that Mr Tucker is not as well known today as some other singers.  These recordings demonstrate why he was a beloved figure at the Met for many years.  I highly recommend them to all opera fans. For those who have come to opera recently, I suspect it will be revelatory in terms of the type of voice that was heard during a golden era of vocalism.

reviewText: As other reviewers have discussed and debated the merits of Pirates' songs and Rickie Lee's vocals, I will limit these comments to the quality of MoFi's remaster.  The album itself was beautifully recorded, with veteran Warner Brothers producers (Bonnie Raitt, Randy Newman et al) Lenny Waronker and Russ Titelman at the helm and a number of skilled engineers, such as Elliot Scheiner, at the board.  Many of the backing musicians, such as Randy Brecker (of BS&T and jazz fame), Victor Feldman, Steve Gadd (of "Aja" fame) and Chuck Rainey, were (and remain) the finest studio and touring musicians in the U.S. and were also used by Steely Dan; indeed, Donald Fagen himself also appears on the album.  In short, this remaster is the closest to quality vinyl that I have heard, it is a notable and significant improvement over the regular "redbook" CD and it does real justice to the album's stellar production and the high quality of the songwriting and performances. The differences are readily notable from the first song, "We Belong Together," in which Gadd's drums finally regain their depth and power, and similarly for the joyous bouncing bass on "Woody and Dutch . . ."  For those who don't have an SACD player, don't worry.  I played this MoFI version on both regular redbook and SACD playback and I prefer the regular version, as it sounds a bit warmer and less harsh but with all of the sonic detail intact.  If you do have at least a decent playback stereo system and get a thrill out of clearly hearing individual instruments and how they interweave and combine in the final mixdown, and (of course) if you enjoy Rickie Lee's music, then I would recommend reaching deep in the pocket and spending the requisite dollars for this MoFi hybrid SACD remaster.  BTW, the "mini-LP cover" packaging is made of high quality, thick cardboard and the booklet is nicely manufactured as well.

It took four years for the band to write and release Hooray for Boobies, but when they did, it was a massive success. Fueled by the radio-friendly single "The Bad Touch," Hooray features not only thirteen full-length songs (the most on any BHG record), but also the return of the notorious "non-song tracks," which are -- get this -- funny this time around. Track three, "Mama's Boy," is a recording of an actual (and unscripted) phone call between Jimmy Pop and his mother.
The clever songwriting remains, and it's as filthy as it ever was - possibly the filthiest moment is the bit about masturbating to a picture of a missing child on a milk carton while driving a speeding trailer. Just listen to "A Lap Dance Is So Much Better When the Stripper Is Crying," and see if you don't burst out laughing at least once.
Most eighth-grade boys should get a kick out of the album once or twice just from the jokes alone, but there is so much more to appreciate than that. Any mild headbanger should love Lupus Thunder's heavy guitar hooks on songs like "I Hope You Die" and "Take the Long Way Home." But if you're looking for bone-crushing speed guitar (Metallica's "Master of Puppets," for example), don't look here.
Hooray for Boobies is an astonishing creation by far. Consider it a longer, heavier, nastier version of "One Fierce Beer Coaster," only without Rob Van Winkle on guest vocals.

reviewText:
In re Szell Brahms, I think of his concerto recordings first. All of his assets in this great group are prominent in this orchestral set:  convincing tempi, fire, great orchesral sound and interplay, understanding
of and ability to communicate Brahmian complexity, tragic depth, wildness, idiosyncratic beauty. In his equally great concerti, I think of the piano concerti with Serkin, Fleisher, and Curzon and the violin+ double concerti with Oistrakh and Rostropovich- just as in Mozart I think first of his accompaniaments for Serkin, Casadesus (on the whole), Firkusny, Peter Frankl, Annie Fischer et al.
There is no weak link in this set, though I admit to loving the first two symphonies per se a bit more than the
final two.  He conducts the outer movements quickly and intensely in #1, mastering the transition between the final movements and not meandering unnecessarily.  #2 is more pastoral and tender // its neighbor-the violin concerto, though all the Brahms DNA appears as well. And for those who consider Szell's conducting icy, try
any of the slow movements which he rarely rushes or skims. Both the Cleveland and Amsterdam thirds are passionate and explosive in the outer movement-the fourth movement is as driven as that in #2. The fourth symphony
is characterized by more calmness, solemnity, and intimations of tragedy, none of which Szell slights. Of course
he faces enormous competition from other sets or individual readings. For sets , I also recommend Jochum/DG nd EMI;
Van Beinum/RCOA/Philips, Klemperer/EMI, and Steinberg/Command. For non sets, Bohm/BPO #s 1 and 2 on DG (my favorites for both-see my reviews).  Also Munch/BSO #s 1 and 2 (RCA). Bohm 1953 #3 (Eloquence), Jochum/Dresden #2, Carlos Kleiber #s 2 and 4. (From Bohm's later set with the VPO, I recommend only the #4.)  The other works on this set are equally fine.

reviewText:
Obviously there's some controversy here.  You'll understand why when you hear her sing and even more so when you read the lyrics.  In the reviews you find the devoted, protective fan who thinks it's his place to protect his dream girl who he envisions to be an angel (a touch of blind devotion).  And you find those who have fallen in other directions under Karie's spell ... and have lost touch with reality.  (Again, when you hear her, you will understand both ... but hopefully maintain your sense of reality and avoid becoming creepy.)

OK, here's the unbiased straight deal from a lover of all good music:  There's no denying Karie's appeal.  Her unique voice and style is ... well, POWERFUL.  She'll make you believe in Sirens.  Once you hear her sing, you'll NEVER forget her.  Since I bought this CD, all I want to do is listen to her sing.  She could sing ANYTHING and it would mesmerize you.

There's much more to her than simply a baby-sexy, feminine voice (although that's Way Spankin Cool too).  For one, her French is BEAUTIFUL!  It will transport you to a sidewalk cafe in Paris or an evening boat ride on the Seine.  And the 60's/70's style European influenced music (with FunKy horns, whistles, clapping, la las, etc.) will have you thinking of a movie from that time in which a girl (with straight hair curled out on the bottom and false eyelashes) is driving her convertible along the cliff-side villages of the Cinque Terra; all in soft pastel Technicolor ... and you'll halfway expect Austin Powers to be hiding in the trunk.  You'll be whistling and snapping too (you can't help it) and saying, "This is SOOO COOL!".  Her English is also beautiful with the added fun of her French accent.  You will smile and laugh (in a 'I Dig It' kind of way) when you hear her say "Coca-Cola" and "Burger King".  And then she has an incredibly sweet side, which you hear in songs like, "The Way You Close Your Eyes" and even "Candyman" (... yeah, in some way, very sweet).

The music is equally unique.  It's amazing that they (all involved) combined the various influences and Crazy sounds in a way that's a Blast, perfect for her unbelievable voice, and most of all is FRESH, FUN, COOL, and yeah - GROOVY.  You can't get the songs out of your head ... even Ozzy couldn't BLAST her out of my mind!  You'll be singing in French even if you don't speak it ... guaranteed.  And you'll be doing Crazy dances like the Monkey and the Fists Over Your Head thing.  Don't try to resist; you can't.  I bet if I could play it for him, even Ozzy would start doing the Monkey with me.

The writing is also unique and is not only perfect but is the way it has to be to complete the spell.  Nothing too deep, meaningful, or dramatic; but ranging from Sweet to Seductive to Crazy to Freaky ... but a perfect ingredient.

And about the FREAKY element; nothing that's gonna BLOW YOUR MIND or Knock Your Socks Off like a Charlie Brown line drive.  Just Cool-Fun-Freaky and just enough of "Way Out There".  And there's a 60's Free-Spirited/Free-Love kind of flavor to some of it (well, more than a flavor in "LolitaPop Dollhouse").  And to that I say, "Groovy Baby!"

This is a great SOLID CD.  Every song is different and just COOL!  It's a great trip.
label: positive

reviewText: Certain things -"growth" for instance, or "breadth"- cannot be said about artists who are still so young, and only a few albums into their careers. Yet with Ms. Laura Veirs, the exquisite breadth that she is already showing  -from Troubled By Fire to Carbon Glacier- and her growth as a performer, are remarkable, however young, however "untenured" she may be. There are, like the prior reviewer says, laments, yet not they are not only that. They are explorations, impressions, musical poems. Jewels as diverse as "Ether Sings," "Lonely Angel Dust," "Shadow Blues," Snow Camping" or "Chimney Sweeping Man" alone justify, and fully prove, Veirs' talent, sensibility, and the astonishing maturity of her  compositions. Another important mention is the "dead-on" production by Tucker Martine who does what even some great producers forget to do, at times, he disappeared behind Laura Veirs' music, and yet has taken it to a new poetic and expressive plateau. I personally has heard enough to vow to follow Laura Veirs to whatever layers this album is still to take me, and whatever new depths may it have still unexplored.

reviewText:
Somewhere along the way the comparison struck me, but in a way it fits.  Dio, like Shemp Howard, was a talented individual who, taken in their own right, should be respected for what they accomplished, but will forever be overshadowed by their predecessors.  Maybe I come at this from a unique perspective.  Most stooge fans seem to be either Curly or Shemp, and Sabbath fans seem to be either Ozzy or Dio.  Personally I like them all and take each of them for what they were.  In the case of Sabbath, Dio allowed the band to finally reinvent themselves with some sort of cohesive vision, and his operatic growl was the perfect foil for Iommi's ever-darkening guitar riffs.  They did away with much of the experimentation and occasional acoustic dabblings, and became a more straight forward metal band.  On this album the quartet of Dio, Iommi, Butler, and Appice have captured a bit of the old black magic.  Though I find myself favoring the first disc, the entire album is about as solid a live performance as you can get.  The new material even fits in seamlessly with the old, a rare feat when old bands try to add to their back catalog.  In the end I will always love Sabbath with Ozzy or with Dio and this Live masterpiece is a welcome addition to the collection. It's one of those albums perfectly suited to driving with the windows down, the volume up, and your foot feeling a little on the heavy side.
And for the record, I'll let someone else sort out who the Joe and Curly Joe of Sabbath are.

reviewText:
The aptly titled three CD set PANDORA'S BOX, name lifted from the groovy song on their sophomore outing, has something for everyone no matter where they fall in Aerosmith affinity.  First of all, up front, I happen to think the first four albums were the cream of their musical crop and own them on CD, so the fact that this set contains 4 album cuts each from AEROSMITH and GET YOUR WINGS, 6 from TOYS IN THE ATTIC, and 5 from ROCKS, all directly lifted album versions sprinkled around this non-chronological compendium project, is not a detractor at all.  Then there are a very few album tracks, little more than a handful really, of the best beef from DRAW THE LINE, NIGHT IN THE RUTS, and ROCK IN A HARD PLACE, none of which compared to the first four masterpieces, but did squeak out some good tracks between the speed bumps.  There is also the non-album single (only on Aerosmith's Greatest Hits), their screaming to die for cover of The Beatles' Come Together.  As you can tell, this set released on Columbia's Legacy label only covers the ground assembled on Columbia Records, which for the old timers like me, was their golden era (until Perry left, with Whitford soon to follow, and the era of Aerosmith Best Of rehashes began to fill the void while the band had reached their nadir, and thankfully they arose again with both guitars in tow, but that was another time and another label).

So if you have the 3 or 4 masters from this era (and even if you have Draw and Ruts, and maybe even the awful Hard Place) you can still be in the market for this assembly since it boasts fully half of its material as demo's, rarities, and live performance tracks, all of which are fully engaging and well-engineered and mastered (there are no muddy hoof prints here).  The bookshelf box is attractive as well with a lot of photos and artwork and a well written band bio dishing up everything you need to know about Aerosmith from 1966 to 1986.  Rarities? There is a terrific oldie of Steven fronting his 60's band Chain Reaction, a Perry&Tyler-less Aerosmith (Tom Hamilton, Joey Kramer, Brad Whitford), as well as Joe Perry's and Brad Whitford's extra-marital affairs released during the hiatus (or nadir as I call it).  The alternate version of Movin' Out and another Beatles cover (Helter Skelter) are absolute necessities, Draw The Line and Last Child are remixed to sound better than the originals, and there's a whole lot of other sleazy smithy goodies to lay your hands on if you are an Aerophile, including Rattlesnake Shake and Walking The Dog as live radio broadcasts, All Your Love (Otis Rush blues jam), and On The Road Again (a Lovin' Spoonful cover), as well as live versions of album favorites (the live versions of Kings & Queens and Adams Apple are just stunning).  Downtown Charlie and Riff & Roll are previously unreleased jams.  You can even get a sense of how the band crafted tunes: listen to Soul Saver and see how it served up a preliminary look at their apocalyptic Nobody's Fault, or check out Let It Slide, the rough cut slice of Cheesecake.

Since the three disc set tried to cover a lot of bases for the musical fan who has a lot of Aerosmith, for the musical fan who has little to no Aerosmith, and for the rabid musical fan who will eat up everything Aerosmith, and spells it all out as a huge casserole with no chronoly at all, other than getting the grooves to flow, I think Columbia did about as well as could possibly be expected.  Oh yeah, and there is a fine gem of a hidden track at the end of it all.  Don't miss it because there is no hint whatsoever in the packaging to tell you.  It is supposedly a "new" song Aerosmith composed just for the set (but that might be a contractual problem so the probability is that it is a retooled jam with a Tyler intro; in any case it rocks!).  If you are a neophyte looking for a solid "best of" collection, you can't do any better than this, it beats any of the "greatest hits" or essentials collections hands down and the price is terrific for 3 fully loaded CD's (I paid three times the current low price back in '93 when this was first released).  Sweet Pandora!

reviewText:
Dream Theater has been making progressive metal albums for years and people are still buying them, so I figured they must be doing something right.  I picked up Octavarium without hearing any of the songs first besides the single "I Walk Beside You", and while I wasn't blown away, it's still very good.

One thing you should be aware of is that these songs are long, and I mean LONG.  Not wimpy six-minutes long, more like, the final two tracks run over a half hour combined long.  Dream Theater takes their time getting where they're going, and they spend significant time milking the better hooks they come up with.  If eight songs that are over an hour in length combined don't sound like your thing, then don't get this record.

"Root of All Evil" is a good opening track which shows the band's metal sound, and is followed by "The Answer Lies Within", which doesn't.  "These Walls" contains probably my favorite guitar line on the album.  The aforementioned "I Walk Beside You" doesn't sound much like the rest of the songs, but it's still enjoyable and has a great pre-chorus.  "Sacrificed Sons" is a strong track about 9/11 with perhaps the strongest rock out section on the album.  The title track is an absolutely mammoth twenty four minute, five part epic.  The first and last few minutes are mostly instrumental, and in between, Dream Theater manages to hold your attention amazingly well with a series of changes in style and tempo. reviewText:
There are those times when true music listeners must be sure that record company executives suffer from some form of tin-ear syndrome.  Why Mathis fans have had to wait this long for JOHNNY'S MOOD and FAITHFULLY on compact disc remains a mystery.  We can only hope that Mathis' eclectic and diverse recordings of Soul/Pop/R&B/Traditional albums of the late 1970s well into the 1980s will someday be reissued on CD.

While it shouldn't be necessary to say, Mathis delivers his own special brand of ethereal magic on classic standards like "How High the Moon", and "April in Paris" on JOHNNY'S MOOD.  On FAITHFULLY, he delivers much of the same on songs like "Tonight", "Maria" and "You Better Go Know" that at the time of their recording were merely on the verge of becoming standards.  Both recordings were orchestrated by Glenn Osser, an underrated arranger whose orchestrations weaved disparate songs together so well that an album had the thematic cohesion of a great movie score.  (Who can forget the unified feel of Mathis' Osser-orchestrated album HEAVENLY?)

It is still anybody's guess why FAITHFULLY and HEAVENLY, which were released back-to-back, were not included in a two-CD album package?  Both albums had a similar synthesis and offered title tunes ("Heavenly" and "Faithfully") written by a then unknown composer named Burt Bacharach; and HEAVENLY and FAITHFULLY both charted at No. 1 and 2 on the Pop Album Charts in 1959 and 1960 respectively.  Nevertheless, JOHNNY'S MOOD and FAITHFULLY work well as a package.

This remastering is absolutely crystal clear.  This set is also a welcome addition to anyone seeking to preserve their old vinyl copies, and it is a perfect introduction for younger fans who are only beginning to scratch the surface of Mathis' prolific discography.  Buy with confidence.

reviewText:
This is a veritable treasure trove for fans of this too-often forgotten era of pop and pop-rock (1959-1963) between the first wave of rock & roll and the British "invasion" that followed the Beatles in early 1964.  Here are 90 of the most forgotten records from this period [total running time: 3 hours, 35 minutes] - ones that NEVER get played on oldies radio because they not only missed reaching the pop Top 40, they missed the entire Billboard Hot 100!  (Most oldies radio avoids anything that wasn't at least Top 20.)  The case with many of these records is that they were quite popular in some markets, but for some reason were unable to get the radio airplay elsewhere needed to generate broader demand.

A real advantage of a collection like this is that there should be very little duplication with any other CD collection you own.  I especially enjoyed the fact that I knew so few of these records, even though by around the mid-point of this time frame I was starting to become aware of everything that was being played on the radio.  This is a trip back in time that one can hear with fresh ears.  And that reminds me of another advantage: the sound is astonishingly good given the age and relative rarity of these records.  Two more advantages: 1) a 16-page booklet with an informative paragraph devoted to each and every artist and record (that's 90 records by 90 different artists); and 2) every record is presented chronologically, giving one a greater sense of the musical flavors of each year.

For anyone who might think that such lesser hits as these must have been throwaways, let me point out that 13 of the 90 recordings were by future Rock & Roll Hall of Famers.  Here's the list: Johnny Cash, Ray Charles, Sam Cooke, The Crickets, Duane Eddy, The "5" Royales, The Flamingos, The 4 Seasons, Barry Mann (in the R&R HOF as a songwriter), Del Shannon, The Temptations, Ike and Tina Turner, and Stevie Wonder (13-year-old Little Stevie Wonder in 1963).  Johnny Cash is also in the Country & Western Hall of Fame, as are Glen Campbell, Sonny James, Webb Pierce, Hank Snow and Conway Twitty.  And Sarah Vaughan is a Grammy Lifetime Achievement honoree.

Other artists of note appearing in this collection include Arthur Alexander, The Angels, Paul Anka, Bobby Bare, Gary (U.S.) Bonds, Johnny Burnette, Vikki Carr (her competing version of The Crystals' "He's a Rebel" from 1962 is on the unconvincing and borderline shrill side), The Chantels, The Del Vikings, Jackie DeShannon, Ral Donner, Shelley Fabares, Barbara George, Clarence Henry, Brian Hyland, Jay & the Americans, Hank Locklin, Aaron Neville, Tony Orlando, The Robins, Tommy Roe, Neil Sedaka, Bobby Vee  and Baby Washington.

There are 14 Billboard "Bubbling Under" one-timers who never appeared on any other national chart with this or any other record.  Ever heard of the Kenjolairs, Aki Aleong, Vicki Tasso, Doug Warren & the Rays, or Jan Burgens & His New Orleans Syncopators...?  I didn't think so.

My Top 20 from this collection (the highest positions most of these records have ever seen!)
1) Nolan Strong & The Diablos -  "Mind Over Matter" (1962) - Detroit proto-soul classic (penned by Devora Brown) with a phenomenal lead vocal by the ethereally high-voiced "Daddy Rockin'" Strong and the stellar electric blues-rock guitar of [sounds like it could be Lonnie Mack/Jimi Hendrix icon Robert Ward! (?)]  It broke through on WLS (50,000-watt Top 40 radio) in Chicago, reaching #16, but surprisingly went no further.  Definitely for fans of Nathaniel Mayer & The Fabulous Twilights' "Village of Love" (on the same Fortune label) - and definitely (IMO) one of the best records of 1962.

2) Little Stevie Wonder  "I Call It Pretty Music But the Old People Call It the Blues Pt. 1)" (1963) - dynamic and propulsive, and by an unmatched talent, but it somehow got lost in the immediate wake of Stevie's phenomenal début single, the #1 pop and R&B smash "Fingertips, Pt. 2"

3) Robert Parker  "All Nite Long (Pt. 1)" (1959) - cookin' and jivin' sax instro that should never have stalled at #113 in its only week on the chart.  This was Robert Parker five and half years before his Top Ten hit "Barefootin'."

4) Johnny Cash  "Johnny Yuma, the Rebel" (1961) - one of the best vocal TV theme songs of all time (from the Western series "The Rebel" starring Nick Adams)

5) Big Al Downing  "The Story of My Life" (1962) - harmonica-powered Southern-style R&B take on Marty Robbins' 1958 country and pop hit (an early Burt Bacharach-Hal David composition).  Like "Mind Over Matter," it was a hit on WLS in Chicago [#15] but failed to break nationally.

6) Googie René  "The Slide" (1960) - sizzling and grooving organ-&-sax-propelled R&B dance-call tune

7) The Temptations  "Paradise" (1962) - This Temptations chart début record was obviously inspired by The 4 Seasons, with Eddie Kendricks taking the high-voiced lead vocal (in other words, the Frankie Valli part, but in his natural voice, as opposed to Valli's falsetto)

8) Ray Charles  "No Letter Today" (1963) - Ray in his brilliant country-soul period doing credit to the 1944 Ted Daffan country ballad hit.  This one got buried on the flipside of "Take These Chains from My Heart."

9) Conway Twitty  "What a Dream" (1960) - This otherwise rather ordinary ballad serves as a showcase for seemingly all of the Twitty bird's trademark vocal tricks, especially his guttural croaks.

10) Baby Washington  "Handful of Memories" (1962) - #16 R&B hit by one of the all-time great voices of the genre

11) Aaron Neville  "Over You" (1960) - cool, relentlessly rhythmic New Orleans R&B with a neat horn chart. The great Allen Toussaint produced and co-wrote it.  It was Neville's first chart record (preceding "Tell It Like It Is" by six years) and a significant national R&B hit (reaching #21).  [On a very sad note, Toussaint passed way 13 days after I submitted this review, Nov. 10, 2015.]

12) Sam Fletcher  "Time Has a Way" (1959) - big ballad by the big-voiced Roy Hamilton sound-alike called "The Man with the Golden Voice" (which later became Paul Carrack's sobriquet)

13) Jack B. Nimble & the Quicks  "Nut Rocker" (1962) - original recording of the classic instro by an alternate incarnation of B. Bumble & the Stingers

14) Del Shannon  "I Won't Be There" (1962) - a good, if not particularly memorable one penned and performed by the talented Shannon, who followed his big chart début year ("Runaway" was a breakout #1 smash in '61) with a major chart slump in '62

15) Tony Orlando  "Chills" (1962) - That's right...Tony Orlando!  The 18-year-old New Yorker had an appealing soulful-pop style, and this is a solid Gerry Goffin-Jack Keller-composed song.

16) Duane Eddy  "The Battle" (1962) - This twangy-guitar version of "The Battle Hymn of the Republic" was likely intended as Eddy's answer to his signature instro smash "Rebel-'Rouser from 1958.

17) The Chantels  "Here It Comes Again" (1962) - graceful girl-group harmony

18) Eddie Quinteros  "Come Dance with Me" (1960) - an all-out rockin' tribute to Ritchie Valens who had been gone one year

19) Hank Snow  "Miller's Cave" (1960) - not a wasted syllable in the telling of this blood-curdling tale set in a forbidding Southern Georgia locale - a #9 country song by one of the greats

20) Bobby Vee  "One Last Kiss" (1960) - 17-year-old Robert Velline from Fargo was on the cusp of a major breakthrough (with "Devil Or Angel"), but only the most comprehensive Bobby Vee collections on CD have ever included this appealing cover of a number from "Bye Bye Birdie."

The only ones I loathed upon first listen:
1) Gus Backus  "Wooden Heart" (1961) - truly terrible Teutonic twaddle (inexplicably, Joe Dowell's version got to #1)

2) The Swe-Danes  "Scandinavian Shuffle" (1960) - entirely sung in idiotic vocalese (which is redundant) [Beware of the ear-splitting final note - if you are able to make it that far]

3) Robie Lester  "The Miracle of Life" (1960) - insipid [Beware of bloated song titles that promise more than they can deliver]
label: positive

reviewText:
Most of you have your favorite era of his music. I like them all in different ways, but I like the sixties best, and this box shows why. There were many aspects to his music, but this set focuses on those secular recordings that were made in the studio and which were not connected to a movie. The best of the movie music is available on Command performance - Essential sixties masters volume 2, which I've already reviewed, while the gospel and live recordings are also available separately.
With those exceptions, every song Elvis recorded during the sixties is here. These include most of his big hits from the period, among them It's now or never, Are you lonesome tonight, Surrender, His latest flame, Good luck charm, Suspicion, She's not you, Don't cry Daddy, In the ghetto and Suspicious minds. Of course, there are a few missing, because they were from the excluded categories, but anybody who wants a Greatest hits collection will find plenty to choose from.
Apart from the hits, you get all the album tracks, many of them long forgotten except by fans of Elvis. These include covers of Fever (Peggy Lee), Memphis Tennessee (Chuck Berry), And the grass won't pay no mind (Neil Diamond), Just call me lonesome (Eddy Arnold), Gentle on my mind (Glen Campbell), I'm movin' on (Hank Snow) and I'll hold you in my heart (Eddy Arnold) among them.
Among the songs written for Elvis but which remain obscure to all but his fans, there are many good songs, any of which might one day be rediscovered and used in a movie or TV advertisement. The song Gently, from one of his early sixties albums, was translated into French and recorded by Petula Clark. I can't ever remember another cover of this song in any language, though there probably is one somewhere - just one of many great songs in this set that you're not likely to hear on the radio.
The last half of the final CD is made up of selected alternate takes of some of the songs, although the most famous alternate take, his laughing version of Are you lonesome tonight, is not among them. Nevertheless, this is a fine collection which will appeal to a far wider public than just his dedicated fans.

reviewText:
The late singer Tim Buckley left brief, but very strong catalog of music before his untimely demise in the mid-70's.  To my ears this record, DREAM LETTER: LIVE IN LONDON 1968 is the crown jewel of his recording career.

When this was recorded in 1968, Buckley was metamorphisizing from a mystical folkie, towards a more avant-garde jazz based style.  Whatever the style was, Buckley was an otherworldly vocalist, capable of emiting low animalistic grolws or hitting ear-piercing high trills at the drop of a beat.  His vocal fireworks are both breathtaking and supportive of the feeling of the songs, something few artists manage. As he sings on this fine two disk set, you can hear him mold his voice in the same way Coltrane molds the sound of his sax to reflect the pure emotion of his material.

Standouts include the opening number BUZZIN' FLY, the epic WHO DO YOU LOVE, an amazing version of the folk standard WAYFARING STRANGER and a powerful medley of PLEASANT STREET merging into a couple verses of The Supreme's classic YOU KEEP ME HANGIN' ON.  He ends the set with a gentle, yet powerful version of his most famous song, ONCE I WAS.

The spare, intuitive backing from Danny Thompson (Bass), Lee Underwood (guitar) and David Friedman (vibes) frame these performances perfectly.  The instrumentl ebb and flow mesh perfectly with Buckley's emotion rollercoaster vocals creating a live recording that still sounds powerfull and fresh thirtysome years after it was recorded.

As a life long Tommy Shaw fan I held high expectations for this release. Considering that 8 of the tracks are among my all-time favorite songs I held very high expectations for this release. However, considering Jack Blades' had such a poor showing on his recent solo debut, I had some reservations about this forthcoming release. I did not listen to any of the streamed audio online as I wanted to listen to the cd with a fresh set of ears unprejudiced toward any or all of the disk.

Aside from the incredibly sparse liner notes, this cd is a monster of an album. From the very first notes of SUMMER BREEZE on through to the end of DANCE WITH ME, I was simply amazed. Though Jack appears to sing lead vocals on most of the tracks, he sings with his natural voice (as revealed on the DAMN YANKEES debut and early NIGHT RANGER releases) and never tries to sound 'too different from Tommy Shaw' as he began doing on the DON'T TREAD release and throughout his SHAW BLADES and solo releases. As such, the songs sound fresh, vibrant and natural... albeit individualized for Tommy and Jack.

I despise cover tracks where in the musicians try to 'make the song their own' by changing the sound and arrangement of the track so much that it hardly resembles the original. I believe that with genuine vocal and instrumentation talent that a true artist can 'own' the song and yet honor the original recordings by staying true to the basic style of the original. Tommy and Jack do just that.

Never does Tommy stray too far with his guitar solos and never do the boys' vocals perform in any way other than admiration for these classic tracks. DANCE WITH ME and I AM A ROCK offer distinct changes to the styles of the songs, yet never too much to dishonor ORLEANS or SIMON AND GARFUNKLE.

Many critics have regarded this release as being an "acoustic" album, which could hardly be true. While the majority of tracks feature the acoustic guitar, this album has more than enough electric six-strings, keyboards and drums to be a rollicking rock and roll album. Never could this be considered an 'unplugged' cover album as one critic remarked.

This is a GREAT covers album. It met my expectations and exceeded them. I tip my hat to Tommy Shaw... this album exemplifies his genuine artistry through and through.

Cutting his teeth, so to speak, on 3 excellent discs featuring songs of romance i.e. " Romance ", "Segundo Romance " and " Romances " he has won over the hearts of women the world over. That being the case, it is truly interesting that on " Vivo" the highpoints aren't necessarily the three romance medley's but the slighly more uptempo numbers! Beginning with the startling " Quiero " things get off to a fast start and only slows down moderately with " Tu Solo Tu ", definitely one of my favorites.... in a disc filled with favorites! Obviously the audience is here to listen to Luis sing songs of love ( natch! ) and he doesn't disappoint. Medley No. 1 takes off and the fans are in a state of ecstacy! Generally I find audiences to be slightly intrusive on live cd's but I'm willing to forgo that complaint here....besides I'd probably be yelling too. Other highlight's include, " Suave " another uptempo that really swings quite well, thank-you and " O Tu O Ninguna " a mid-tempo that made me wish I spoke Spanish! Plus, throwing in " La Bikina " a mariachi number that was nominated for a Latin Grammy this year, and you get the idea that things are moving along very nicely! Adding to all this is a band that plays extremely well together and seems to stay with Luis every step of the way. Some of the disc does sound as though perhaps the band is slightly over-rehearsed and that they don't leave much room for any spontinenty but that's a small infraction. And as for LM himself....obviously he's in fine voice and playing the consumate entertainer who is very much at home onstage. An artist who truly knows his audience and here gives all of himself for their enjoyment. And ours! Bravo to Luis and bandmates!
In the end, " Vivo " is simply chock full of great music, wonderful packaging and tons of pictures plus a small booklet as well! I will readily admit that there is a hint of 'Las Vegas schmaltz' incorporated in his shows but I won't fault him for that. A lot of thought went into releasing this product and while many might find it slightly calculating, I find everything very much to my liking. So you may wish to look into having " Vivo " added to your 'musical library' as well. And as to where you locate your copy....well, that's up to you!

reviewText:
Radiohead. Politics. I don't know what to say other than those couple of words. I could go on and on about how much I enjoy this album, and how much this band has inspired me and led me to believe that there is some future for the rock industry.
Some tend to think of this as 'going back' to previous recording and experimentation. Not at all. This band constantly amazes me with every minute of this album. Being in a band myself, I can't even comprehend the genius it takes to write such songs. Songs that can warm you heart or make you so frightfully paranoid.
I prefer not to go into a rundown of each song individually, but I would note that every song has superior craft and musicianship. I'm not trying to sound preachy, and I'm not trying to be hip by listeing to this band. But you can listen to this group 10 times and never really hear them. "2+2=5" is a masochistic prog rock song reminiscent of Orwell's "1984". Other highlights include "Sit down, stand up", "Where I end and you begin", and the most experimental track on the disc "Myxamatosis". The sounds of a diseased rabbit never felt so morbid.
I would, however, like to sing out one track in particular. "A Wolf at the Door". Of all the tracks this album throws at you, it comes at you the fastest and with the most emotion. So incredibly melodic, but so very violent. "Steal all the children, if I don't pay the ransom." If this album has a most brilliant moment, I feel it would be in this track.
I'm not sure if this album will stand the test of time, as OK Computer has (and it certainly isn't as good), but this band will most definately come to be the most recognizable band in the world.
For those of us who listen...

'There But For Fortune' is an omnibus album of 18 tracks from three important Phil Ochs albums. Unfortunately, 'Pleasures of the Harbor', the album for which I always had the highest regard is not among them.

Ochs, along with Richard Farina is one of the two great pretenders to Bob Dylan's throne (inherited from Woody Guthrie), as the great American folksong singer / songwriter, after Dylan went electric.

Unfortunately, both Ochs and Farina died long before they were able to achieve their full potential. It is especially interesting with Ochs to imagine if he would ever outgrow his tendency to write songs which rapidly became dated. In this album, there is an odd mix of references and subjects which are probably totally unfamiliar to young people today, with some other songs, such as 'Cops of the World' which have become remarkably more relevant with recent events.

In contrast, Dylan's genius was in writing so many great songs which, like many of Guthrie's songs, have all the earmarks of enduring for a long, long time.

With some caveats, I agree with other reviewers that this is about as good as it gets for Ochs collections. Enjoy them often.

Stanley Turrentine's distinct blues drenched yet crispy hard swinging sound and tone fronts a session padded by a dream rhythm section... with ultra grease and groove layed on by the late great Shirley Scott, who could have just as easily have called the session her own. reviewText:
Traffic had one of the most original (and interesting) sounds in British rock, and not only because of their eclectic musical influences, which embraced psychedelia, folk, jazz, soul, R&B, and even classical.  Their unique sound was also the result of their unusual instrumentation.  While the group went through a number of personnel changes, its constant core members were Steve Winwood (vocals, keyboards, guitars), Chris Wood (sax, flute, and organ), and Jim Capaldi (drums & percussion).  With no regular bass player, Winwood often filled in with the bass pedals on his organ.  And, while there is no lack of guitars on most Traffic recordings, the guitar is not emphasized or particularly important to the group's sound.  Dave Mason came and went in their early years and, on other recordings, Steve Winwood would switch to guitar, with Chris Wood taking over organ duties.  In short, Traffic was anything but your typical guitar-bass-drums rock outfit.  And, with "white Ray Charles" prodigy Winwood at the helm, and with their willingness to experiment with virtually any sound or musical style, they cut some of the most distinctive and important records in British rock.
"Last Exit," their third full-length release, is actually a record-company creation.  With Dave Mason gone and the band temporarily disbanded (while Winwood joined Eric Clapton in Blind Faith), Island Records cobbled this LP together from tracks that didn't make it onto Traffic's earlier albums, along with two extended live jams ("Feelin' Good" and "Blind Man" - neither of which was ever recorded in the studio).  The result, while not as cohesive as Traffic's other releases, is nonetheless exceptionally strong.  While Mason's cut "Just For You" is disposable pop, Winwood's studio tracks are some of his strongest:  the swirling psychedelic soul of "Shanghai Noodle Factory," the haunting blues-rock of "Withering Tree," and the Beatlesque rocker "Medicated Goo."  And, while their sound quality is sub-par, the live tracks on side two are the group's most convincing experiments with the blues, as well as their most essential concert recordings available.
In short, "Last Exit" isn't Traffic's best album, but it's not far behind.

reviewText: As a jazz buff, I had very little exposure to Cheryl Bentyne other than through her stellar work with Manhatten Transfer. Her performance in " The Book of Love" is a revelation on many levels. This collection of beautiful ballads is one of the most poignantly romantic recordings I have heard. The lush arrangements of husband/keyboardist Corey Allen and the backing of the Prague Symphony Orchestra are magical. Ms. Bentyne's vocal quality and range are near perfection--her phrasing and enunciation are models of clarity. She is coquettish without being cloying. Listen to her alluring treatment of Let's fall in love and you too will get weak in the knees. Her classic treatment of "Be My Love" is exceeded only by Wayne Johnson's beautiful acoustic guitar and a jewel of a solo by cellist Armen Ksajikian. The high water mark of the cd in my view is "You taught my heart to sing". This romantic ballad is perfected by Bentyne backed only by husband Corey Allen's piano. The feeling and emotion between the two is palpable. Bentyne and her arranger husband have indeed made beautiful music together.  Highly Recommended!

On this recording, Norbert Leo Butz as Jamie is incredibly alive and vibrant, showing emotion after emotion (even on a recording!) as his character develops.  If I had to pick an antagonist, it would go to Jamie, even though you can't discount his intentions and the delicacy of his situation.  Sure, he gave into his weaknesses, but he's human and imperfect, and still comes off as somewhat noble.
I can't praise Sherie-Rene Scott's Amneris (from Aida) enough, and her interpretation of The Last Five Years's Cathy is nothing short of astounding.  She creates a character who is not only likable, but applaudable in her efforts and daily struggles, and consequently, her successes.
My next props have to go to Jason Robert Brown for the most incredibly innovative story line/narrative structure I've heard of produced on the stage to date.  I can only describe it as sheer brilliance, how the characters are developed, details revealed, little by little throughout.  How Jamie goes from desparate to smitten to anxious, to despair and confusion is thrilling, but even more genius is how Cathy goes from lost and hurt to repressed to frustrated to SO in love (all backwards of course).  During the finale, when Jamie's saying goodbye forever and Cathy's saying Goodbye Until Tomorrow, I'm truly impressed how the stories manage to come together, even if it's not really in any kind of similar time frame.
All in all, I highly recommend this recording.  Except for a couple of seemingly gratuitous curse words (in case you're wondering), this is a psychologically enlightening, romantically involving, emotionally driven piece of work that stands not only as a memento for those who have experienced the show itself, but also a delightful album of modern, varied musical theater.

reviewText:
This album isn't perfect, and I have to be in the mood for it, but I do appreciate it as a work of art on its own and a compliment to the Beatles' original music. It's a collage of sorts or perhaps a panorama on the music and sounds they made.

I am a Beatles fan and was familiar with their catalogue long before finally hearing this album, but I also come to Love as an eclectic person and a lover of the arts. My tastes in music range from the Beatles to classical opera to Welsh folk singing, all of which I love for different reasons. I'm also keenly interested in theatre, including musical, and the performing arts. I long for the opportunity to see this or any Cirque de Soleil show but at this time in my life, that is not foreseeably forthcoming. So it's possible my perspective is quite different than that of some other Beatles fans. The fact that I'm interested in a broad variety of stuff and enjoy new and different things likely contributes to my attitude.

I also really want to defend this recording from some of the flak from some big Beatles fans and self-labeled "purists". Firstly, I would never consider myself to be a purist about anything in a general philosophical sense, but that aside, I cannot agree that this remix constitutes sacrilege, though I suppose I understand the ire about the fact that this happened to coming along before the original albums were fully remastered. Still, we shouldn't take that out on this album. As the musical accompaniment to the Beatles-themed Cirque De Soliel show Love, this album can stand as a worthy piece of art on its own and quite justified in its creation. To elaborate further, as a surprising number of one-star reviewers really seem to have not understood what this is or how it came into being, Cirque De Soleil is a French Canadian-founded performing arts troupe crossing acrobatics dance. It's based upon aerial ballet and performance art of that sort. George Harrison, who seems to have been a keen appreciator of art and beauty, was friendly with the creators of Cirque De Soleil and was the first one interested in a project like this. It was George, a Beatle, who was responsible for initiating this. It didn't end up happening until several years after his passing, but the musical collage to accompany the cirque show was mixed and edited by George Martin and his son Giles and approved by all of the surviving Beatles and their estates. With that in mind, I don't think purists have that much a case here.

Love is the Beatles via Cirque. It's not meant to be a hits collection or a Beatles remastering project. And it doesn't have to be. I find it to have moments of real beauty and artfulness and I recommend to open-minded Beatles fans, music fans, or lovers of the arts who like to experiment and are willing to try something different and new. Being familiar with the original albums is helpful but inessential. All you need is love and an open heart-mind.

reviewText:
A Matter Of Life And Death (2006.), Iron Maiden's fourteenth studio album

The new millenium has been a huge revitalisation for Iron Maiden. It cannot be denied that the `90s was a barren period for the heavy metal gods. The departures of guitarist Adrian Smith and later frontman Bruce Dickenson left a huge hole to fill in the band. `Virtual XI', released in 1998 was an extremely disappointing album and marked a low point for the band. However brighter days were ahead as Bruce Dickenson and Adrian Smith both returned to the band. The restored line up then released `Brave New World' and `Dance Of Death' which were both fantastic albums. So could Iron Maiden, heavy metal giants of more than just a generation pull another serving of classic metal out of the bag? With the band's popularity again surging, `A Matter Of Life And Death' couldn't have been released at a better time...

Over their career, Maiden have had more than  a fair share at successful attempts to push musical boundaries. Their early career, sparked during the New Wave Of British Heavy Metal was revolutionary and then their progressive and conceptual stuff at the end of the `80s was revelatory. `A Matter Of Life  And Death' is very much a progressive album but it goes one step further and incorporates a grand, epic feel giving it an imposing, `magnum opus' style. There is plenty of life in Maiden yet and this album is an awesome expansion of their classic sound. For me and a number of other fans, this album is definitely the best of the band's work since the re-union of the classic line up but it is in many ways one of the best albums of Maiden's career, full stop. This brilliant album deserves more than just a mention alongside `Powerslave' and `Number Of The Beast'. In terms of songwriting, there is some extremely impressive stuff on here which can easily be put down as some of the band's best. There are giant epic songs which ooze the prog metal style that Maiden often incorporate into their music throughout the album. However, I personally find that what really makes this album a result is how the band performs the music. The album has that great `live' feel to it and the chemistry of the band seems better than ever. You can see this on the DVD which comes with some versions of the album. The band seem to be loving playing their new music and the new directions it takes them in. All of the band have a hand in the songwriting through the album which furthermore makes this work a proper band effort. Guitarists Smith, Murray and Gers all play out some fantastic riffs and memorable melodies across the album and Steve Harris' bass work always adds to the colour of the songs. Bruce is on top form with the operatic vocals and Nicko McBrain exhibits some of his finest drumming on this album, providing a mix between beats with heavy prescence and the more understated lines.

`Different World', the album's opening track has proved to be an immensely popular track. The main riff is inescapable and some of the melodies in this brilliant opener are great. `These Colours Don't Run' is a classic heart on sleeves song from the band. Bruce gives an expressive vocal performance in a song dedicated to those serving in wars. `Brighter Than A Thousand Suns' is the first epic of the album, with a theme about the Manhattan Project. The song has some rousing choruses and plenty of varied sections which weave together seamlessly. `The Pilgrim' is equally strong  musically, with an eastern flavoured riff. Bruce Dickenson returns us to the themes of war with `The Longest Day', a song about the D-Day landings. There are some beautiful melodies in this one as well as racing guitars and a gripping chorus.

`Out Of The Shadows' is more archetypal Maiden, with a nice mix of electro acoustic sections and heavier choruses. A song about birth and entering the world. The curiously titled `The Reincarnation Of Benjamin Breeg' was another single off the album. The song opens and closes with a slow, atmospheric guitar work whilst the main part of the song features more classic riffs and inspired Dickenson Vocals. `For The Greater Good Of God' is a slower, more reflective epic which grows much more enjoyable with repeated listens. `Lord Of Light' features more impressive solos and melodies and a galloping section; something we haven't seen from Maiden in a few albums. `The Legacy' is an amazing closer, my personal favourite track on the album. This final epic is built up into different sections, each with their own melodies and themes. However this doesn't break the flow to the song and each section stands tall in their own right, lyrically covering humanity through time and the trail left from war and opposition. The acoustics are fantastic on this one!

`A Matter Of Life And Death' is Iron Maiden's finest album in a long time and a classic in it's own right. Easily one of the best metal albums of 2006 this work is an epic journey of massive proportions and never loses it's life or spark. The band embarked on a great tour for this album, often playing the whole thing right through at some of the gigs - testament to the greatness of the material on here I guess. If you like Iron Maiden or music with an epic style, this album is a must!

MY RATING: 9.5/10

reviewText:
William Smith Monroe of Rosine, Kentucky (1911-1996) wrote these tunes for fiddle.  Many fiddlers passed through Monroe's definitive bluegrass band, Bill Monroe and the Bluegrass Boys during an approximate 50 years of true bluegrass music....however, it was Kenny Baker, a great fiddler in his own right (having put forth numerous fiddle albums of his own), who, along with Monroe's band of 1976, laid down the definitive recordings of many of Monroe's greatest melodies--from Jerusalem Ridge to Ashland Breakdown, Fiddler's Pastime, Big Mon, and many others.

If you purchase ONE album of Monroe instrumentals, this is the one to buy. It was rumored that Kenny Baker played an original Guarneri violin--but whatever it was, he made it sound like one! A violinist-fiddler myself, I caught on to this album just as I began 5 years of work earning a living playing bluegrass fiddle, and Kenny Baker was, and still is, one of my greatest inspirations on the instrument, along with Stephane Grapelli, Stuff Smith, David Oistrakh, Dave Swarkbrick, Peter Knight, Yehudi Mehuhin, and a short list of other great recording artists.  Many of them probably never heard of Kenny Baker--but you should listen to him if you have any love for the violin, because he elevates Monroe's tunes into the stratosphere!

Most highly recommended.  Incidentally, I bought the CD, but wore out about 3 LPs as this album first appeared in 1976, and I had to slow it down to 16 2/3 r.p.m. to catch some of the subtle licks that I would eventually play--today, you can slow CDs down 1/2 speed without changing the key!!! And, the iPhone is only 5 years old. What will the next generation of fiddler's play? They will still have to listen to "Kenny Baker Plays Bill Monroe."

Last weekend she muffed the words to at least half a dozen songs, two of which had to be started from the beginning. If you are a fan of their's I wouldn't expect too many years of live performances.

True, this is a "live" album, and not the original stuff.  But then, this is folk music.  You need acoustic guitars and voices, and that is all that is needed to carry it. reviewText:
Hats off to Avid Jazz records for putting together this great compilation of The Chico Hamilton Quintet's classic recordings. The lineup's are as follows: Chico Hamilton, drums, Fred Katz, cello, Buddy Collete, flute, clarinet, tenor and alto sax, Carson Smith, bass and Jim Hall on guitar. Lineup 2 is Chico Hamilton, drums, Paul Horn, alto, tenor, flute and clarinet, John Pisano, guitar, Fred Katz, cello and Carson Smith on bass. For the trio offerings you have Chico Hamilton, drums, George Duvivier, bass and Howard Roberts on guitar. All cream of the crop, top notch innovative and brilliant musicians and composers. Chico does a great brush and mallet solo on Drums West. Chico was not a flashy drummer but instead used his brilliant skills for melodic, ryhthmic and time keeping cohesiveness. He was a genius with the mallets and brushes. The combinations of instruments that this ensemble chose to use was fantastic producing a fresh and new sound that would later become legendary in the jazz world. The recordings took place between 1953 and 1956 and sound as fresh today as they did when recorded. I agree with the other reviewer that Chico don't seem to get his just recognition in the jazz circles but hopefully more people will come to appreciate the many great accomplishments that these musicians created together and producing a very tight, inventive, exploratory and unique unit. Katz's cello throws this quartet into another realm of adventureous sounds, tonalities, harmonics and melodies. If you enjoy cool jazz in it's finest light you will love this release. All of the musicians involved offer their brilliant technique's and skills at their apex of their game. I have many drummers that I admire and love to hear play as I too am a drummer, but Chico ranks up there with some of the best. Do yourself a favor and check this magical set out. I highly recommend it and give it a very strong and high 5 stars. Check out my other reviews.

John W. Shearer
(ART MULE SNAPFISH)

Produced by DJ Mark and the .45 King, "All Hail the Queen" is unlike any hip-hop debut, since it includes guest appearances by many of the genre's top stars including Monie Love and De La Soul, which add to he album's diverse appeal.
The best track on this album has to be the Hip-Hop/Techno classic, "Come Into My House," which is one of the first hip-hop songs to be certified a club classic. Latifah's vocals, the fast beats, and the hints of techno make this the most danceable song on this entire album. Overall, "All The Hail Queen" is a landmark album for a woman in rap/hip=hop music. Before Latifah, few women had achieved the success and fame she has gained due to her charming personality, professionalism, and her desire to be the very best she can be. reviewText: Amazingly under-rated when it premeiered in 1951 (Admittenly against such competition as Guys and Dolls and THe King and I that same season) and forgotten today, "A Tree Grows In Brooklyn" has one of the finest scores of the 1950s, and possibly even of all time. The overture medley of Arthur Schwartz's music alone must be one of the most beautiful ever written for the theatre, and the lyrics by Dorothy Fields capture character and the period setting of the show (turn-of-the-20th century Brooklyn tenemants) while being hilarious and deeply moving in their own right. The other reviewers have mentioned the highlights ("Make the Man Love Me," "I'm Like A New Broom," "Love Is the Reason," "He Had Refinement"), and they are all correct. The catchy and delightful "Mine 'Til Monday" and "Look WHo's Dancing," and the lovely period song "If You Haven't Got a Sweetheart" and "I'll Buy You a Star" also stand out. I want to talk about how two songs, "That's How It Goes" and "Growing Pains," capture the humorous yet truly bittersweet and oddly haunting quality of the famous Betty Smith novel on which the show is based. "That's How IT Goes" is a "local color" song for the chorus of immigrants who live in the tenements that describes the various uses of clothes, most of them boring and seemingly unneccessary, yet part of the never-ending cycle of life. "You wear 'em, you soil 'em, you stoke 'em, you boil 'em, you dry 'em, you iron 'em, laugh in 'em, cry in 'em, live in 'em, die in 'em, that's how it goes... Why?  The Lord knows, but that's how it goes...." And with that the song ends. It's just something you live with; life goes on in spite of everything. "Growing Pains" is sung by Johnny Nolan, the charming but weak alcholic n'er-do-well unable to provide for his family, to his daughter Francie as she is coming down with "a bad case of growing up." There are the charming "warnings" of what to expect (Mom dropping the hem of your skirt, etc.), but there is also the underlying sadness in the idea that Francie will soon lose her childhood innocence. "We all must get to know things we don't want to know," but in the end "you'll be awfully glad you had these growing pains." A potentially cloying moment is handled with restraint and knowing intelligence. It may even jerk a tear or two out of you. As for this cast, they certainly do the score justice. Shirley Booth is the standout as the loveable, childlike, even sexy, yet wise Aunt Cissy, bringing charm and depth to the character and possessing one of the strangest yet most adorable voices you're ever likely to hear. However, a flaw of the production in general, aside, apparently, from a weak book, seems to be that her star presence distorted the focus of the show, originally centered on Johnny and his wife Katie, which probably explains why the people playing those roles, Johnny Johnston and Marcia van Dyke, possess fine voices and a good sense of emotion but register more as excellent vocalists than as memorable characters in a show the way Booth does. I guess you just can't steal a show from Shirley Booth, even if your characters are the real focus of the story. A pity, but perhaps an unavoidable one. Still, they and the rest of the cast do wonderful justice to this incredible score, brimming with melody and emotion. Kudoes also to Goddard Liberson for doing a great job producing the recording; the sound is great and we even get six full minutes of ballet music, unusual for the early days of LP records when this was made. Obviously, Lieberson loved this score almost as much as you probably will. The time is ripe for a revival, or at the very least a concert staging by Encores! or some similar organization. Broadway, are you listening? Come on and rediscover one of your lost treasures!

reviewText:
A lot of people only know ELO from their later and admittedly oft-cheesy post-"Out Of The Blue" work and from the handful of their late-period upbeat pop tunes that get recycled in commercials and movie trailers. And these people probably regard ELO as a variant of Styx, but with occasional orchestral arrangements. But there was a time when ELO actually rocked out and brought a novel sound, and not always an uplifting and happy one.

"Face The Music" is, on the whole, a dark album. It kicks off with an unsettling intro with minor keys, backwards vocals (which apparently proclaim "The music is reversible, but time isn't...turn back..turn back...turn back.."), an ominous choir, and strange sound effects. (Mini-overtures of this type can also be heard on 1974's "Eldorado" and 1981's "Time".) We then leap into "Fire On High", a complex and musically quite interesting instrumental with high-speed guitars and what sounds like a harpsichord. Not often heard these days on the radio, this is one of ELO's best numbers.

The big hits from this album were, of course, "Evil Woman" and "Strange Magic". The latter is also one of the group's strongest songs in their entire repertoire, perfectly capturing a certain melancholy longing that makes it an ideal companion to "Can't Get It Out Of My Head" from the previous year's "Eldorado".

"Poker" is a high-octane tune with some clever lyrics, and "Waterfall" and "Night Rider" also have their merits. The weakest cut is "Down Home Town", which isn't precisely bad, but it's a bit odd to hear a bunch of Brits chanting "Wish I was in the Land of Dixie", and for most rock groups of this type, playing around with country music is generally a bad idea.

The album closes with the wistfully yearning "One Summer Dream". It's no secret that Jeff Lynne has often been accused of wanting to be the fifth Beatle, but I suspect these lusher and romantic ballads are equally close to his heart. (Lynne remains active to this day, by the way, having just produced the latest Tom Petty album.)

"Face The Music" is an impressive work and a great antidote to some of the saccharine excesses of their "Discovery". Not cheerful by any means, but happiness is overrated.

reviewText:
This is by far the best version of this album yet! I have most versions of this LP, including the just released 2014 ORG version on 2 45rpm 180g discs.
Going back to the beginning, this album was recorded at A&M records in 1970. A&M was known then for being cheap-o from the recording studio to the substandard pressings by Monarch Record Pressing in L.A. The studio was pretty plain with not the best equipment. A&M was also known for doing strange things to the material recorded there with Howard Holzer as the chief engineer. So, most recordings made there were not nearly as good as recordings made at other studios like GoldStar, etc.
The original pressings of this album were made by several different pressing facilities. Most common are the Monarch pressings(marked M1), Columbia Terra Haute(T1) and the best pressings by Columbia Santa Maria(S1), etc. The Columbia pressings are by far the superior.
The also new ORG 45rpm release was pressed by Pallas and is a waste of money.
This new MFSL release was pressed by RTI and is the first to cut through the muffled A&M sound. The original recording sessions are with minimal musical instruments and with competent, but not the best, musicians. The "Wrecking Crew" was not used. Other musicians and singers guested on the recordings such as James Taylor.  The highs are there and the bass is there. The superior RTI pressing makes for a quiet groove. If you like Tapestry, this is the definitive version!

reviewText:
A bit over the top? Well quite frankly, NO! This is the kind of record that haunts you in the shower or when you are in the sack with your girl/boy/mother/whatever works for you. As far as searching for that compilation that Digweed has been trying to visualize his entire two and a half decades look no further. If you are new or not all that familiar with Digweed please allow me to try to give a humble sketch.

John Digweed is a DJ from the UK with a most unusual and not at all popular niche. In a nutshell, what he does is use his uncanny ear for music to create jaw-dropping mixes with tracks you'd never think of listening to. Look in whichever country, club, bedroom, or dorm but you won't find anyone who has such a steady grip over this formula like Digweed. This is a tough formula mind you. Sasha tried it using a Holden approach with Fundacion NYC but this trial failed miserably. It failed for a lot of reasons but an interesting and an allegorical one is that he literally put his ego before the music. Digweed does the exact opposite. Indeed at first glance you think there is little mixing going on but that is classic Digweed for you; you don't seem him but he sure as hell is there, crafting a mix that should be boring and repetitive into a sort of solo by Miles Davis.

Indeed a good description of the Digweedian style of mixing would be elusive, confusing, cerebrally hypnotic and perpetually innovative. It was Diggie who introduced the rest of us to Adam Spears' track Crayons. He has always utilized, and championed the genius if Holden. If you send him a demo this evening, there is a 90% chance that he'll give it a go before the end of the month. The man is a rare breed indeed... But there is no denying his brilliance and it is his experience and his uncanny ear of music that makes this minimalist monster of a compilation shine.

Now, I must say I am a bit, weird when it comes to music. This mix is not for everybody. I mean a friend of mine and a fan of Digweed has mixed feelings about Digweed and asked me to sample it and was interested in my opinion. His was four stars out of five. Four stars!!?? For this jaw-cracker? But.. to each to his own.

The mix starts out with some teaser tracks. The track names themselves explain what they are meant to do to you; disorient you, discard whatever preconceptions you had about this mix. The tracks also serve as nasty tension builders and indeed you wonder where he is going with all this. It is sometime when you are having these thoughts that he chooses to drop Guy Gerber's remix of the Chaim EP track Dana. I have given it a lot of thought and I have come to a decision; This is one of the most emotional, awe-inspiring tracks I have ever heard. If you think this review is long and meandering fine. Ignore it. That is fine too. Just add, "Listen to Digweed mix Dana into Camino De Sol" to that things to do before I die. For those still with me, the mix gets even better. The inhuman breakdown that Digweed illuminates around 4 or so minutes into this Joakim remix demon? Words cannot describe. The mix transitions nicely (bad pun I know) into the shivering, a nice ominous, experimental track. He basically hits you with syncopated, minimalistic tech gems until you can't help but grin stupidly (if this genre is your taste. I hope Tiesto lovers aren't misinterpreting). Aerial is easily Kate Bush's best work since The Hounds of Love. My only small quibble is that it is a bit bloated and some sort of editing down would have helped it.

It is on the second disc that the album really come alive however, and makes this an essential album. Kate lets the songs breath, but they never feel too long or meandering. Really the entire disc flows as one suite of music, a true "concept" album that even Hounds of Love wasn't (maybe it would have been if that album had been a double LP as planned). "Sunset" brings in some of that "world music" feel that really didn't work so well on "Eat the Music" but here is sublime. "Somewhere in Between" stands out as a song that should have been a single. But the tour de force here is "Nocturn." It mixes an almost funky bass line with Kate's more typical ethereal voice and music.

I would place this album next to Talk Talk's Spirit of Eden in terms of density and layers, and almost endless listenability.

reviewText: Like all Cohen's early albums, Songs of Love & Hate has grown in stature down the years. Other singers seem to like the songs more than Cohen does; for the collection that he compiled, Essential Leonard Cohen, he selected only one track from this album, Famous Blue Raincoat. Among those who highly esteem Songs of Love and Hate is Jennifer Warnes who covers Famous Blue Raincoat on her album of the same name which also contains a duet with Cohen on a longer version of Joan of Arc. The Handsome Family interprets the same song on the soundtrack album Leonard Cohen: I'm Your Man whilst Tori Amos performs it on Tower of Song: The Songs of Leonard Cohen. Famous Blue Raincoat is a great favorite, as Judy Collins included it on her Cohen tribute album along with Dress Rehearsal Rag and Joan of Arc. And on the appealing 1991 tribute I'm Your Fan, there is a French version of Avalanche by Jean-Louis Murat. Sing Another Song Boys is Cohen at his bitter best, its harsh chorus atypical of the image of the poetic folkie but pointing to later songs like Lover Lover Lover on 1974's New Skin for the Old Ceremony. The fierce and uptempo Diamonds in the Mine is in the same vein, where the celestial female vocals are particularly effective in balancing Cohen's raw voice on this tale with its striking imagery. In tone, theme and delivery Diamonds in the Mine and Sing Another Song Boys are not too far removed from tracks like Iodine, Paper-Thin Hotel or Don't Go Home with your Hardhat on his much-criticized Death of a Ladies' Man (1978) that was produced by Phil Spector. Besides the second more vibrant version of Dress Rehearsal Rag with full instrumentation & a denser sound, the original tracks are typical early Cohen. With astonishing elegance and simplicity, the haunting melodies, melancholy lyrics and ragged voice have a way of establishing themselves in the consciousness of the listener. Few other musicians touch the strings of the soul in the way that Cohen does. Dylan can do it; Nick Cave does, as do Nick Drake, Lou Reed, Richard Thompson and definitely Swans on their more gentle songs. Songs of Love and Hate is another jewel in Cohen's crown of ageless music.
