reviewText:
Five years ago Poe made waves on modern rock stations all over the country with her sexually charged breakthrough hit, "Angry Johnny."  She has made a triumphant return this Halloween releasing her sophomore album, Haunted.  Over the course of the disc, Poe attempts to make sense of her relationship with her dead father, famous documentarist Tad Danielewski.  The album was inspired by and works as a companion piece with the acclaimed horror novel House of Leaves (Pantheon Books, 2000), penned by her brother Mark Z. Danielewski in his own attempts at coming to terms with their father.
Uniting each of the tracks thematically throughout the album is Poe's sampling of cassette recordings of her father's lectures.  She originally unearthed the tapes in 1993 after going through her father's things following his death.  They sat next to her stereo for a few years, as she was emotionally unable to bring herself to listen to them.  When she did, she couldn't quit playing them as they released a wave of emotion within her that propelled her to make the album as a tribute to her father.  Also running throughout the disc are fictitious phone calls between her father, her estranged mother, and a young Annie Danielewski (Poe's real name before she took on the moniker after her favorite author).
Haunted begins with one of these phone call tracks, "Exploration B," where Poe leaves a message on her mother's answering machine about the death as she sings, "I thought you should know, Daddy died today.  He closed his eyes and he left here at 12:03."  "Exploration B" segues beautifully into the first song and the title track (also featured in Blair Witch 2). One of the strongest cuts, "Haunted" blends soaring psychedelic rhythms with a danceable drumbeat behind swirling guitars.  "Control" and "Hey Pretty" return Poe to the harder rock sound that drove much of her debut album, Hello.  The first single, "Walk The Walk," with it's franticness and faux-rap jumps off the disc while the nine-minute "Wild" refreshes the opening chords of Poe's own song "Hello" before turning into a funktified raver-friendly remix of itself.
Not only does the ghost of Danielewski haunt the album, but another fallen performer as well.  The memory of Josh Clayton-Felt, formerly of School of Fish, who died earlier this year from testicular cancer floats through the acoustic song "5 &  Minute Hallway" as he helped contribute to the track.  "Not A Virgin" features more pseudo-rap and the album's best wordplay as she sings about the loss of her feminine flower claiming, "It's gonna be a new experience if you wanna play with me."  "Lemon Meringue" is literally introduced by her father and features the chamberlin of renowned studio player Patrick Warren while "Spanish Doll" is tinged with a trip-hop flamenco flare.
"House of Leaves" roars with all the horrific haunting of her brother's book of the same name.  The album closes with its most poignant song, "If You Were Here," as Poe and her dead father find a mutual understanding with and love for one another.  The track's sparse sound ends with a conversation between Poe, on the verge of tears, and her father.  The elder Poe confesses, "I love you" while the younger version of herself closes with, "It's okay.  You can go now."  Just like her brother's novel, House of Leaves, she has found redemption and salvation by the close of the album.  Poe and her brother, Mark Z. Danielewski, are currently touring the nation spreading their newfound love for their father. (originally written fall of 2000)

reviewText:
Taken from her one woman show which recently premiered in London at the Donmare Warehouse, Patti LuPone's "Matters of the Heart" is a first rate recording.  Her nuance, her style, her personal flair are all  embedded into the songs represented here, making this a nice addition to  any musical theatre library.  With a solid powerhouse voice that  electrified us in "Evita" and mesmerized us in "Sunset  Boulevard," Patti LuPone makes every track her own, leaving her own  indelible mark.  From Sondheim to Jimmy Webb to John Lennon and Paul  McCartney, it is a love story, told from different characters through the  magic of song.  There are surprisingly funny tracks such as "Shattered  Illusions" and "I Regret Everything" to the somewhat  touching moments taken in "Air That I Breath" "Sand and  Water" and "My Father," the Judy Collins hit.
Patti LuPone  is a star of the Broadway and London stages, having contributed heavily to  the musical theatre world with the creation of roles as Eva Peron,  Genevieve in the Baker's Wife, Norma Desmond, Fantine from Les Miserables,  and has left her mark on the music of Irving Berlin from playing the role  of Reno Sweeney to releasing an album with the Hollywood Bowl Orchestra  (entitled HeatWave).  The only detraction for this album is that it came so  late in her career, yet without that time, there was no way she could have  brought the multileveled layers to each and every character choice and  song.
If you are a fan of Ms. LuPone, you will not be disappointed.  An  intimate recording of a one woman show that was exceptional in person.  I'm  glad I have this keepsake.

reviewText:
In 1963-1964 Judy Garland attempted a weekly television variety show as hostess/performer.  Regrettably it wasn't renewed past the first season due to a variety of reasons too lengthy to discuss.  However it still provided an invaluable filmed record of the last positive sustained effort of her checkered career.  Sadly, after the failure, which was very traumatic for Ms. Garland, both her professional and personal life began a downward trajectory, despite occasional flashes of the old magic, that ultimately resulted in her untimely death in 1969 at the age of forty-seven.

Thankfully, I believe almost all of her episodes have been released to DVD, usually in pairs of two per DVD.  Some are brilliant, others merely good, with a few mediocre ones, none were truly clunkers.  The Christmas Show filmed on Friday December 6, 1963 and telecast on Sunday December 22, 1963 falls somewhere between good and brilliant.  What's unique about this show is that the viewer gets a glimpse, albeit a filtered one, into the private world of Judy Garland as a mother.  All three of her children are on the show:  seventeen-year-old Liza Minnelli, an eleven-year-old Lorna Luft and eight-year-old Joe Luft.  The studio set where the show was taped was a reasonable facsimile of Ms. Garland's Hollywood home.  It's an amusing snapshot of what was at that time probably very fashionable; split-level architecture and "modern" furnishings that now look very quaint and dated.  Regardless, having both her family and familiar surroundings around her made Ms. Garland very relaxed and at ease, there is a delightful, cozy, informal atmosphere to this show that is quite beguiling.  Getting an early peek at the incipient vocal talent in both of Garland's daughters, particularly Liza Minnelli is an additional bonus.

The show opens with a graceful nod to the past; Ms. Garland is framed in her living room window singing "Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas" to Lorna and Joe as all three sit in the window seat.  This was exactly how she had sung the song originally to Margaret O'Brien in the 1944 film classic "Meet Me in St. Louis".  After introducing her children to the audience, she invites us in to her home as all of them perform a lively rendition of "Consider Yourself" from the stage musical "Oliver!"  Next up is a solo turn from Joe singing "Where Is Love?" also from "Oliver!" with Ms. Garland in the background gazing lovingly at him.  Unfortunately he is the only one of her children that didn't inherit some of her vocal ability, but since he was a little boy one can overlook it.  Still, it's unlikely you'll want to view it a second time.

The guests then begin in earnest, first Tracy Everitt, a young dancer on the show, introduced as Liza's "beau".  Together they perform "Steam Heat" a famous dance number originally choreographed by Bob Fosse, this is Tracy's choreography.  While not up to the Fosse version, for a fledgling choreography effort and their extreme youth, it's a cute number with some nice touches.

Popular singer of the day Jack Jones arrives to sing a speeded up arrangement of  "Wouldn't It Be Loverly?" followed by one of his own hits "Lollipops and Roses", a sweetly charming ballad, that probably in this less innocent age would be considered condescending to women.  Ah well, you can decide for yourself.  The final guest is Mel Torme, the singer/arranger who wrote the special musical material for "The Judy Garland Show".  He also was one of the writers of the evergreen "The Christmas Song", upon which Ms. Garland and he duet.  Torme arrives with a group of carolers and the entire company does a medley of Christmas carols.

Ms. Garland is in fine form indeed, her numbers include besides the ones mentioned above, "Little Drops of Rain", "Winter Wonderland", I think her simple straightforward rendition is my favorite of all the versions I've heard of this song, and in the medley "What Child is This?".  At the program's conclusion she sings for the first time on her show, her trademark song "Over the Rainbow" as a Christmas lullaby to the two younger children.  My only complaint is that she doesn't sing her lovely "Merry Christmas" song that she had performed in the film "In the Good Old Summertime".  This would have made a nice encore after "Over the Rainbow" to close the show.  She looks very sleek and attractive in an elegant fur trimmed red brocaded hostess gown, and besides being in good voice is witty, warm and generally entrancing, sharing a wonderful interplay with her three children.  You will also enjoy her impromptu dance with a chorus line of manic Santa Clauses that zip in and out of her living room.  The title of the review is her deadpan-bemused farewell to them.

Misses Minnelli and Luft both have their individual numbers in which to sparkle.  There is a jazzed up version of the old song "Alice Blue Gown" that Minnelli does at full throttle, while playfully sashaying in her full skirt around the room. Ms. Minnelli is not yet the polished superstar, but she is endearing in her artless enthusiasm.  Lorna Luft belts out a socko version of "Santa Claus Is Coming to Town", very surprising coming out of a little girl unless of course Judy Garland happens to be the little girl's mother!

The DVD is digitally remastered and restored, with a newly created 5.1 surround sound track, and the loving care shows.  The black and white images are razor sharp and crystal clear, probably looking as good if not better than when originally aired.  Besides the original mono soundtrack, the other special features are some holiday outtakes.

Supposedly Judy Garland travelled with an audiotape of this show, she loved it that much.  There were plans to do a similar show for Easter that unfortunately didn't materialize.  But there is this special, it's like attending a good friend's holiday house party, so get a cup of eggnog or hot chocolate and some Christmas cookies and settle back and enjoy your visit!  And, and if you liked this, which I hope you will, try some other episodes of "The Judy Garland Show" such as the Lena Horne, Liza Minnelli and Barbara Streisand ones, you won't be sorry!

reviewText:
Notice the play on words in the title, for all the hood savvy people out there. Ludacris has got to be one of the most underachieving artists ever to step foot in the world of Hip Hop. I say this because he's so talented, yet for the fist half of his career thus far, he put out material like "Money Maker" all the time, at least up until Release Therapy, where his true talents starts to shine. He follows up that album with Theater Of The Mind, a supposedly conceptual album, but with little more to the actual concept of a theatrical performance aside from a few "theater-esque" moments like a movie preview, an impressive ensemble cast, or a live performance. By no means does that detract from the goodness of the album.

Luda opens it up with his always bombastic and fiery intros, followed immediately by "Undisputed", his official declaration that he is Hip Hop's champion. These are the few songs on here that Luda is by himself, and he takes those solo moments and shines like the sun on steroids.

There are many noteworthy cameos on Theater Of The Mind, one most notably being Luda's colabo with former rival T.I. in "Wishin You Would". While neither artist really shines, its still a fun banger to put in the car. Luda also teams up with T-Pain on the catchy "One More Drink" to get his club on on a very smooth drinky lust track that shows off his swagger. He takes another stab at pleasing his lady fans with help from Chris Brown and Sean Garette on "What Them Girls Like" with a successful style similar to what he had back on Chicken & Beer.

Luda's MOST noteworthy guest stars no this album fall under three songs. The first being with The Game on "Call Up The Homies", a Cali power ballad you cant not bump in the ride, and given Game and Luda's great chemistry, the song is catchy as fly paper. The second being "I Do It For Hip Hop" with living legends Nas and Jay-Z. Being no slouches themselves, Luda brings his A game on this track to keep up with the lyrical titans, and actually outshines them (which is hard to do with both Nas AND Hov at the same time). Kudos to Luda on that one. The third song is the closer of the album, "Do The Right Thing", an aptly titled track featuring Common and Spike Lee (yes, THE Spike Lee) who opens and closes the song with quotes from his classic film of the same title.

While this album general does very well, it has some draw backs that prevent it from reaching the ever elusive "classic" status. Tracks like "Nasty Girl" feat. Plies, "Contagious" feat. Jaimie Fox, and Southern Gangsta fall short of likable, only because of the guest on the songs. If not for them, they would all be great. I was especially annoyed at "Nasty Girl" because the song is tight, but the minute Plies speaks the entire song is ruined. Every other song on this album not mentioned falls under the category of so-so; not bad, could be better.

Overall this is a great album, a true sign of growth from a immensely talented artist. Get ya grown man on Luda, keep doin what it do.

Call Up The Homies
One More Drink

This is the best album Jack White has ever been a part of. And the White Stripes are probably my favorite band. But there's so much more to this album than just White. Patrick Keeler is a beast on drums throughout, LJ has some good basslines and keyboard parts, and Brendan Benson absolutely shines, especially on songs like Many Shades of Black, Attention, and Consoler of the Lonely. Everyone talks about how much more this album sounds like the Stripes than Broken Boy Soldiers did, but probably the biggest improvement to this album is how much stronger Benson sounds both on vocals and guitar. The overall sound to the album is stronger. There's a lot of start and stop/push and pull rhythms going on, and it's a lot harder than BBS was. There's some strings and Mariachi on a few tracks too, changing things up a little bit. It has some great softer moments as well. You Don't Understand Me is great, and I still get goosebumps listening to Carolina Drama.
This is easily one of the best albums of the year, if not the best. Jack White is one of those once in a generation talents in songwriting, and then when you combine it with the rest of the guys on here it sounds even better. If you like music just in general pick this album up, and go see them live. I saw them about a month ago. It was unbelievable.

I went into this CD not being a huge Pearl Jam fan but, quite literally, came out being obsessed with buying everything they've put out. I've always been a fan of acoustic music, and I've always been fond of Pearl Jam. So while browsing their section in a local CD shop I came across this. It looked good enough so I bought it. From the first few notes of Of The Girl, I knew I was gonna wear this CD out. I kept true to that thought, playing it at least twice a day, every day, for about a month. I think this is a fairly justifiable collection for newcomers, I mean it's got a few landmark songs, (Black, Daughter and Yellow Ledbetter), but it's really the lesser known tracks that make this what it is. Ed's voice is top notch, I would even venture out and say his voice sounds better here than on some studio discs. McCready, of course, is simply astounding. This is one of the few bands that I can sit through a guitar solo and just say, "Man, now that was good."

Having gone into this CD not hearing many complete studio discs, I hadn't heard of many of these songs. After first listen, Masters Of War jumped out at me the most. It's Ed's voice that makes this song what it is. He's got the intensity in his voice that few other singers have. Sleight Of Hand was another song that kind of grabbed me. Just the overall feel to this song was really touching, a definite stand out. Now I had never heard Lukin before this CD so I really didn't understand what the introduction was all about, but this song is amazing. It's not long at all but even acoustically, it's very intense. Fatal, a B-side, is also featured here. This is one of my favorite songs on here. I can't explain why either.

A few of my favorite songs on here are Of The Girl, Thin Air, Fatal, Sleight Of Hand, Lukin, Masters Of War, and Crazy Mary. For the price you pay for this you definitely get your money's worth. I have absolutely no complaints about this CD. Every song, and I mean every song, is down right amazing.

reviewText: Count Basie Vol. 2: Seven Classic Albums covers the period1956-1961. The joys of this set are many and varied. Disc One kicks off with a live "Basie In London" Jumpin At The Woodside from 1956. What do you get when you mix a Thad Jones led trumpet section with arguably Basie's finest sax grouping of the era-Marshall Royal, Bill Graham, Frank Foster, Frank Foster and Charlie Fowlkes? Disc Three offers the equally strong "Dance Along With Basie" and "Just The Blues (with Joe Williams). It had to Be You features Thad Jones soloing in just perfect time for dancing along with the Count himself. Makin' Whoopee is a creamy chart featuring the saxophone section, while Cant We Be Friends is notable for its tongue in cheek wit. Just The Blues is a vehicle for Basie & His #1 Son Joe Williams and they are 10 magical tracks indeed. Confessin The Blues is my favorite rendition of this standard, ditto for Mean Old World and the ancient Key To The Highway, revivified by Basie & Co. IMO there's nothing more wonderful than scraping acquaintance with tunes like Lyin Woman and Mean Mistreater as rendered by this team of great blues-steeped musicians. I could go on & on -this anthology deserves a place in any lover of Big Bands library, especially if you're a serious fan of Count Basie.

reviewText:
The recordings on this 2 cd set represent a Bernstein-Kennedy connection of sorts, and is a treasure trove of great Mahler performances never to be forgotten. All three works have some link to either JFK or RFK, or the Kennedy family in general. And this link makes these spectacular works all the more emotional, moving and meaningful. Perhaps more than they ever had been before.
  The 2nd Symphony "Resurrection", was recorded in September of 1963, but after the tragic events of November 22nd, it was decided by Columbia that the recording would make a fitting tribute to the slain John F. Kennedy. Bernstein had conducted this very same work on television just a few days after the assassination, and the speech he gave that night is one of his most powerful examples of his ability to communicate to the average man, woman and child on such profound matters. The music, which is of course for two female soloists and full chorus, in addition to the huge orchestra, is justly considered one of the best Mahler 2nds on record. In the opinion of this reviewer, it is the best ever made. (Sony released a different version of the 2nd on their Royal Edition line back in the early 90's, featuring the London Symphony Orchestra from back in 1973. They made a major goof in not releasing this version back then). Bernstein is in his total element in this music, and never for a moment do you doubt that he was born to make this music sing like it had never sung before. This was the first Mahler work LB was introduced to, and his passion for it is evident. When you reach parts of the text in the last 2 movements: "Man lies in deepest need, man lies in deepest pain" and "Rise again, yea, thou wilt rise again", the extra-musical meanings applied at that tragic moment in American history become unbearable, yet also inspiring beyond all human comprehension.
  Also included is the 1st part "Veni creator spiritus" from Mahler's 8th Symphony "Symphony of a Thousand". This was performed live back in 1962 at the grand opening of Lincoln Center (then known as Philharmonic Hall). President and Mrs. Kennedy were in attendance, and LB caused a bit of a scandal when he planted a big, Bernstein kiss on Jackie Kennedy backstage after the show. (Imagine if there were TMZ back then?) The whole point of the concert was to show something that still is true 55 years later: JFK was the greatest friend the arts ever had in this country's history since perhaps Jefferson. I gravely doubt you will ever see that happen again in this country. All the more reason to preserve this recording for posterity. Let's hope that posterity won't always have to be in the past.
  The one other work on this 2 cd set is by far the most moving. It is the Adagietto from Mahler's 5th Symphony, performed at the Funeral of Robert F. Kennedy at St. Patrick's Cathedral back in June of 1968. This music was played as the Kennedy family brought the sacraments up to the alter for the Holy Communion. Jackie Kennedy herself had asked her good friend Lenny to play this music at the service, which of course he did. There is a beautiful letter from Jackie to Lenny thanking him included in the wonderful book "The Leonard Bernstein Letters". Jackie didn't have the greatest sophisticated taste in music, but she knew that this music would be perfect. And it was. You can hear from the ambiance in the cathedral the intense emotion involved. The Adagietto is music that has sometimes been called schmaltzy. This is because of repeated exposure in pop culture, such as films like Death in Venice and Rules Don't Apply. You could even say that LB plays it a bit too schmaltzy here (listen to the tiny little hitch in the violins at the very beginning of the climax at the end. No accident). But, considering the occasion and the intense grief involved, I don't think you could ever find a better and more powerful version of this movement if you tried.
  As for the sound, it's very good all around. The Super Bit remastering is done to great effect here. As I mentioned, there is a lot of ambient noise in the Adagietto. But these performances could hardly ever be bettered. My one quibble, as I have with other Royal Edition and Bernstein Century releases, is the dividing of the movements into many tracks. This can sometimes be annoying if the beginning of a new track happens right in the middle of a big moment in the music. Your mp3, iPod, iPhone or whatever often leaves just a split-second gap between the end of one track and the start of another. If it happens at just the wrong time......Oh boy! But, as I said, this is a trivial complaint. This music rises beyond that. It Is the music that drew too many people to Mahler's music to count in the first place. (Yours truly included). It is for fans of Gustav Mahler, Leonard Bernstein, the Kennedy family, and just a time when the arts and culture actually had a chance in this country.----------------PEACE
label: positive

reviewText:
When you're on a limited budget and have no immediate friends who share your taste in music (I'm 52, way past the normal age most of my friends will still listen to really heavy music, preferring to hide in their classic rock world where everything is safe, repetitive and dull).  Not me.  As a guitarist and sometime keyboardist, my appetite is insatiable, but inevitably some groups fall through the cracks when I'm interested in other stuff, and as a result I get to some of them later than I would have liked to.  Cathedral is one of those bands I was aware of but until I finally watched a video on YouTube of a song off "The Last Spire" was I actually impressed enough to buy "Forest of Equilibrium".  Now I'm hooked, and I'm snatching up Cathedral CD's as fast as my wife will let me.  They are (were) the best doom band ever, and I hate to say it, do it better than even Black Sabbath, who invented the genre!  That's really not that unusual - consider Jimi Hendrix, who was steeped in delta blues, but interpreted them along with Bob Dylan tunes into something on a new level.  True, Cathedral couldn't exist without the mighty Sabbath, but there are no rules saying they couldn't play their style of heavy doom metal more viciously or with more imagination.  In the doom metal family tree, Sabbath is the top of the chart, and then a direct line goes to Cathedral before branching out any further.
  "The Garden of Unearthly Delights" follows in the vein of "The Carnival Bizarre", with more mid paced tempos, but is in a world of its own especially when you get to the title track, a 27 minute multipart opus that covers more territory musically than you can shake a stick at, injecting surreal female vocals with equal parts of ultra heavy passages.  It's a very interesting piece and does not get boring.
  The rest of the CD like all Cathedral is chock full of their signature riffs, courtesy of Garry Jennings, a phenomenal player who blows the competition out of the water, Tony Iommi truly his only peer.  Lee Dorrian is his always charismatic and expressive self, and "The Garden" for its experimental side, tinged with dark psychedelia, is a great album in a series of albums that are as close to doom nirvana as you'll ever get.

reviewText: Wow.  I received this CD as a gift, and haven't stopped listening to it.  It starts with the sound of the surf, in the Great Pacific Northwest--home of the talented Gary Stroutsos.  This CD is really a suite, so several of the pieces flow from one into the other, and the overall feel of the CD is mellow, timeless, and musically very interesting from end to end.  Gary Stroutsos is best known (at least to me) for his Native American flute music.  He has also done a flute and synthesizer CD with the Space Music master, Jonn Serrie.  This CD reflects time spent in Oregon at Falcon Cove Beach, which Mr. Stroutsos describes as a *sacred place*. On this CD Stroutsos plays altus alto flute, bamboo flute, ratan bass flute and wood flute.  He is joined by: Glen Velez, Elizabeth Falconer, Larry Mahlis, Ed Pais, Jonn Serrie, and Nonda Trimis.  This is a new release by the label *Paras Recordings*, a *new* label.  I've received other recent releases from them, and the quality of the music is GREAT.  Try out this CD as it takes you through all the times of day, starting with *Dawn* on the coast, and ending at evening on *Zen Beach*. Take your time....

reviewText:
I love this album and just got it in the mail today.  I've always wanted it on CD.  Why is it some of the best albums haven't been re-issued yet on CD?  Thank goodness that is not the case here anymore.
Every track on this album was worthy of being issued as a single.  You'll remember every song after first listen...I know I did.  The album is crafted very much in the style of it's predecessor 1979's "Dionne" (another great, memorable album) though I prefer this one.  A great mix of uptempo, ballads and some updated covers.  I'm a huge fan of "We Never Said Goodbye"...if you liked "Deja Vu", I think you'll like this track, too.  My favorite track is "Easy Love", the album's opener...it makes for a nice bridge/segue from "Dionne" to this album.
You also get 3 bonus tracks...2 additional tracks produced by the original album's producer, Steve Buckingham & one produced by Michael Masser (whose prolific production work I'm usually a big fan of).  The Michael Masser produced track on this album, "This Time Is Ours", is just a bit too generic for me although Dionne hits some good high notes on it.  But I don't think even Whitney Houston or Diana Ross (who also have fantastic Michael Masser productions in their catalogs of work) could've saved or elevated this track.  It's sung well & produced well but the song itself just isn't anything special.  As for the other two bonus tracks...I believe "Dedicate This Heart" may have originally debuted on "Hot, Live & Otherwise" (thought did not appear on that CD's re-release, perhaps because it was licensed for this reissue).  It's a nice, up-tempo number.  Then there's "Only Heaven Can Wait", a pleasant cover of a Roberta Flack song.
While the bonus tracks are nice, I would've paid the same price just to have the original album alone it's that good.  I do, however, appreciate the fantastic liner notes that accompany this re-release.  I'm going to hit the repeat button right now on the CD player!

reviewText:
Jay Z is one of the most recognizable names in the history of hip hop. The author of 11 studio albums and counting he is notorious to hip hop fans of all generations. Unfortunately, his past few efforts have left much to be desired, and don't compare to his masterpiece 1996 release, Reasonable Doubt. Per the title of my review, I firmly believe that this album is one of the greatest releases of all time. The production is simply immaculate, and lyrically Jay Z is on another planet. The album is a portrayal of the life and thoughts of a street hustler, from first hand experience. The rhymes clearly show Jay's cockiness which he tempers with light-hearted witty commentary and he delivers with a smooth, precise and cool demeanor. Think Big Daddy Kane mixed with a little Barry White.

The album itself is 14 tracks in length, 10 of which I would classify as superior. The production is handled by 3 main producers - DJ Clark Kent, DJ Premier and Ski which allows a nice consistency to develop. My favourite song on the album is track 6 D'Evils, produced by DJ Premier. The piano loop is infectious and the chorus cleverly samples the vocals of Prodigy from the I Shot Ya remix and Snoop Dogg from Lil Ghetto Boy. Other favourites include Can't Knock The Hustle ft. Mary J. Blige, Brooklyn's Finest ft. Notorious BIG, Dead Presidents II and Bring it On.

All in all, an iconic 90's hip hop release that has aged like a fine wine. For those newer hip hop fans I suggest you go back and listen to when Jay Z was a real rapper, not the sell out that he has become today.

reviewText:
SUBDIVISIONS:  A very witty, accessible discussion of the restlessness of suburban youth.  As always, Rush looks for balance.  Kids feel the need to escape the suburbs and go to the city.  When they get to the city, they feel the pull of the quieter times back home in their subdivision.  Not the most brilliant proposition, but told with great lyrics, and their best (up to that point) keyboard dominated song.  Still gets lots of radio play.
ANALOG KID:  The most upbeat song on the album, and a feel good song all round.  Another "yearning of youth" song, but with a majestic, dare I say romantic feel.
CHEMISTRY:  Although lyrically quite strong, it may be the weakest musically.  Talks about the attraction between people. No deep thoughts, but again, clever analogies that we come to expect from Neil Peart.
DIGITAL MAN:  I'll admit it...I'm not real clear on what this song is about.  But it's got some great lines anyway and a really great Geddy Lee bass solo.
THE WEAPON:  Part II of "Fear" the pseudo-song cycle that began with Part III on MOVING PICTURES and concluded on GRACE UNDER PRESSURE.  Again, the lyrics, about resisting oppression, are great.  "The Knowledge that they fear is a weapon to be used against them."  Cool!
NEW WORLD MAN:  A brief, peppy rarity...a radio-friendly Rush single.
LOSING IT:  A sad song with a great violin solo in the middle.  It's about achieving greatness, and then losing it.  Terrific, sad lyrics, sung very effectively by Geddy.
"The dancer slows her frantic pace in pain and despairation
Her aching limbs and downcast face aglow with perspiration."  What great lyrics to set up the fatigue of the dancer.  Then we come to realise she's not fatigued from her dancing but from just trying to make it across the room because her body has betrayed her.  It's a fairly obscure Rush song, never done in concert, but has always been a personal favorite.
COUNTDOWN:  A wonderful tribute to the brave men and women who go into space in the shuttle.  It does a great job of making you feel the excitement of being there at the launch site.  The shuttle is compared to a "smoking white dragon."  It's a sweeping song that actually has the power to make your hair stand on end just a little.  A very strong closing song.
Although album doesn't rock as hard as any other Rush album, it is still a great showcase for their skills.  Highly recommended.

reviewText:
I bought this because it was high on Elvis Costello's recommended records list (always a good source for new discoveries). I've since found out McCartney and others have raved about it as well. I hesitate to give something I just bought five stars, but it's hard to think of another rating for this record. The main drawback is that it's only 40 minutes long.
On first listen Sexsmith seems too simple and maybe a little dreary. He's patently un-hip. Yet he's also unaffected, so much so that when you'd ordinarily find reason to dismiss him he has a hook in and the material starts building in your head. These are the kind of songs that keep you up at night. His melodies are spare and pretty. His lyrics have a direct innocence that is not naive but more like a haiku, stripped down and poignant with a pervasive hint of sadness ("So young we had no choice, we were pulled along by the ancient voice of girls and boys"). His singing is young sounding and direct, like Brian Wilson or maybe like McCartney without all his affectations.
This album has a weird intimacy, not like he's talking to you but like you're listening in to his thoughts--even the passing observations ("Standing on the side of the road near the overpass with a sign around his neck that says 'Carwash, Free Balloons' is a clown in broad daylight").
Producers Mitchell Froom and Tchad Blake never get in Sexsmith's way; they avoid their tendency to overlay density and textures to the production. You can hear the grass grow on this record. It's quiet and gentle--and sometimes harrowing.

reviewText:
Recorded in 1956, Sun Ra's first album (here in its entirety)
is a welcome addition to anyone's musical library. Along with
streamlined swingers like "Brainville" or "Future", sly
finger-poppers like "Lullaby For Realville", and speculative
serenades like "New Horizons" or "Sun Song", the Delmark CD
presents the previously-unissued dance call, "Swing A Little
Taste". With its tip to the orchestral romps of Fletcher
Henderson, Tadd Dameron, and Dizzy Gillespie, bearing a
chromatic savoir faire worthy of Duke Ellington himself,
the landmark session is classic Sun Ra, pointing the way
for the instrumental voicings of the next half-century,
and beyond.

Arkestra perennials such as tenor giant John Gilmore and
maverick baritonist Pat Patrick take their place alongside
unsung titans such as the bright, buoyant trumpeter Art
Hoyle. Others, such as the renowned trombonist Julian
Priester, gained fame elsewhere, only to rejoin the fold
decades later. All and more are a treat for the ears.

As for the pianist (who doubles on haunting organ for the
title song), his playing is joyously bright with sobering
skill; always gentle in his fierce determination.
As the Myth-Realist stated in the 1950s, "There is a
great need for America to give all of its creative
artists a chance". A gauntlet in the face of everything
from that period's McCarthyism to current fund-cutting
and other forms of censorship, Ra's words and music
have always held true to this idiomatic creed.

If you've experienced Sun Ra's artistic diversity
over the years, this disc comes as a powerful
addition but no surprise. If, however, you are
among those who dismiss Mr. Mystery as an eerie
noisemaker, I offer you this delightful shock,
an accurate pointer to what this grandmaster
of Jazz has always been about.
label: positive

reviewText:
No album ever had such a grandiose impact on music culture and the industry as Nevermind did. Following the release, sales exploded for this album, and also enabled upcoming alternative bands to finally get their moment of fame. I wanted to avoid the Guns n Roses Nirvana feud, so I'll just state that Cobain was a selfish, ignorant human being responsible for some of the bashing put towards an incredible metal band that highly influenced Nirvana in many ways. That being said, he knew how to pen an incredible rock song, produce inducing guitar hooks, which were catchy beyond imagination, and highly contribute to the release of one of the greatest rock albums of all time.

Opening with a song that in many ways defined rock for the 90s, Smells Like Teen Spirit is viciously punk infused rocker, with a guitar riff that's catchy as hell. However, I myself am more fond of the powerful follow up In Bloom, with its downkey guitar smashing and explosive drums creating a delicious rocker(my favourite). Come As You Are opens as a dark, disturbing tune, breaking into another classic rocker which ultimately earned a great deal of airplay and still does. Breed is simpler, very fast paced and punk influenced. Lithium was arguably the second biggest hit on the album, with the awesome chorus, and captivating guitar melody through the verses of the song. Polly is a darker side of Nirvana, in a sense showing Cobain exploring with a more delicate tune with great effectiveness. Territorial Pissing is a dangerous rocker, with speedy drums from Grohl and an awesome lyrical delivery. Drain You stays with the consistency of the rest of the album, another solid rocker. Lounge Act lacks some of the rock righteousness that was perfectly executed in the tracks prior to it. Nevertheless, it isn't worthy of a skip. Stay Away certainly provides more energy, opening similarly to Territorial Pissings with the drums, and building into just another great rock song, which is basically in summary the truth to this album. Ending with the most depressing song on the tracklisting, Something In The Way, we hear a most disturbing lyrical delivery, with a gripping chorus.

Overall rock n' roll fans cannot pass up this album, easily a landmark album in rock history which still resonates through music today. Sadly it was taken the wrong way, and music culture was ultimately destroyed by disgusting interpretations. Highly Recommended to all.

reviewText:
Chuck Mangione plays the flugelhorn, you know, that bigger brassier trumpet that blows the tops off mountain peaks and in this case blows the clouds away.  In 1975, long haired progressive rock college kids were dipping their toes, and many other appendages, into the fusion jazz pond, even though jazz "purists" were still looking cross-eyed down their noses at anything remotely fusion (and that, given the fact that jazz by definition and from its earliest inception was "fusion" since jazz created music by fusing ethnic, cultural, and cross-genre motifs together into improvisational playing).  CHASE THE CLOUDS AWAY quickly drew attention from us as this superb flugelhorn and keyboard player, together with his three extraordinary sidemen on sax, bass, and drums, drove jazz musings into Latin and Manhattan Italian based explorations, enveloped by a kick-butt ad-hoc orchestra, and then put to bed by "Soft" vocal intonations from Esther Satterfield.  Chuck was proud in his liner notes that this record was a "live in the studio" recording, so you won't hear electric piano and flugelhorn duets since he had to lay one down to hop on the other.

CHASE THE CLOUDS AWAY has no extra-progressive leanings (a la Mahavishnu Orchestra), nor does it wind down a bossa nova path (a la Deodato), nor the easy listening jazz-rock of say Tim Weisberg (also from that era).  This is real fusion jazz that sits expansively right in the middle of 52nd Street clubs.  Some critics have overall dismissed Mangione in general as nothing more than another smooth-jazz crossover act and this is, in my opinion, highly insulting.  Anyone who listens to this masterpiece with an ear to good music, no matter what genre it comes from, will be immediately clued into some of the best jazz music of the second half of the 20th Century.  It is no wonder that A&M Records co-founder and trumpeter extraordinaire himself, Herb Alpert singed this act to his label.  While LAND OF MAKE BELIEVE on Mercury Records two years earlier had some very slight pop leanings (only so much as would predicate the soaring success of FEELS SO GOOD two years after this album), CHASE THE CLOUDS AWAY is truly jazz served straight up.  Despite all of the applause and accolades heaped upon FEELS SO GOOD, a true crossover gold and multi-platinum release, CLOUDS is by far the better disc, especially if you are looking for "jazz".

In 1975 I was still endeared to Creed Taylors CTI Jazz label with all his stable of varying and hugely talented creators nearly to the point of exclusivity.  Yes, nearly, though Miles, Herbie, Mclaughlin, and others were to be found on Columbia and a few others scattered across the universe, CTI was a wellspring of Effin-Fantastic music for the best part of a decade.  So stumbling across this album was pure accident and if you are here reading this review you are either replacing vinyl (like I did) making you an already seated fan, or you are a new convert and maybe you too stumbled across this accidentally.  If you heard a track on an FM jazz station, you are curious, you liked what your ears heard, by all means, please take the plunge.  This is a dynamite record, doesn't get boring, every track is a different experience from different jazz perspectives, and the four piece, plus orchestra, are riveting, spectacular, and spot on perfect.  If you remind yourself that this album was recorded live, with not a single overdub, stagger back at the incredible sound, the tight showmanship, the pure energy and the ambient heartfelt laid back OMG that is a good feeling muse, you will appreciate it all the more.  Like Ol' Blue Eyes, who also required live in the studio recording, Chuck and his mates really prosper going to tape.  Gerry Niewood, sax and flute; Chip Jackson, bass; Joe LaBarbera, drums.  Buy this, one listen and you will be addicted.  He has some other terrific albums, but this one will probably, like it did to me, spoil you and others will come close but not be a hole in one.  This is a CD you are going to Dig Man!

LL Cool J is one of hip-hop's living legends, a link back to the days of Kangols, shell-toes, and bugged-out breakbeats. But LL is also a survivor, and unlike a lot of old school cats, he's still viable in the commercial marketplace, as the recent radio success of "Love U Better" proves.
"Love U" is the lead single from LL's latest release, the aptly named 10 -- which is not only his tenth album, but his tenth album for Def Jam; fulfilling a contract he signed with the label 18 years ago at the tender age of 16. Appropriately, 10 is a return to form for LL (especially after the ill-received combativeness of 2000's The G.O.A.T.), and the album finds him doing what he does best: Making relaxed, radio-friendly jams while giving the ladies a little something extra.
He gets help from the Neptunes on both scores here, as the Virginia super-producers contribute five out of the album's 14 tracks. Aside from "Love U," Chad and Pharell supply beats for the smoothed out, Kandace Love-graced "Amazing," the Marc Dorsey-backed love jam "U Should," the club banger "Clockin' G's," and the knuckleheaded old school goof, "Niggy Niggy Nuts." Longtime LL collaborators the Trackmasters get their chance in the producer's chair, too, providing the raw material for LL to spit over on "Mirror Mirror" and "Born to Love You."
LL also gets love from some old friends, too, including P. Diddy on "After School," Amerie on "Paradise," and Dru Hill on LL's touching tribute to the grandmother that raised him, "Big Mama (Unconditional Love)." But for all the producers, guests, and collaborations, 10 is all about LL, and he shines the brightest on solo tracks such as the club banger "Fa Ha" and the ... "Lollipop." 10 may not break any new ground for Mr. Smith, but it sure is nice having him back again.

reviewText:
Mavis Staples says of her early days singing with the Staple Singers: "When we started our family group, The Staple Singers, we started out mostly singing in churches in the south.  Pops saw Dr. Martin Luther King speak in 1963 and from then we started to broaden our musical vision beyond just gospel sings.  Pops told us, "I like this man. I like his message.  And if he can preach it, we can sing it."

This album focuses on songs in that spirit.  The songs take us back to the 1960s, but they remain relevant today.  Indeed, Staples says: "With this record, I hope to get across the same feeling, the same spirit and the same message as we did with the Staple Singers--and to hopefully continue to make positive changes."

The backing group includes some estimable veterans, such as Ry Cooder and Jim Keltner.  "Down in Mississippi" features good rhythm and is well and expressively sung.  The focus of this song is the problems in Mississippi, including blacks being able to drink only at water fountains labeled "For colored only."  The story of the singer helping to integrate Mississippi and the pride her grandmother feels in her.

"We Shall not Be Moved" begins with the repetitive phrase "We shall not be moved."  Each verse, a new line is added and the cumulative effect is profound.  Key lines:

"We shall not be moved
Like a tree planted by the water
We shall not be moved
The union is behind us
We shall not be moved
We're fighting for our freedom"

The power of repetition, propelled by the smooth and expressive voice of Staples makes this a riveting tune.  The beat is simple and instrumentation is spare.

"In the Mississippi River" tells the tale of Civil Rights activists being thrown into the Mississippi River.  Key line:

"Into the river they go,
They don't get out alive."

The backing vocals weave together with Mavis Staples' voice to powerful effect.  One fragment remains in my memory, as the agents of death noted that killing these people "ain't no crime."

Finally, as one additional example, "We'll Never Turn Back."

"We've been mute and we've been scorned
We've been talked about. . . .
But we'll never turn back
Until we walk in peace."

A simple song, but with a powerful message, well sung by Staples.

This is a wonderful, powerful CD that hearkens back to the grim days of the 1960s, when the forces of reaction and racism met the voice of equality and civil rights.  The songs testify to what was at stake and the price sometimes paid for fighting for equality (note the roll call of martyrs and those "who put their lives on the front line and died just trying to live and breathe" in "I'll Be Rested").  A must buy recording, in my view.

reviewText: I first discovered Paul Hardcastle via a Website streaming "Smooth Jazz" music. I enjoy certain performers in that genre and avoid others like the plague. While Hardcastle is certainly a purveyor of the form (it would be kind of hard to deny that with song titles like "Jokers Wild (Smooth Jazz Version)"), he's not offering run-of-the-mill, generic "quiet storm" music here. I own this CD as well as The Jazzmasters V,The Collection,Hardcastle 3,Hardcastle 4, and Hardcastle 5. I prefer the instrumental tracks over the vocal ones (although some instrumentals do feature wordless "vocalizing" or a spoken line or two). There is a level of melody, of tension, of complexity, something memorable in Hardcastle's music that isn't normally found in this genre. My top tracks from this CD are "Shine," "London Chimes," and "Peace On Earth." I've culled 13 other tracks from the CDs above for a CD-length playlist on my iPod, and I listen to it often. There's some guitar, but it's not "Nils / Pacific Coast Highway" or a Norman Brown album. There are horns, but they never have that honking, screechy, nails-down-the-blackboard feel that's in some of the Rippingtons' self-described "high energy" tracks. The music is "balanced" without being "sanitized" or "homogenized." This is a good CD to start with...representative of the range and variety in Hardcastle's music. Chances are you'll want more, just as I did.

reviewText: Lincoln Memorial offers anything but the sort of music crafted for timid listeners or commercial breaks, but what sets Lincoln Memorial apart is the context and musical experience of the musicians. Jimmy Herring is perhaps the most talked about talent on electric guitar who's gained notoriety with both jazz and rock audiences in recent years, having gained attention touring with the Allman Brothers, Aquarium Rescue Unit, and more recently Phil Lesh, and The Dead. Two other well known leading younger players that are consistently dropping jaws at festivals and gigs are saxophonist Greg Osby and drummer Jeff Sipe. Not as well known are two other players that lock in to make this a special-if not overtly telepathic-quintet: the late bassist Ricky Keller and keyboardist Jason Crosby. And the notion that this is fully five musicians locking into a myriad of spontaneous journeys is at once scary, ridiculous, and awe inspiring. The selections run the gamut from the introspective, the quirky and hilarious ("Ol Bugaboo"), to the controlled hyper-burn of multiple hydrogen stage harmonic boosters ("Departure'). Throughout Jimmy Herring works wonders on guitar-he has a full rich tone that at times evokes the melodic turns of Allan Holdsworth, and just as often blistering runs that are entirely his own. Drummer Jeff Sipe, who has collaborated on numerous recordings with ex-Mahavishnu bassist Jonas Hellborg-demonstrates his mastery in both listening to his cohorts, and edging them forward into unexplored new vamps. Sipe's playing and originality here-as in many other settings-is gaining him a reputation as one of the rarest of drum talents today-who can establish a voice and sensibility in the most challenging musical settings imaginable. Osby's performances are equally amazing with his free-flowing inventions always seeming to bring exactly the right contrast to Herring's guitar. Certainly many tracks on Lincoln Memorial require the listeners patience as modal explorations start out as musical conversations, and then morph and evolve into the synergistic plasma of five-engine freight train hurtling down one perilous musical track, with a new twist around every corner. These are musicians of the caliber that listeners will want to hear how they interact in the most daring and vulnerable setting possible-and there are very few if any deliberate or false steps in the mix. It's never going to see a spot on the "Smooth Jazz" charts. Lincoln Memorial dishes out over 70 minutes of music originally edited out of more than three hours of expertly recorded jam sessions. Musicians and listeners who inherently understand the potential of great jam sessions will not want to miss this one, and jamband fans who think they've seen God at a Phish concert, will want to think again after this. Hopefully this recording will find its way into the hands of an audience that can appreciate both the interplay, musical risks, and delights that happen along the way, but I suppose listeners who crave a neat and tidy compositional structure may flee the scene screaming. Few recorded electric band excursions into free improvisation since Weather Report or King Crimson have produced such a powerful and whimsical result.

reviewText:
Overall, these are exceptional performances.  For several of the symphonies, they are my favorite or second-favorite recorded versions.  The concerto performances are also fine and noteworthy, though only one of them is at the top of the list of available recordings.

Klemperer's versions of all of these pieces are monumental and yet provide exquisite attention to detail.  He is famous (notorious to some) for his slower tempos in most allegro movements.  The slower tempos permit a greater level of precision in attacks and in unison playing; if sloppiness in performances is a major issue for you, then you will love the studio versions of Beethoven symphonies and concertos that are found in this collection.  (The fact that his adagios and andantes tend to be a bit faster than most has attracted less attention.)

There are times when a slower and more monumental performance misses the point.  Before getting to the performances on this collection that I love and admire, I'm going quickly to dispose of the ones that, in my opinion, are not very good.  I've talked about those in other reviews so will simply mention them here.  First, and most conspicuously, a slow and monumental approach to the Eighth Symphony just doesn't work very well.  To see what I mean, play the first few measures of the first movement of Klemperer's Eighth and then immediately play the same passage from the Casals performance with the Marlboro Festival Orchestra.  Less problematic, but still unsatisfying, are the performances on this set of the last two movements of Beethoven's Seventh Symphony.  As with the entire Eighth Symphony, the ideal performance of the last two movements of the Seventh should be light and electric.  It's hard to do that without eliding some of the notes out of existence; but Klemperer isn't interested in lightness and electricity, here or elsewhere, so intent is he on making sure that you hear every note.

I also find Klemperer's tempos in the Fourth Piano Concerto to be too slow for comfort - including, in an exception to the pattern noted above, the Andante con moto, where Klemperer pretty much ignores the last two words of the tempo marking.

With those few exceptions, I find every performance on this set to be somewhere between excellent and extraordinary.  One of the special joys is hearing how much unlike Mozart and Haydn the early works can sound under Klemperer's direction.  The most conspicuous example of this is the earliest work on this collection, the Second Piano Concerto in B flat, which was written before the First Piano Concerto, though it was published after it.  Every other performance I've ever heard makes the Second Piano Concerto sound like it was composed by some imitator of Mozart or Haydn.  But Klemperer makes the piece sound like the work of Beethoven - a young Beethoven, to be sure, but a Beethoven with a well-developed sense of the power that an orchestral work can generate.  Try listening to this performance and then listening to the Solti-Ashkenazy performance with the Chicago Symphony, for example.  I think you will be astonished by the difference.  Because he captures the power and force of the work so effectively, Klemperer wins the nod from me for best performance of it.  (It is perhaps unfair of me not to mention Klemperer's collaborator on the concerto performances, Daniel Barenboim.  But it seems to me that Barenboim wasn't given much opportunity to shape any of the concertos to his liking.  These are Klemperer performances in every respect.)

Similarly, Klemperer's performances of the First and Second Symphony are monumental and powerful rather than light and electric.  Most performances of the First, and many of the Second, make them sound Mozartean or Haydnesque; so any true Beethoven fan will find much to appreciate in these versions.

A similar point could be made regarding Klemperer's version of the Fourth Symphony.  Although most conductors have rightly ignored Schumann's characterization of the Fourth as "a slim Greek maiden between two Norse giants" (the Third and Fifth), Klemperer's performance here is the most effective refutation of Schumann that I've ever heard.

The symphonies that are most famous for their monumental power, the Third ("Eroica"), Fifth and Ninth ("Choral"), all receive extra infusions of enormous force in these Klemperer performances.  I recommend all of them without reservation.

As an aside, I'd have loved it if Klemperer had repeated the exposition section of the opening movement of the Eroica - few conductors ever do that; but the one or two performances I've heard where it was done make the ground-breaking scope of the symphony even more evident.  Repetition of the first-movement exposition does make the fourth movement seem disproportionately small - but having a first movement of a symphony on a far larger scale than the last was really automatic until Beethoven's Ninth changed all the rules.

Finally, I have to mention a special favorite among the performances in this collection -- the Sixth Symphony ("Pastoral").  The symphony is a monument of loveliness -- perhaps the most exquisite expression of joy (in the happy sense rather in the triumphant sense of the Ninth's finale) that can be found in music in any genre.  In my opinion, and to my taste, Klemperer's studio performance of this symphony is the best to be found anywhere.

reviewText: This album is not a collection of hit singles but more of a thematic album, which makes it all the more special. Whatever the inspiration, this is a deeply heartfelt album that flows seamlessly. With an absence of lightweight pop tunes, it didn't rocket up the charts, but the mournful, passionate songs stirred a cauldron of emotions within the souls of many listeners, making this album a favorite for many Sam Cooke fans. "Night Beat" also featured a 16-year-old organist by the name of Billy Preston who would soon record many noteworthy albums of his own. In the liner notes for this CD reissue, Peter Guralnick raves about this album, calling it "one of those moments of pure transcendence that can only arrive mysterious and unbidden even in the midst of the most fully committed creative life." reviewText: This is the first album on which Kirk started to really push the boundaries of jazz in ways other than the multiple-horn trick.  While the saxophone was always his base, Kirk plays plenty of flute, manzello, stritch and nose flute on this one, and what is more impressive is that he didn't just try to force each instrument to fit some preconceived traditional bop phrasing.  He alternated between instruments because sometimes one horn is better suited to the specific phrasing he wanted to use than another.  This album, then, is the beginning of Roland Kirk's truly eclectic approach to jazz, drawing openly on multiple traditions, breaking them down and putting them back together again in interesting, and what were then new ways.  He could play swing, bop, cool, avant-guarde, or whatever he wanted, but what makes this album so interesting is that he didn't just play a hard bop piece, then a "cool" piece, and so on.  He would mix and match elements within the context of the same piece in unexpected ways, which would later become his trademark.  This album shows how he got started with that approach.  It is probably not a stretch to suggest that the experience of playing on this album would help Herbie Hancock and Andrew Hill clarify their own ideas, which were still forming at the time (1962), and it is difficult to see how this would have remained as cohesive without a drummer like Roy Haynes on board.

reviewText:
This is not the band in its physical prime.  Plant's voice is strained, and Page seems to have (permanently) lost something in his fleet fingers.  While Bonham is as good as ever, I get the sense that more tracks than normal are being overdubbed.  Page has a difficult time making sessions the way he used to, his presence isn't what it used to be.  Also, with the death in Plant's family and the move in England towards synth rock (which was to swallow bands like Queen whole, with Robert somewhat following suit in his solo career), synthesizers are put on display on this album in a way they never had been before.  So, there are problems with this record.

But this is no ordinary band. There is no rock band, ever, that matched the cohesion and individualized skill at each position, as this one.  The Doors, the Allmans, the Jimi Hendrix Experience ... there's a lot of great things I could say about them, obviously, but for the total performance from each person in this band, I think it was the tightest and most cohesive.  And they were strong enough to accommodate the forces moving against them.

For Plant's gravelly, weakened voices, there is strengthened insight and poetry.  He can still notes, but it sounds strained, and I find myself rooting for him,  One thread of Zep's songwriting always had JPJ coming up with principle ideas and Jimmy elaborating, e.g. Black Dog, No Quarter.  So, it's a winning strategy, and it works here.  For Page's loss of performing standards, he begins using a device called a B-Bender, which bends his B string and gives his performances a country-music flavor - which he'd always had, but now even more pronounced.  JPJ's synthesizer work is majestic.  So, the totality is something that in some way pales, and in other ways reigns supreme.

It's perhaps worth noting that over the years, I've come to value this more than its predecessor, Presence.  I had once had Presence as my favorite, for its tight guitar playing and bluesy lyrics.  It's still great of course, but In Through The Out Door is a richer listening experience for me now.  In fact, ironically, there's nothing quite like it from them for feeling like the dumps, than this and .. their first album.

reviewText:
Trent Reznor is clearly not a happy person. Nor is Nine Inch Nails, the creative title of his tortured music, a happy product on any of their numerous albums. The Downward Spiral's title is fitting, though, taking rank as the darkest NIN release in the bands almost 20 year catalog, it's future bleak, its outlook hopeless, and its aura enough to drag even the most optimistic of listeners down into the void of human despair which Reznor evokes within his walls of superior sonic production, twisted samples, abrasive guitar playing, and unconventional synthesizer manipulations.

The album begins with Mr. Self Destruct, an exercise in...well...self-destruction, as Trent wails off a list of vices for which the society he despises secretly live by, shaming ourselves on the altar of sex, drugs, gratuitous violence in entertainment, and religiion. Ending with Adrian Belew's psychedelic guitar manipulations, it is the perfect way to start the album and lays the blueprint for the subject matter to come; a myriad of sex, drugs, violence, and the contemplation of suicide which will leave the listener drained and devoid of hope once the album finishes.

Taking an unexpected turn, the music mellows into the bassy undertones of Piggy, bringing the image of despair full circle with the eerily whispered lyric "nothing can stop me now, 'cause I don't care anymore..." After a guitar solo full of fuzz distortion cranks across the bridge of the song and brings the almost human sounding drum machines bashing into Piggy's closure, Heresy begins, Trent's screams of rage at God and the powers that be over the AIDS virus dominating the track, making it one of the most brutal tracks presented here, alongside March Of The Pigs, it's followup song and a continuation of the pig theme which seems to wholeheartedly encompass the artists view of society.

Other noteworthy tracks are Closer, the single which only proves you have been living under a rock if you can't sing along with its sexually explicit and non-radio friendly chorus and The Becoming, an industrial beast of a song featuring Reznor lamenting over the pathetic inhuman machine he has become, using samples of human screams instead of music as a backing track. It is one of the albums most disturbing moments and will infect your mind if listened to closely (or frequently) enough. And of course there is Hurt, one of the most powerful songs of the 90's generation, an anthem which epitomizes regret and despair in the most dire of ways. Not to be missed is A Warm Place, a hauntingly beautiful piano piece spreading its warmth across a few brief minutes of the middle of the record before plunging the listener back into insanity.

Machine-like and human at the same time, Trent Reznor began his breakthrough as the king of darkness with this album, using inhuman production and manipulation of his instruments (one of which is the studio itself) balanced with some of the most daring and depressing lyrics ever composed to create one of the darker contrasts yet presented in electronic music. Although the drums sound real, they are really samples and keyboards all run through an effects processor to attain a quality which is almost personable. The guitar playing is primitive, lacking much technical skill, but perfect for the cold, icy vibes which this music requires. The Downward Spiral does not need a Steve Vai-like guitar sound, whizzing by on 32-note-per-second technical solos, but rather imperfectly executed tones of madness which fall perfectly into place with the rest of the "band", no matter how slow or fast. Creating mood is key to the playing of not only the guitar, but Reznor's vast array of keyboards, which he puts to much more original use than on Pretty Hate Machine, opting for original and unconventional sound effects to fit the drearinesss and ugly face of his tortured psyche rather than the standard synths employed on his debut album.

Though many hardcore and 'original' NIN fans will dispute it, The Downward Spiral is a progression from Pretty Hate Machine. But a progression into what? Reznor has clearly mastered his production skill and ability to create a conceptual mood piece with his second album, but at what cost? His voice only sounds more tortured than on his previous album, and though he appears to have mastered his craft, one can tell through the depression in his voice that he has more than a few demons to exorcise, and that this music is not being made simply to sell records. If you have ever hit the lowest of lows in life or know what self-hatred is, Reznor is right alongside you here, lighting the path of the individuals lonely journey across time.

As others have said, this was Eurytmics' return to experimental technopop. Annie tries out a lot of different vocal moods on this album, from speak-singing in "Beethoven," to cool pop-soul vocals on "I've got a Lover Back in Japan," to bruised torch singing on "Savage," to a blues wail on "I need a Man."  And Dave comes up with the right musical backdrop for all of it.  At a time when they could have taken it easy, and repeated the massive success of "Revenge," they chose to experiment, and do something new.

This experimentation means that it will not be a favorite of everyone.  But for those who are fans of Sweet Dreams and Touch, Savage should prove very satisfying.  These three albums are, in my opinion, Eurythmics at their best.

reviewText:
Toumani Diabat, the kora guru of Africa, has outdone himself with this collection of solo instrumental pieces.  The virtuosity in fingering the kora, the richness of the rhythms and range of melodies is unmatched by anything this Malian musician has done previously.  I enjoyed his earlier solo collection, "Kaira", produced twenty years ago and his "New Ancient Strings" (1999), with which he and the younger Ballake Sissoko paid homage to their fathers' musical genius. Yet now, with this CD he has reached a level of maturity, depth and musicality not previously achieved.  For fans of the West African kora, this is a must in their collection; for the "newbies", this is a great introduction into a mesmerizing aspect of Malian music and treat to enjoy over and over again. It will very likely become addictive. This is music to lose yourself in.

Toumani Diabat comes from a long line of Malian musicians. His father was the most famous kora player of his time and Toumani often pays credit to him through his music. Nonetheless, the younger Diabat has refined the abilities of the instrument and enriched the playing techniques over the years.  Elements of these could already be detected in the award winning "In The Heart of the Moon", a collaboration with the legendary guitarist, the late Ali Farka Tour.  Toumani, being largely self-taught, has been open to experimenting with this traditional instrument, without abandoning its unique sound and complex harmonies. As he traveled the world, he absorbed and learned from other musical cultures, such as Indian classical music, flamenco and blues. The compositions on this CD harmoniously integrate such influences with melodies and rhythms of the past. All are his, or presented in his adaptation. Soft melodies that seem to tell gentle stories alternate with more vivacious and energetic pieces.  Not surprisingly, a special homage is included for Ali Farka that he would have treasured. Toumani's extraordinary technical skill lets him expand the fingering to incorporate the bass line as an accompaniment creating the impression that two koras are playing. Furthermore, recently Toumani has been experimenting, successfully as the pieces here exemplify, with two differently strung koras, one for the traditional melodies and harmonies, the other for his more "modern" compositions. The photos in the included booklet show the details of the finger settings. The explanations of the background to the two kora stringings and insights into the stories behind each piece are written by the musician himself.  A beautiful gift to yourself or for people you care deeply about.  [Friederike Knabe]

reviewText:
In the genre of prog rock, one of the norms is that debut albums tend to be rougher in terms of their sound, with more "edges" in a sense. Granted that Marillion came out with very clear influences (a musical advantage, so to speak) stemming from Pink Floyd, Genesis, Yes and even King Crimson, this, their debut album sounded very polished, serving as an exquisite musical framework to Fish's very particular lyrics and voice.
Though the band in their Fish period has been almost inextricably tied to the Scottsman (so much, that when he departed in 88, most people deemed them doomed to breaking up), the strength of the band beyond Fish has been present in their music since day one, giving enough room for each member to contribute to his fullest. An example of this are the guitar solos Steve Rothery delivers for the opening track and "Chelsea Monday," Mark Kelly's upbeat keyboards in "Garden Party," Pete Trewavas' characteristic bass line all through "Chelsea Monday" hand in hand with Rothery's mourning guitar and even the drum work of short-lived Marillion member Mick Pointer (he would only be a part of the band until the recording of this album).
The way I see it, this album, along with their "single" prior to it ("Grendel," which fortunately is part of the Disc 2 on this remastered edition of the original 1983 album) constitute the band's formal tribute to their predecessors, serving as a musical platform for what the band would later show to the world, peaking in 1986 with the genius of the concept album 'Misplaced Childhood,' which introduced most of the bands fan base to them, thanks to the more radio-oriented single "Kayleigh." In a sense, after 'Script...' the comparisons between them and the groups that influenced them more directly would become more subtle, making room in the fans' ears and hearts for what would become the Marillion sound.

reviewText:
A few years ago, when I wrote a review for "Three Chord Opera", I had said that Neil Diamond had recaptured some of his former glory with that disc.  Little would I know that in 2005, he would release "12 Songs", which would surpass anybody's expectations and instantly become one of the best in his entire discography.

Like many, I awaited "12 Songs" with much anticipation, because of the collaboration with uber-producer Rick Rubin.  Surely the lyrics would be solid; that has always been Mr. Diamond's strength.  But, Mr. Rubin would challenge Mr. Diamond from a musical sense, force him to step outside of his creative comfort zone, and produce a disc that would ultimately be much more intimate, raw, and uncluttered than we have grown accustomed to.  Mission accomplished.

Much of the advance press and thinking was that "12 Songs" would hearken back to Mr. Diamond's early days, when he reeled off acoustic hits such as "Cherry Cherry" and "Solitary Man".  I thought that a much more apt comparison would be that this would be similar to his output around the time of the "Stones" and "Moods" albums, where his songwriting had matured, but the acoustic element was still very much present.  I would like to think that I was right, judging from this collection of songs.

The tracks on "12 Songs" are somewhat varied in terms of theme and presentation, and remain strong throughout the disc.  The sparseness and simplicity of the production - combined with Mr. Diamond's reflective, introspective lyrics - provide a lot of punch.  As much as I have tried to find a clunker or two in the song, I honestly have not been able to identify any.  From the opening chords of the hypnotic "Oh Mary" through the lighthearted closing track "We" (as well as the two bonus tracks for those with the Digipak edition), the listening ride is fun.

There are several standout tracks.  "Hell Yeah" seems very much to me like Mr. Diamond's "I Am, I Said" for the 21st century.  "Evermore" is as beautiful and striking a ballad as Mr. Diamond has produced since "Play Me" - even evoking memories of that classic song with the use of strings accompanying the tune.  "Save Me A Saturday Night" is a wonderful love song in the simplicity of Mr. Diamond's message.  "Man Of God" is a strong spiritual that continues his pattern in recent discs of including at least one semi-religious track.  Late in the disc comes "Face Me", which again echoes the lyrical style and musical arrangements of the "Stones" and "Moods" era.  For those with the Digipak version, the bonus track "Men Are So Easy" is amazingly strong, making me wonder why it was left off the standard version of this disc.

Of course, for those with the Digipak version, there is the evaluation between takes of "Delirious Love", a fun rocker with a good, classic shuffle beat.  The bonus version that was enhanced with vocals and arrangements from the great Brian Wilson is very enjoyable, though the added production does make it feel more like a Beach Boys/Brian Wilson song than a Neil Diamond song.  So, it is probably best that this take was a bonus track, leaving the simple acoustically-driven track on the standard disc; to have used the Brian Wilson track would have been a jarring distraction from the overall flow of "12 Songs".

All in all, "12 Songs" is a remarkable disc, and puts the Neil Diamond fan on notice that, at age 64, he is not done yet.  One hopes that his collaboration with Mr. Rubin lasts for a while and results in several discs, because the results are outstanding.  Neil Diamond fans will, of course, love this disc, as with most all of his output over the year.  However, I would strongly recommend this to those who have not listened to Neil Diamond before.  I would also recommend this to those who have drifted away and become slightly disenchanted with Mr. Diamond's music over the years.  Give "12 Songs" a spin in your player.  I don't think you will be disappointed.
label: positive

reviewText: When I heard that Mel Brooks was making a Broadway musical out of his movie classic, "The Producers," I was intrigued. I always thought that this story would be perfect as a musical, since the first time I saw the movie. Of course, I was also worried it wouldn't live up to my expectations. I haven't yet seen the show, but if it is as amazing and brilliant as the music and the performances on the original cast album seem to indicate, it may be heading on its way to be a musical masterpiece. I am dying to see it. First off, let me say that there just could never be as perfect choices to play Leo and Max as Nathan Lane and Matthew Broderick. On this recording, they are absolutely perfect in capturing the spirit of Gene Wilder and Zero Mostel's performances but making the parts all their own. From what I have heard, they are superior to them. Their voices are extremely strong, and most importantly, show-bizzy. But since this review is really about the music, I'll get on to that. The score is absolutely brilliant. No other word to describe it. Never in my memory has a score so perfectly parodied and celebrated the scores of old Broadway. Even scores such as Sondheim's "Follies" falter, in my opinion, in that they are too self-deconstructing and intellectual for their own good. This score is not cynical like shows such as that. It is light, breezy, and fun...the proper approach, I believe to satirizing Broadway. Musical theatre enthusiasts can appreciate the allusions to Broadway scores. Examples include "The King of Old Broadway," with shades of "If I Were A Rich Man," from "Fiddler on the Roof," and even "Reviewing the Situation" from "Oliver." The beginning of "I Wanna Be A Producer" is a subtle and hilarious parody of "Old Man River" from "Showboat," and in the indescribable "Keep It Gay," a bunch of theatre queens chanting "Tony, Tony, Tony," while they are referring to the award, instantly brings to mind Maria from "West Side Story." And these are only a fraction of the myriad parodies within parodies within parodies. But the music also has great heart, making it approachable to people who are not "in-the-know" and even though it sounds like old-fashioned Broadway music, it has freshness and life all its own. And there has never been an old Broadway show with lyrics like, "We're marching to a faster pace/Look out, here comes the Master Race!"  The lyrics themselves are incredibly clever, with great wordplay, rhymes, and a sophisticated sense of humor. The best dirty humor needs sophistication. That separates the crass and obscene to the type of dirty humor that is above criticism: This overall feeling of innocence that surrounds the entire score can make even a chorus line song about Adolf Hitler seem sweet...Adolf ELIZABETH Hitler,  I mean, of course.
