reviewText:
As an OGT and proud member of the Tool cult I am utterly aghast at all the negative comments about their latest release. I think a large segment of fans miss the old days of primal rage and hostile aggression when Maynard would scream his vitriol and stare into the audience ready to kill someone. I was a young angry twenty-something at the time and relished the shows from the Undertow/Aenima era but I've grown older and wiser as has Maynard who appears to have attained some form of spiritual enlightenment that was reflective of the tranquil transition that is Lateralus. While his performance and demeanor was still rough around the edges he chose to "let this go" whatever that horror was that's always haunted him. Lateralus was a moment of pause, reflection, disposition, and at the end of The Grudge a catharsis. The "stone" was purged. I'm just guessing of course, Maynard has always been an enigma.

Many fans however didn't care for the more laid back, soothing, meditative moments of the Lateralus shows which continues in 10,000 days by far the most eclectic, complex, deeply layered, cerebral release yet. I suspect they just wanna rock out and punch someone in the mosh pit like the old days. Alas, Tool's nonstop evolution and metamorphosis to sublime beauty and artistic apotheosis has surpassed them leaving us to enjoy this special moment in musical history.

I was breathless when I first embraced the CD and hit the play button. It didn't take several listens to comprehend it I was immediately overwhelmed and carried away far beyond this world. Every listen is an ethereal, visceral, transcendental journey to the divine and I can't stop listening to it. Being an old metalhead Jambi and Vicarious were early favorites because they rock so immensely but within a few days Right in Two and 10,000 Days have taken over as I am so moved and almost in tears every time I hear them. I cannot even imagine what these songs will be like in concert with the amazing visuals to accompany them. Right in Two may go down as Tool's masterpiece. Beyond words. The Pot is a nice change of pace with the obligatory bashing of the current administration which is now a requirement for every new rock album. Justin has always been a tremendous bass player but this is his finest work so far. After a more laid back performance on Lateralus Adam is back with the raw gusto and forceful fretwork that was all over Aenima.

Before being dismissed as a fanatic who can find no wrong I do have some criticism. It's usually a bad sign when a band decides to produce themselves as Tool has done here. Every band no matter how good needs an objective listener and co-producer. Which begs the question- where is David Bottrill??? His work on Aenima and Lateralus is nothing short of amazing. Why on earth would they not bring him back?! The overall sound and mixing job is average at best. Danny's drum sound is a bit weak compared to previous albums especially Lateralus which just knocked your socks off. Yes, Maynard's voice takes a backseat and not nearly as dominant as before but maybe it's on purpose. His vocal chords have taken alot of abuse over the years. Rosetta Stoned is so reminiscent of Third Eye in sound and style it seems like an inferior sequel to that song and turns into a jam session that doesn't go anywhere.

Aside from those minor setbacks they have surpassed the great things I expected. This album as well as the entire Tool catalog has altered me and had such a profound positive effect on my life I cannot even describe it. Thank you gentlemen.

reviewText: A serious contender for the title of best Wu-Tang solo album. Only Built 4 Cuban Linx is also perhaps the most influential, thanks to Raekwon's cinematic imagination. If the Genius is the Wu's best overall lyricist, Raekwon is arguably their best storyteller, and here he translates the epic themes and narratives of a Mafia movie into a startlingly accomplished hip-hop album. RZA contributes some of the strongest production work of his career, indulging his taste for cinematic soundscapes in support of the album's tone; his tracks are appropriately dark or melancholy, shifting moods like different scenes in a film. Cuban Linx's first-person narratives are filled with paranoia, ambition, excess, and betrayal, fast rises and faster falls. There are plenty of highlights along the way -- the singles "Criminology" and "Ice Cream," the gentle "Rainy Dayz," the influential posse cut "Wu-Gambinos" -- and everything culminates in "Heaven & Hell" and its longing for redemption. Like the Genius' Liquid Swords, Only Built 4 Cuban Linx takes a few listens to reveal the full scope of its lyrical complexities, but it's immensely rewarding in the end, and it stands as a landmark in the new breed of gangsta rap.

For those who have followed the musical production of Spanish-born Alberto Iglesias, you will be surprised with his work the score he did for the film "The Constant Gardener". Famous for scoring the five most recent movies by Pedro Almodovar, Iglesias reinvented the style that made him famous, blending in sounds and instruments from Africa. The result is a soundtrack that ranks alongside 2005's great soundtracks, which made last year one of the most prolific ones for movie music.

"The Constant Gardener" is a solid body of music that serves as a great place from which director Fernando Meirelles (City of God) can launch the visual concepts that make this one of the best movies in recent times. Along with the work of Alberto Iglesias,  you can spot the voice and strings of Ayub Ogaba contributing the the uplifting musical mix. Overall, this is a soundtrack not to be missed.

reviewText:
This is a wonderful opportunity to compare the art and craft of four great song stylists--Billie Holiday, Sarah Vaughan, Ella Fitzgerald, and Lena Horne.  The songs were recorded over the period from 1935 to 1950.  The CD works not so much as a seamless piece of art, but it works as a means of introducing people to four great singers, while--at the same time--allowing those listeners to make their own comparisons of their respective talents.

Overall, I think that this works pretty well.  One can wish that other selections had been used on this CD, but with so few cuts available, this works about as well as one could expect.

Some samples:

Billie Holiday begins the CD with her "The Man I Love."  This Gershwin song is done justice by her wonderful voice, as she imagines a love to come and considers how she "can make him stay."  Evocative singing.  There is the hope of coming love.  On Monday?  Or Tuesday?  This cut also features some nice backing orchestral work.

Ella Fitzgerald follows with "My Melancholy Baby."  This is an up tempo rendering of this song.  Teddy Wilson's Orchestra backs Fitzgerald most ably.  Her voice is in fine form and she provides us an estimable rendition of the work.

Lena Horne, "Prisoner of Love."  Teddy Wilson and His Orchestra provide terrific backing.  Her smooth voice serves this song well; the voice almost caresses the words as she sings lines such as:
"I need no shackles to remind me
I'm just a prisoner of love."

Sarah Vaughan, "Nice Work if You Can Get It."  Another Gershwin song and another great voice to sing it.  Once more, superb orchestral support for the singer.  And what lines!

"Nice work if you can get it,
And you can get it if you try."
....
Where two hearts become one
Who could ask for anything more?"

There are other fine songs on this CD (such as "Ain't' Misbehavin'" and "East of the Sun (and West of the Moon)."  All in all, this is a fine CD that allows listeners to compare four talented singers and four rich voices.

Kanye West has given us a classic, I think.  It's hip-hop at its truest.  Not 50 Cent, not Chingy, but it brings you back the 90's, the best era of Hip-Hop.  The only thing is there's only 20 tracks, but it says there's 21 on your CD player.  Here's the listing with my rating:
Intro
"We Don't Care"- A sound for the kids, and the song that starts his smarta$$ persona(no offense).
Graduation Day(interlude)
"All Falls Down"- I'm not a fan of the video, but the song is very catchy.
I'll Fly Away(interlude)- A good short sing song.
"Spaceship"- A good song.  Kanye raps about robbing the store he works at, Consequence and GLC rap about the struggle, and the chorus samples Marvin Gaye.
"Jesus Walks"- One of my favorite songs.  The second verse is very influential, because he talks about how people get in trouble for discussing Jesus.
"Never Let Me Down"- Jay-Z delivers two tight rhymes(especially his last rhymes on his second verse).  I don't like J. Ivy, but Kanye drops a very influential verse, and almost outrhymes Jay.
"Get Em' High"- Not one of my favorites, but it is a good song.  Talib Kweli and Common both drop excellant verses.
Workout Plan(interlude)
"New Workout Plan"- It isn't one of my favorites, but it is a fun song, with crazy humor and nice ans surprisingly nice singing by Kanye when he does.
"Slow Jamz"- A smooth song.  One of my favorites.  Twista and Kanye both drop tight verses, and Jamie Foxx delivers a great chorus.
"Breathe In, Breathe Out"- I would've liked to hear Luda drop a verse, but he does drop a cool hook while Kanye drops humor on the verses.
School Spirit Skit 1(interlude)
School Spirit- It's a good song but I don't like that it's edited.
Lil' Jimmy Skit
"Two Words"- My other favorite song.  It's a tight beat and Kanye, Mos Def, and Freeway all deliver tight verses.
"Through The Wire"- An emotional song to listen 2, because Kanye's mouth is wired shut when he's rappin it.  It is one of my favorites though.
"Family Business"- My last favorite song.  Kanye talks about his family and manages to make fun of himself a bit.  Nice beat.
"Last Call"- I like this song, but it's not one of my favorites.  If you keep listening, Kanye spends alot of time at the end talking about how he got to where he's at.

One Amazon reviewer, giving this recording one star, stated this material by Bruce Palmer was not for Buffalo Springfield fans.

If you appreciate the genius of the band's individual members, you will treasure this recording.

The four tracks feature instrumental improvisation, which is so reminiscent of 60's bands like The Grateful Dead or Jefferson Airplane--maybe a reminder of Ravi Shankar's influence without exotic instruments. All songs remind me so much of the psychedelic genre from that time period.

I have been a Buffalo Springfield fan since the band's early beginnings, and words can't express how happy I am to have my copy of Bruce Palmer's recording.

I immediately added all four tracks into a playlist with my favorite songs from Springfield, a few from early Poco featuring Richie Furay, songs from Jim Messina, some from Neil Young's first solo album as well as the first one, where he had players from Crazy Horse, and I also added a song or two from Supersession, an album where Stephen Stills added a song or two.

The result was that Palmer's recording is something for a "real" Buffalo Springfield fan.

It is creative. It is incredible.

reviewText:
Gama Bomb are a band principally from Northern Ireland, who play a very strict 1980's influenced form of Crossover/Thrash Metal and incorporate a lot of humour into their lyrics.

Tales From The Grave And Space is their third full-length studio album, after 2006's Survival Of The Fastest and 2008's Citizen Brain. It was released in 2009 (re-released in 2010) on Earache Records and is currently available for free legal download off of Earache's website.

The musicianship is absolutely top notch and even more surprisingly, the production is of the absolute highest quality. This album sounds as almost as good in terms of production as other Thrash Metal albums from 2009 from long established bands like Exodus's Exhibit B and Megadeth's Endgame.

Highlights include `New Eliminators Of Atlantis B.C.' as well as `We Respect You,' and album closer `Mummy Invasion,' all of which are fast and straightforward thrash metal numbers; mostly with more of an East Coast feel than Bay Area if you want to get more specific, although that is reversed on tracks like `Polterghost.' The album is twelve tracks long, clocks in at half an hour in length.

As singer Philly Byrne has been known to say live `I hope you like songs that sound exactly like that one.' Gama Bomb don't incorporate anything else into their sound other than pure thrash metal; there are no ballads, no atmospheric buildups, no eastern scales and no fifteen minute progressive songs.

If you are a big fan of Nuclear Assault, S.O.D, Sacred Reich and more modern acts like Municipal Waste, SSS and Evile then Gama Bomb are certainly a worthwhile proposition that you should check out.

This album is very strong and no serious complaints can be made about any aspect of it other than the simple fact that it doesn't come from the 80s and that there isn't a whole lot of variety on offer, but if you expect any you may be missing the point of this band a little. If you hate humour in your thrash, you also may want to give it a miss, otherwise however Tales From The Grave And Space is a very good album that thrash fans should seriously enjoy

reviewText:
Kim Carnes Caf Racers, released in 1983, was the singers follow up to 1982s critically acclaimed but commercially lackluster Voyeur. On this effort Carnes does a complete 180 and goes from the straight forward rock of Voyeur to electronic synth dance pop on Caf Racers, along with some breath taking pop ballads. Taken as a whole, this was probably not the best move on Carnes part but it appears that the singer was desperate to fit in with the times and 1983 was the year of synth pop. Replacing the reliable super producer Val Garay with Keith Olson on this project was supposed to bring Carnes back to the top of the charts, where she was barely 2 years ago with her eternal anthem Bette Davis Eyes. That was not to be as Caf Racers floundered badly. But the albums commercial failure does not tell the whole story. Hurricane is a solid slice of Dance Pop and should have been a Pop and Dance smash. You Make My Heart Beat Faster, Young Love and Invisible Hands are all Carnes attempts to be hip to the times with these up-tempo Dance Pop ditties but all of them failed to generate a hit for Carnes as the songs all sound frighteningly similar to each other. These are by no means bad songs but they unfortunately do try too hard and as a result none of then work. Universal Song is Carnes attempt to recreate Draw Of The Cards from 1981s blockbuster Mistaken Identity and it too does not live up to the marginal to begin with original.

Kim Carnes voice is really her greatest strength. It is an instrument that Carnes uses to make you feel every emotion that she sings about. The ballads on this album are what makes Caf Racers worth a listen. Just listen to I Pretend, a chillingly beautiful power ballad about a love that can never be. I Pretend became an Adult Contemporary Top 10 hit and should have been an across the board smash but lack of promotion and radio stations and programmers over all reluctance towards the Caf Racers album and all the songs on it hurt Carnes chances of scoring a hit with I Pretend. A real shame since Caf Racers has so much to offer and further showcases Carnes talents as a singer, particularly on slow songs. A Kick In The Heart is another criminally overlooked ballad on Caf Racers that has all the goods needed to have become a huge commercial hit. Same story with Met You At The Wrong Time Of My Life, as beautiful as anything offered in 1983 by way of balladry. Ill Be Here Where The Heart Is was originally featured on the Flashdance soundtrack and received some air play and is rightfully also included on Caf Racers.

Many Thanks to Culture Factory for doing such a beautiful job of re-mastering this gem. This series is called a Vinyl Replica Collection but this is actually a great High Definition Remaster. The sound here is amazing. And preserving the iconic album cover art front and back is simply genius. The over all look is sleek and has a feel of a vinyl record in mini form. Even the disc it itself looks like the original vinyl record and the original vinyl sleeve is also beautifully re-created. Thanks Culture Factory for a job well done.

reviewText: On the relatively obscure 1986 album Inside Story, Grace turned away from Sly & Robbie's reggae/dub to an elegant style of melodious and soulful pop in a delightful variety of ballads and uptempo songs. The 1970s legend of intelligent disco Nile Rodgers, producer of amongst others Chic, Sister Sledge and Norma Jean was the co-producer. These songs & sounds have passed the test of time with flying colors. Almost everything here could have been a hit, like I'm Not Perfect (But I'm Perfect for You), a mid-tempo number with clever lyrics & memorable hooks and Hollywood Liar with its poetic put-downs and witty turns of phrase. This is also the track with Grace's trademark French lyrics that recalls La Vie en Rose on the debut Portfolio, Autumn Leaves on Fame, Amado Mio on Bulletproof Heart and Pars on Warm Leatherette. Chang Hitchhikes to Shanghai with its sublime synth lines is a lovely story song as is Victor Should Have Been A Jazz Musician, a slow atmospheric ballad with plaintive sax and tender, sometimes whispered vocals. The catchy Party Girl has a lilting beat and expansive feel, whilst Crush is a funky track with an edgy beat. One of the highlights is Barefoot In Beverly Hills, an impressively arranged composition with sublime vocals in various styles. There's another arresting ballad in Scary But Fun whilst the stirring Inside Story is a spiritual masterpiece with a powerful gospel sound. This melodic and moving title track is the most explicit statement of a theme that runs throughout her work, also finding expression on the 2008 album's track Love You To Life. How sweet it sounds to hear Grace SINGING again after all the growling, talking & chanting of the preceding works of the early 1980s. If Portfolio is her best Disco album, Nightclubbing her best Torch Song one and Living My Life her best Avant Garde excursion, then Inside Story rivals 1989's Bulletproof Heart for her best Pop album. After 19 years of silence, Grace returned in 2008 with Hurricane where Sly & Robbie, but also Tricky and Brian Eno, lend a hand on a difficult but impressive and mostly autobiographical album.

Still, to a minority who happen to know him, this record is the best he released even though it was his first solo work. Fans of Queen have probably picked it up at the time it was released (1992) and a ballad 'Over and Over again' has even received some airplay in Holland and some other European countries. And that was pretty much it.  Maybe things would turn out differently, had it been releases a decade earlier, who knows.
The album though has a lot more to offer, melodic rock of a highest quality (Queeneesh vocal layers and songwriting are evident) and cannot go unnoticed. The absolute majority of songs are true gems especially 'Broken Dreams', 'I believe in You', 'Heaven is Calling' and 'Love is alive'. The only filler song presented here is 'Live Your Life', which probably meant to draw more attention from media.
If I just say I recommend this CD to a true melodic music fan that would be an understatement.  In my opinion it's a must have for anyone's collection

reviewText:
BANG. This quick little EP is over in nine minutes and you wonder where your eardrums went. You bend over to search for them on the floor, but as you do, your nose begins to bleed. Suddenly your stomach feels a trifle off kilter as the carpet begins to swim in front of your eyes. Your hands tingle as the sensation in your feet floats away. If you didn't know any better, you'd swear that there were fish hooks in your lungs pulling in opposite directions. Air becomes sparse as your eyes dart in a futile attempt to locate escape. You would stand up, but your spine has been removed. Your flaccid body flops to the ground as vultures begin to land on your windowsill. Ants start a pathway to the tender spots of your face. It's over now. In just nine minutes, you have been eviscerated by five guys from Jersey. And it only cost six bucks.
It's amazing that the same band who recorded this EP went on to make the debacle of the full length known as "Soundtrack to the Personal Revolution". I love Burnt by the Sun, but this EP just wipes the floor with the full length. But, this review isn't for trashing "Soundtrack..". Anyway, this EP was released in August of 2001, not 2002 as it is stated above. These four songs will decimate any preconceived notions one might have of noise core. The guitars rage in an oil-sheened slickness that slices with precision and dices with pretension. Everything flows with ease, yet still sounds like absolute insanity. The vocals are impenetrable; try and follow along with the lyric sheet and you will get lost in a haze of aural antagonism. I can't say enough about the veneer BBTS painted in my mind for the full length with this EP, but as I said, "Soundtrack..." should be used as a coaster. Play it safe and stick with this. "Soundtrack..." is terrible. Did I mention to get this instead?

reviewText:
Finally in 2008 "Winger" fans have something to stand up and cheer about. In the 20 plus years that "Winger" has been rocking they have amassed a legion of loyal fans that just can't get enough of them and their metal sound. Winger "live" is the bands first entry into the DVD concert market and fans won't be disappointed by what they see and hear. The Song list and level of musicianship by the band is sure to please any casual or hard core "Winger" fan. From the second they take the stage there's no doubt why Kip Winger, Reb Beach, John Roth and Rod Morgenstein have been able to hang around for so long.

The DVD concerts 19 song set list is really impressive and the level of showmanship and precision of playing from the guys makes for a great concert experience for those lucky to be in attendance. Kip Wingers voice seems to have stood the test of time and the backing vocals and harmonies are as good as they ever were. The music is tight and the band seems to really be having a great time on stage and the audience is with them song after song.

While this DVD release from Shrapnel is very good it could have been much better. For one thing the Audio mix is only in 2.0 Stereo, so there's no 5.1 Digital or DTS. The picture is really clear but some segments switch from color to black and white for a different effect. I would have preferred they just present the concert straight forward and in color. In my opinion the camera editing could have been so much better, there's a little to much crowd shots for my liking.

When I buy a concert DVD I want to see more of the band performing and less of the crowd. Aside from a couple minor complaints this is an excellent entry into the DVD concert forum for "Winger" and their fans. I highly recommend it!

reviewText: There are a lot of great Wagner conductors. I have heard a lot of them on the same music. Personally I think Wagner may have been the greatest melodic master I have ever heard. Maybe the most creative since Bach. So what a pleasure to hear his forever popular overtures and preludes. I have heard Barenboim, Levine, von Karajan, Szell, Tennstedt, Boult, to name but a few. These were all very good. (The MET opera orchestra may be the most disciplined and finely tuned orchestra under Levine that I have heard since Cleveland under Szell!)  Many are just excellent. But whose do I listen to the most?  Otto Klemperer's Philharmonia recordings of the early 60s may be the superlative among many excellents. His Rienzi reading knocks the lights out. The physical recording does not seem to lose much to our digital sound. If you are a fan of Wagner's overtures and preludes, get it while you still can. This one has stood a long time. It may stand a while longer with prolonged remastering. But who knows when financial belt tightening will have an impact? Get it.  Available on Amazon.

reviewText:
Achtung Baby is a sensational rock album that every music lover should own. U2 created this 12-track CD in Berlin in 1990-91 around the time of the collapse of the decrepit socialist state of East Germany, and this "zeitgeist" is reflected in the style of the record. Heavy emotional lyrics about love, lust and loss, driving guitar, and clattering dance and techno rhythms are brilliantly fused together in one of the most powerful records ever released.

My Track Review of Achtung Baby:

Zoo Station - Groundbreaking lead track uses a jagged industrial rhythm and distorted vocals . The Zoo Station was an East Berlin landmark railway terminal back in the Communist era that the U2 crew visited as the album took shape.

Even Better Than The Real Thing - One of the key songs of the whole decade, this fantastic recording has that "wow" factor that made it truly memorable. Brilliant video, and it heralded U2's 1992-93 Zoo TV media & information blitz. Even Better... came with a groovy dancefloor remix by Perfecto that had a chart life of its own. A big hit in July 1992.

One - A very special song, One is an emotional ballad that has taken on many layers of meaning over the years, and reveals raw emotions that U2 are so good at displaying. At once, a great pop hit in April 1992, an anthem for the ages, a heartbreak song, and a statement of unity and solidarity. My favourite song on the album.

Until The End Of The World - An awesome rock song. This has dramatic introduction, almost-apocalyptic lyrics, dense rhythms and it works superbly as a concert track. Really exciting.

Who's Gonna Ride Your Wild Horses - A medium paced track with Bono's vocals bathed in a wash of hazy electronica and featuring memorable choruses. A 5th single from the album , it hit the Top 10 in December 1992.

So Cruel - This song is a masterpiece and shows U2 at the very height of its songwriting powers. This slow, compelling song builds to an unforgettable crescendo in the third verse and its superior lyric reveals the power of obsessive love.

The Fly - An immediate attention-grabbing single released in advance of the album in November 1991 and reaching #1, this was our first glimpse of U2's radically-different new sound for the new decade. In amongst the slogans and the shades, there is a killer pop song here with that familiar spine-tingling moment in the chorus when U2 rises to a plane no other band can reach.

Mysterious Ways - I never grow tired of this terrific funky song. What a great bassline! I think this mid-paced track is alluring and accessible while still sounding suitably exotic (the shimmering North African scenes on its video and the concert belly dancer add to the mystique!) A Top 3 hit in December 1991.

Tryin' To Throw Your Arms Around The World - I don't listen to this one as much as the first eight classics, but it's still pretty good. A medium-tempo track.

Ultra Violet (Light My Way) - This has a great sound to it and is a relationship song with heavy lyrics and a memorable refrain

Acrobat - Many reviewers like this one, though it isn't a favourite of mine. Again a powerful lyrical song.

Love Is Blindness - Brilliant slow track to close this landmark album, this lays bare the bleak emotions of a difficult and painful emotional entanglement.

Overall, this album succeeds as a work of art, as an extension of the band's previous work, as a dance record and as a rock record. I enjoyed it as much as ever before when I played it through in running order a few days ago; such great music never goes out of date. It is my pick as the best rock album of the 1990's.

5 stars

reviewText:
"(What's The Story) Morning Glory?" is rock and roll stripped down worse than a porn star at prom. It's in your face and blurry, a collection of sounds and rhythms so rapidly spit, they knock you in your face, breathless en route to a jazzed up headache.

The disk has songs that cry out to you - "Don't Look Back In Anger" - tunes that ride a high - "Roll With It" - as well as a merge of the most influential genres music chucked out since it was a toddler in Elvis' "Heartbreak Hotel".

Oasis, rolling through the high stylings of MOD, their resemblance uncanny with folded shirts and a soul made out of rubber, release a dance pop riot, and make it fight tediously with sore throat grunge.

Call them slaves to the Beatles, even back ally copy cats of the great Brit-pop movement, but do so with hypocrisy. Oasis have attached themselves to music that fought against the administration. They've recreated the Summer of Love, and I say, here, here to such a concept. With "(What's The Story) Morning Glory?", Oasis have created a pot smoking disco ball, with Noel blending in styles so different they blush when together.

When Noel sat down and wrote it, he may not have been thinking about the impact it was going to have in the `95, "oh, we're in the nineties now", society. He may not have thought his cough ups about pop culture hysterectomies would matter. How wrong he was, because Oasis didn't just define a generation, it nailed it down with a hammer, taking the living breath out of the mainstream sounds of grunge. Irony intended every bit.

Noel keeps an attitude about him that is rough and innocent, his voice flustering as he ponders to either hit the notes, or let the notes hit him first. By the time he gets to "Champaign Supernova", you find yourself pondering how you are able to dance to raw sound. Emotions are chopped up and delivered in liquor shots as "Morning Glory" rolls through "Wonderwall", "Some Might Say" and "Hey Now!".

It's an album that doesn't beg to be recited. It doesn't want you to classify it, and in no way does it want to be put up on a pedestal. It's just a wicked nice piece of non fiction, from a band that seemed to carry the world on their British backs during its release.

There are some rock and roll discs that hold on to listeners through lowly punch lines, between a muddled mess of off beats and boring tunes. "Morning Glory" is all a muddled mess, but the hottest sounding and looking mess on the shelves of HMV.

And this dirty mess infects the listener with tunes that seem to come out of the planet..

Oasis performs "(What's The Story) Morning Glory?" like it is a show on Broadway, because after the first track, every other has a life by itself. The actors, each taking on a personality for the play, hurry throughout the acts, picking away at the un-expecting audience.

Oasis is not standing out in the rain, asking to be Shakespearean.. Most of the rock and roll on the market - oh, pardon me, sire, most of the "rock" on the market - is rubbish, over hyped, "next big thing" retaliation to our society's need for Glamour and People's magazines. They is nothing glamorous about Liam singing about booze, Noel bopping his head in tune and Paul Arthurs , Paul McGuigan and Alan White rocking out to the steady passed rock. Here's to raw sound.
label: positive

reviewText: I've read the reviews and I've listened to the petty complaints, so I finally decided to buy this set and formulate my own opinion. Before I disclose my findings, I'd like to say that I've enjoyed the music of Genesis since 1973 when I first heard the "Genesis Live" album. From there the whole thing snowballed to "Selling England By The Pound" and then "Nursery Cryme" and finally "The Lamb Lies Down on Broadway." Unfortunately, after that one Gabriel moved on and with very few exceptions the fun was over (for me at least). So I've always maintained a fondness for the Gabriel years; from my perspective they embodied the true spirit of the band. With that said, it should be mentioned up front that this box set is THE definitive release for fans of early Genesis: the artwork, lyrics, photos and even the disc graphics are faithfully reproduced in all their bizarre glory. In addition, the newly remastered sound is absolutely stunning; my favorite example of this stellar difference is on the "Selling England by the Pound" CD---without a doubt the best version of this classic album that I've ever heard---it actually rivals the newly remastered version of "In the Court of the Crimson King". I've carefully listened to all the CDs in this set and have found them to be superior to any other previous releases. Yes, there are a few subtle differences in the mix, but IMO they don't detract from the listening experience. Also included is a bonus disc of rarities which contains some interesting tidbits. Throw in the extensive selection of videos and interviews and you've got one of the most interesting, comprehensive, high quality box sets that I've ever had the pleasure of owning. ***** stars

Jc Chasez's "Schizophrenic" is one of kind; it's diverse with rock, hip-hop, reggae, dance, new wave, and don't forget -- the ballads.
1. "Some Girls (Dance With Women)" - the first single off the album. When I first heard it, I thought it was a dancefloor track automatically. And, of course, two girls dancing in the club, makes a guy turned on or teases the guy.
2. "She Got Me" - Now this song confuses me a little bit. Here, Jc talks about his love affair with an alien (I hope it's a girl alien) and how she got him.
3. "100 Ways" - Now this song's the sh**!! I can picture that song can be used for a model runway show, influencing the "Rock Star" image. Jc gets dirty in the process as he seduces the woman by letting her say what's on her dirty mind.
4. "Mercy" - Jc takes it slow, reggae-style as he plead the girl to be with him 'cause he needs mercy.
5. "Build My World" - the first ballad of the album and probably the third single to be released. It tells about the after hours after a night out at the club, wanting someone to be with him. Heartwarming? Yes!
6. "Something Special" - Uhh...nothing special here, just a bunch of handclaps here and there.
7. "If You Were My Girl" - Now, Jc picks up the pace and this track interests me because he does yell in a sexy way almost at the end of song.
8. "Shake It" - Now, this is what I'm talking about! He collaborated with Basement Jaxx after they collaborate with him with the song "Plug It In" on their "Kish Kash" album. It samples a song that goes "do it, do it, do it 'till you're satisfied".
9. "All Day Long I Dream About Sex" - the second single off the album. It's new wave at its finest; using the synthseizers and all. Of course, people won't forget the chanty chorus, it's an anthem that Jc says, "it's just for fun".
10. "One Night Stand" - Jc's acting like a pimp, making the girl feel special for one night only. He gets a little freaky in the process, so be aware, ladies.
11. "Come To Me" - The dancefloor anthem for after hours. Samples Corey Hart's "Sunglasses At Night", but some people think it samples Eurythmics' "Sweet Dreams (Are Made Of This)". One of my favorites in the album, he talks about being lonely and he's yearning for his lover when he lies awake. Very dirty and sexy.....
12. "Dear Goodbye" - the second ballad of the album. It tells about him and his lover going on separate ways, and he feels emotional when he sings it on stage. He almost start to cry, that poor baby.
13. "Everything You Want" - Back to reggae again. Jc sings like he was from The Police, even though, it's influenced by it. Great party track, play when you're in the beach.
14. "Lose Myself" - the last ballad of the album. One of my favorites and it's heartmelting and very emotional.
15. "Right Here (By Your Side)" - I usually skip this track, nothing usual.
16. "Blowin' Me Up (With Her Love)" - Now, this is the song that starts his solo debut. It was released as a single and the "Drumline" soundtrack on December, 2002 and it's very good, use for a marching band piece.
17. "Some Girls (Dance With Women) (Rap version) - it's featuring Dirt McGirt. Nothing I can say about that.
So that's my review. If you're going to get this album, trust me, it's the best yet!!!!

reviewText: Sarah Brightman's name became synonymous with Andrew Lloyd Webber as his one-time wife and muse two decades ago, but it was her voice that made her a star and would have made her a star with or without Webber. Yes, she became famous for singing his tunes early on, but it was her talent and undying love for her art that made her the biggest-selling soprano of all time. With such masterpiece albums as Eden, La Luna, Harem, Requiem, Surrender and Timeless/Time To Say Goodbye under her belt, this collection is compiled of the greatest songs from those and one Lloyd Webber cast album, Phantom Of The Opera. Brightman already has a devoted following, and if you play this CD for anyone who is not familiar with the superiority of Sarah's vocals, you are sure to add that many more to her fanbase. It's hard to say where to begin on this collection because all fourteen tracks are proven winners. Whether it's the splendiferous opening track of "Phantom Of The Opera," which features her duet partner Steve Harley, to the sensational, spine-tingling closer of "Time To Say Goodbye (Con Te Partir)," complimented by Andrea Bocelli, there's nothing not to like on this magnificent CD with its carefully chosen tracks. In between the opening and closing tracks, we are treated to phenomenal selections that include "Just Show Me How To Love You," "Deliver Me," "What You Never Know" and her gorgeous interpretations on such contemporary American fare as Simon & Garfunkel's "Scarborough Fair" to Procol Harem's 1967 masterpiece "A Whiter Shade Of Pale." Her Italian is perfection on "Nella Fantasia" while her unique interpretation of Queen's "Who Wants To Live Forever" will knock you out. If you already are familiar with these tracks and want to savor them on one splendid disc with gorgeous liner notes and photographs, this one's for you. If you're a visionary and would like to take this magnificent journey one step further, I suggest the DVD companion that contains 20 performances, which include the aforementioned plus superb performances like "Ave Maria," "Anytime, Anywhere," "Wishing You Were Somehow Here Again" and several more. To hear Sarah Brightman is diva divine. To see and hear Sarah Brightman is simply supreme.

I only just heard this track on Saturday Night Live tonight, like a previous reviewer,  but I am in love with it.  Everyone here has picked up on the Bee Gees vibe, but  nobody has mentioned the huge nod to Cerrone's "Supernature" in the beginning of the  song.  Does nobody pick up on the sheer, blissful irony of this song?  Everyone seems  to be missing the mark here, or maybe I am just interpreting it differently than  everyone else here so far.  Pink Floyd are undoubtedly one of the best bands ever, but  that doesn't mean they should be this sacred cow never to be touched, either, and I  actually consider myself a huge fan of everything from Syd Barrett's early material  through to the later Floyd.

To put it bluntly, Pink Floyd's original version of Comfortably Numb is a track I  can't listen to unless I'm in a certain frame of mind, because it is sure to depress  me to no end, which is not necessarily a bad thing.  It's a classic and nobody denies  this.  However, the fact that this cover can make such a well-known, depressing song a  danceable bit of retro disco fluff I actually want to play over and over again... it  really blows my mind.  The fact that they were even able to conceive of meshing the  lyrics of Pink Floyd with Cerrone's "Supernature" and the sound of the Bee Gees is  simply amazing to me.  Anyone who covers "Comfortably Numb" is knowingly putting themselves up for ridicule by the legions of fans of the original song.  It's one of those classics that is so sacred to Pink Floyd fans that I honestly doubt anyone could do it justice in their eyes without keeping predictably close to the original.

Count me in as a fan of this cover.  They really brought something entirely different  to the table with this single, not just another warmed over, boring, safe rehash.  This single took brass ones to make, that's for sure.

reviewText: Quite simply, Stalingrad (2012) is one of the best Accept albums ever, and that's saying a lot. It is a devastating, and brutal experience which epitomizes the best that heavy metal has to offer at this time. There's not a lot of pretense here, and very few surprises, as Accept has had pretty much the same sound for nearly three decades. Forget about love ballads, this is the dark stuff that reaches out and grabs you in the gut, and shakes your foundations. If you want to hear about pain, war, death, struggle, oppression, evil, and destruction, then Accept is speaking your language, and with a maturity and conviction that is powerfully effective. When the core of Accept, guitarists Wolf Hoffman and Herman Frank, bass player Peter Baltes, and drummer Stefan Schwarzmann, reformed with new vocalist Mark Tornillo, some may have doubted that the band could be as powerful as before, and questioned how anyone could replace the legendary Udo Dirkschneider. First on Blood of the Nations (2010), and now on Stalingrad, Accept has clearly demonstrated that the members of the band more than stand on their own merits as musicians and songwriters, and Mark Tornillo is one hell of a singer. Kind of a mix of Udo, Graham Bonnett, and Rob Halford, Tornillo's aggressive singing style meshes perfectly with the band's dark musical tone. Led by DIrkschneider and Hoffman, Accept was one of heaviest exponents of Eurometal in the 1980's. After forming his band U.D.O., and leaving Accept, Dirkschneider has continued to produce the same kind of pile driving metal that the original Accept pioneered. Happily for fans of this crushing genre of metal, the newest version of Accept is arguably as powerful and relevant as ever. Though there is no one completely in charge of the music for THE LINCOLN LAWYER this assortment of themes and music more than serves to highlight the tension and the underlying parodies. Cliff Martinez offers the original music for the score, never in the way, never calling attention to itself, but keeping the movie running smoothly and with adequate tension/relief. To remind the listener of the story the following is offered:

THE LINCOLN LAWYER is a classy, well-written (adapted from Michael Connelly's novel by John Romano), well-directed (Brad Furman) drama that benefits from the presence of a well chosen, first class cast. This is one of the stronger movies of the year, the kind of film that reminds us of the art of cinema.

Mike Haller (Matthew McConaughey in a brilliant performance) is a money hungry smarmy defense lawyer whose brilliant mind is bent toward representing sleazy types who pay well. He works out of his Lincoln automobile driven by his trusted ally Earl (Laurence Mason), lives in a dumpy apartment, works with a shoddy appearing detective Frank (William H Macy), and spars with the beautiful fellow lawyer Maggie McPherson (Marisa Tomei) with whom he has a daughter and an on again off again relationship. One of his fellow workers Val Valenzuela (John Leguizamo) tips Mike on a case of wealthy realtor Louis Roulet (Ryan Phillippe) who is accused of beating a prostitute: the case smells of lots of money so Mike of course takes it on - along with Louis, wealthy mother Mary Windsor (Frances Fisher) and the family lawyer Cecil Dobbs (Bob Gunton). Mike's investigation turns up evidence that suggests his client is not the 'presumed innocent' he appears and there are connections between this case and an old case Mike handled - Jesus Martinez (Michael Pea) - and Mike's usual 'go for the money' attitude takes a turn toward actually seeking justice in the courtroom. A shady dealing lawyer does actually have a conscience and finds a way to prove the truth will out.

There are many cameo roles worthy of mentioning - Josh Lucas plays the prosecuting attorney Ted Minton, Pell James is Mike's girl Friday Lorna, Margarita Levieva is the victim prostitute Reggie Campo, Trace Adkins plays the motorcycle gang head Eddie Vogel, and Shea Whigham inhabits the role of the jail snitch DJ Corliss. But the major attraction here is Matthew McConaughey's Oscar worthy role: he is magnetic in his transformation from a lawyer you want to loathe to a victor you want to hail. Marisa Tomei is once again given the opportunity to demonstrate just how fine an actress she is. This is a fast moving, well-scripted film that is simply one of the better moves to come out in a while. Highly recommended both as a film an as a musical score. Grady Harp, November 12

reviewText:
Well thats what the advertising blurb says. And for once I think its justified. Whether you buy the standard album or the deluxe edition you won't be disappointed. This is clearly an album Elton John made purely from the heart, to give Leon Russell the limelight back he deserves. As Elton says on the DVD there are no egos involved in this. So this isn't a superstar pairing designed to make money (well not for Elton anyway). In many ways Leon is the star on this. Its his Piano fills and licks that feature, where Eltons Piano playing is mostly relegated to rhythm parts - and thats how Elton wanted it.

The songs are written mainly by Elton, Leon and Bernie Taupin and there are some absolute corkers on here. The album starts with the wistful/romantic Piano introduction to Leon's "If it wasn't for bad", which turns into a great little rock tune. Leon (with Bernie Taupin) also contributes another standout track "I should have sent Roses". This is a marvellous song with an aching melody.

However if you think that Elton is outclassed by his hero you'd be completely wrong. "Hey Ahab" is a wonderfully rocking Gospel feel track and the Civil War ballad "Gone to Shiloh" is another standout from Elton and Bernie. A special mention for Neil Youngs contribution on this track, which gives it very much a Band like feel with three different vocalists taking the lead.

If I was being very critical I'd say there are a few tracks which seem like fillers - the sort of thing that would have appeared on a normal Elton John album (so still fine songs). However even these are lifted by the arrangements and T-Bone Burnetts production.

So where to place this in the cannon of these two great artists. Leon hasn't recorded the sheer volume that Elton has and so it must rate amongst his best, though not as good as his eponymous 1970 album. Not much is!

The last ten years have been very good for Elton. The return to form of "Songs from the West Coast" (2001) and "The Captain and the Kid" (2006) mean that you can't just dismiss those albums. But overall this is better than those two, and in a different league to most of his 1980s and 90s material. Even "Two Low for Zero" which I recently bought on CD isn't in the same class. So yes you have to go back to the 70s to find better Elton John albums and even then theres only a few that match or better this.

reviewText:
The compliments I can pay to LCD Soundsystem's "This is Happening" are bountiful, but they all boil down to one thing: If you don't find your head bobbing at least once while listening to it, then check your pulse.

Murphy is an active DJ in the New York music scene. Along with British producer Tim Goldsworthy he makes up DFA, a record label and production team that has produced albums by bands such as The Rapture and Radio 4. As time went on, Murphy also began releasing singles under the LCD Soundsystem moniker. Three albums later, here we are.

Every previous LCD Soundsystem release has received almost universal critical acclaim, and this most recent one is no exception. First came 2005's "LCD Soundsystem." It was made up of two discs -- one compiling all of the singles released up to that point and the other comprised of entirely new material. Next came 2007's "Sound of Silver," and finally, we have 2010's "This Is Happening." What exactly is happening, I don't know. But what I do know is that it's awesome.

According to LCD Soundsystem's biography at RollingStone, Murphy says this will be the last LCD Soundsystem release. I hope, for all of our sakes, that this does not end up happening. But if it is the last we see of Murphy as LCD Soundsystem, then this album was one heck of a way to go out with a bang.

"This Is Happening," like "Sound of Silver," has only nine tracks. That may seem like a ripoff, but given the fact that seven of the nine tracks clock in at over six minutes -- one is even 9:06 -- it balances out.

But lengthy songs can be a bit overwhelming. If they don't vary or stay interesting musically, they can provide a lot of "Is this over yet?" moments.

Long songs need to feel like they are taking you somewhere or that something is being built up to. None of the songs on this album feel long; they feel like they're going somewhere. Take the album's opener "Dance Yrself Clean." In the first three minutes, you know something big is coming. Sure enough, a beat with a deep synth drops around the 3:06 mark. Then, at the end, it loops back around to the simple feel of the beginning -- just Murphy's voice with some single tones and percussion. Very tastefully done, indeed. I appreciate being able to tell when an artist values my full attention for an entire song. I can tell that James Murphy cared deeply about that with every song on this album.

The song "I Can Change" is just plain fun. There are all sorts of interesting video game-esque sound effects, the beat is a perfect mixture between laid back and hammering, and the chord progression is simplicity at its best. Well, it really isn't a chord progression at all but rather the same two root notes alternating back and forth for the entire song. Like I said, simple but great.

I think one of the main reasons the music of LCD Soundsystem appeals to me is because of its melting pot of electronica, dance and rock mixed with Murphy's quirky lyrics. And believe me, the lyrics do not disappoint on "This Is Happening." The song "Pow Pow" stands out not only because it has an awesome beat, but because Murphy literally just plays off of the phrase, "From this position..." for the entire song. Two of my favorite examples are "From this position, I totally get how the decision was reached," and "From this position, I feel affinity for both of them, which is confusing." I really have no idea what he's getting at or what meaning he is driving for, but it doesn't matter because it's random and appealing regardless.

The final track of the album, "Home," feels like a sequel to "Dance Yrself Clean." The overtones and chord progression feel the same and the vocal drawl that is interspersed throughout is almost identical to the one used in the album's opener. I love this idea as a way to end an album. It helps with the cohesiveness of the experience. It's like we're getting closure, as if we're coming full circle.

I'm not a good dancer by any means, and you would almost never see me in a club of any sort. But if, by some freak occurrence, I were in a club and any of the songs from this record came on, I would be the first on the dance floor.

It would indeed be a shame if this were the last we heard from LCD Soundsystem. But it's a safe bet to assume that "This Is Happening" will crop up again on several Best of 2010 lists, and I'd even go so far as to say we'll hear of it again in several years on some Best of the Decade lists.

reviewText:
Sociologically as well as musically the Butterfield Blues Band holds a singular place in American music. They didn't just help begin the driving of the blues through mainstream America's front doors, they kicked open doors for the bluesmen who taught most of its membership the music and the soul thereof, when the key founders were teenagers or collegians captured by Chicago's teeming blues community and circuit and caught the attention---and, often, the mentoring---of the veterans who made that community with their earnestness and savvy. (Stories of the Butterfield band refusing to accept certain bookings unless their blues idols were booked likewise are still legion.) They were also one of the first racially mixed blues groups, were unapologetic in their attack and their presentation, and most of all knew what they were doing once they got the chance to record the material that made them a Chicago club mainstay.

Very little of Butterfield's work has stayed out of print, and everything included here from the sessions for what should have been their first album has since joined up with the remainder to form the famous "lost album" sessions disc. That alone might have superceded this anthology, one of the best such sets assembled, but this anthology will work well for anyone who just wants the meat of the Butterfield legacy, even if a few hardcore favourites---the incendiary jam, "Screamin'," from the seminal first album, being the most notable---are missing here.

Disc One is devoted entirely to the first Butterfield era and, "Screamin'" aside, the absolute best of it is here, including the rip-snorting "Born in Chicago"; the randy "Shake Your Moneymaker"; the harrowing "I Got a Mind to Give Up Livin'" (on which Mike Bloomfield showed once and for all that he wasn't kidding around as the first and in many ways best of the mid-1960s white blues guitar stars); the exuberant "Work Song" (where the entire Butterfield band, Mk2---jazz-oriented Billy Davenport having replaced Sam Lay in the drum chair---showed they weren't kidding about jazzing the blues without pretense); the steady-rolling "Blues With a Feeling," on which Butterfield proves he's up to the challenge of his idol Little Walter as a harmonica stylist and Bloomfield peels off his customary, sleekly melodious lines; and, of course, the groundbreaking "East-West," which ushered in the jam as a serious blues-rock motif and ran the gamut from raw blues to free jazz to raga and back while providing both a confirmation party for Bloomfield and a coming-out party for Elvin Bishop, whose opening solo slot is even more promising than the turn he took in the final third of "Work Song." Paring down the best of "The Paul Butterfield Blues Band" and "East-West," the first two albums, the original Butterfield band lived up to its legend.

Disc Two covers the post-Bloomfield editions of the group, with Butterfield bringing in horns and experimenting as much with soul and jazz as with blues. Bishop comes into his own as a guitarist and Butterfield reimagines himself as a bandleader, a process he'd begun with "East-West," giving his musicians even more of their own head than he'd already begun hinting and getting mostly affirmative results, particularly their bristling "One More Heartache" and their freewheeling live performance of another Little Walter track, "Everything's Gonna Be Alright." Some of the experiments didn't work as well as others, but for the most part Butterfield---who'd lose Bishop after "In My Own Dream" and never again had a guitarist as distinctive as either of his two originals---keeps his swelling eclecticism from interfering with the execution. In Gene Dinwiddie he had an empathetic horn section leader, and between them the pair guided the band through the rest of its existence with music equal in caliber, if not quite in legend, to the original band, even if something essential was lost when bassist Bugsy Maugh and drummer Philip Wilson departed.

Butterfield's own musicianship never suffered through any of those changes, even to the point where he still sounded vital and sure while blowing his harmonica on music that could barely if at all be called blues. Which testifies to the depth of his talent and the dilemna: often as not, his ambition was larger than his resources, and it helped cost the band the success its original rendition enjoyed, though they enjoyed a brief revival after a splendid set at Woodstock. But he left a wealth of fascinating music regardless. And if you're not inclined to listen to the entire Elektra catalog, this anthology puts almost all the Butterfield Blues Band music you'd ever need into one intelligent place. It won't do a thing for his estate (he died in 1987), but sooner or later it should help get him inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

(Clarity time: The whole Butterfield band wasn't up there with Bob Dylan for the infamous Newport Folk Festival set, though the entire band did play at a blues workshop that was part of the festival. Butterfield himself didn't play with Dylan, but Bloomfield, bassist Jerry Arnold, and drummer Sam Lay did, with Blues Project leader Al Kooper behind the organ.)

Some Kansas fans felt that Masque didn't measure up to Song for America. Still, the next album was highly anticipated as Kansas' popularity among Midwestern high school teens was still very high. Their loyalty was rewarded with the release of Leftoverture. The lead off single, Carry On My Wayward Son, blasted over the airwaves and attracted a new legion of fans. At the time, many fans felt that Leftoverture was at least equal to if not surpassing Song For America. You're not going to find pristine vinyl copies laying around these parts. This album was played to death.

Leftoverture continues the practice started on Masque, a mixture of short rock songs among longer prog pieces. What's missing here are the straight forward rock numbers that showed up on earlier albums - songs like Bringing It Back, Down The Road, Lonely Street and It Takes A Woman's Love. The shorter songs are more prog than rock, featuring many prog and classical flourishes.

With Leftoverture and the national success of Carry On, Kansas won back any fans confused by Masque and gained a lot more. I would go so far as to say this was Kansas' finest moment.

If you know Kansas from a greatest hits collection and are looking for the full album experience, I'd start here.

Say what you will about John Mellencamp ... and I'll say that "No Better Than This" is a hauntingly beautiful collection of music, deeply steeped in pure Americana lyrics, floating on simple elegant chords that will reach in and caress your heart, stuttering your voice, and shifts like a warm breeze from across the desert.  This is twilight music, designed for the setting sun, crafted to slow dance with the one you love, or to rock back on two legs of a weathered chair, balanced between here, there, and nowhere.

This album was vintage the second it was laid down, these songs are the stuff of history, honest, simple, and recorded with T Bone Burnett on an old Ampex reel-to-reel recorder, just like they used to do, before things were polished to the point of being uninteresting.  This stuff is worthy of Woody Guthrie, or any number of artists who's ghosts still roam the low end of the radio dial late into the night.  So say what you will about John Mellencamp, but you've got to give him his due here on "No Better Than This," a delightful treasure that's gonna ride with you like the snap-button plaid flannel shirt you've been wearing nonstop since you found it in the local second hand shoppe.

reviewText:
When I heard Springsteen was going to release an album filled with folk covers inspired by the work of Pete Seeger I felt apprehensive. Seeger's recordings are often dull affairs, more interesting as historical document than as album for listening pleasure. Springsteen himself has been known to produce equally droning folk inspired material. Both The Ghost of Tom Joad and Devils and Dust featured material that was melodically uninteresting and needed to be saved by compelling lyrics. So a Seeger album by Springsteen had al the potential for a major disappointment.

All said the end result is quite the opposite. The record is lively and a whole lot of fun to listen to. The music was recorded live in his living room, with the horn section in the hall. You can tell the musicians are really having a ball. The record is about making music first and foremost. The music is nothing like you've heard from Springsteen before. It's as much traditional country as jazz. Where most of Springsteen music is very much thought trough this record sounds spontaneous and absolutely electrifying. It's Funky and joyous. It's a feast.

The choice of songs is interesting. Each and every one of these songs are traditionals. Some of them have been recorded many times over the years. Shenandoah has been put to wax over 260 times in the past 30 years. Yet others as My Oklahoma Home have rarely seen the light of day. Some of the songs Springsteen picked are still relevant to day. Mrs. McGrath is a protest song against the war. Knowing Bruce's stand on the war in Iraq I suspect this is hardly accidental. Some songs have been brought somewhat up to date. In Pay me my Money Down we can hear Springsteen sing "I wish I were Mr. Gates, I'd haul my money in by crates". Mary Don't You Weep has been kept in his traditional form. Others still as the children song Froggie Went A Courting only seem there for comic relief or to show how diverse the canon of traditional American music is.

Although the record doesn't feature any original Springsteen compositions I'm inclined to call it an essential album. Not necessarily because it's Springsteen but because it's Springsteen doing these songs. These songs have the potential to reach a millions audience for the very first time because of him. In recording these songs Springsteen plays an important part in keeping this American tradition alive.

reviewText:
This is surely one of the most rewarding and valuable sets in the catalogue of recorded music. Edgar Varse was hardly a very productive composer, but the music he did compose comprise some of the most innovative works ever penned. Indeed, a case could be made for the claim that Varse almost single-handedly and without precedents (well, there are traces of Italian futurism, Stravinsky, and Scriabin, at least) reinvented music and the techniques for constructing artworks in sound, and most of his innovations were made decades before anyone else attempted anything similar - to a certain extent, Varse embodied the radical avant-gardism of the 1960s some generations before it existed, but as opposed to at least some of the contemporary American ultramodernists his music isn't merely novel but of consistent high quality.

That does not mean that there isn't a romantic streak in Varse's music (despite his interest in mathematical structures as the basis of compositions), but it is a kind of modern romanticism preoccupied with the vastness of space or the strangeness of the world of microphysics, the possibility of new horizons and with exploration. You will look in vain for strong melodies or themes in Varse's music; this is music based on musical or rhythmic gestures, and whatever melodic fragments may occur (especially in the earlier works) function as parts of these (geometrical) gestures rather than being the main focus; this is music of cubes, spheres, curves and shapes interacting with each other, colliding or being pierced and punctured by other intervening blocks, at one point investigating the geometrical properties of the music, at another the topological properties.

But not all of the music is particularly "difficult". The relatively early Amriques and Arcana are relatively approachable (though utterly original), and the first disc opens with the hilariously witty sound study "Tuning Up" (a draft realized by Chou Wen-Chung, and possibly a take on Varse's interpretation of the public perception of his music). Amriques, for large orchestra (with added percussion), here given in its original version but with the added central part for the ondes martenot, sounds like a huge, elemental take on Stravinsky's Rite of Spring, punctuated by massive crescendos, monstrous dissonances and percussive polyphony. It may actually be the easiest Varse work to start with, and it can hardly fail to bowl over any listener coming fresh to Varse.

The famous Pome lectronique (for tape) was created for the Brussels World Fair in 1958 and depicts an evolving musical landscape designed to explore the listener's perception of space. To be honest it may sound just a tad dated (at least in this realization), but it still makes an impact. Arcana (1925-27), on the other hand, based on an ide fixe, develops the style of Amriques further, and is a slightly static (not necessarily in a negative sense) work of constant climaxes and bold juxtapositions. Nocturnal, however, is somewhat disappointing. It was Varse's last (incomplete) work, and more personal than most of them - it is a dark, disturbing setting of words and phrases from Anas Nin's "House of Incest", but sounds unfinished and even somewhat inconsequential, like the first sketches of an still undeveloped idea.

The second disc continues with Offrandes, Hyperprism and Octandre, more modest works for smaller ensembles but exploring (elements of) the same soundworld as Amriques; rewarding, remarkable works they are, if less earth-shattering than Amriques itself. Intgrales sounds like the embodiment of a mechanical nightmare, though offset by some beautiful, lyrical but slightly ambiguous melody. Ecuatorial (1934) is a setting of a prayer from the sacred book of the Maya Quiche, the Popul Vu, and is an absorbing study in primitistic, elemental force, strangeness and fervor.

Ionisation for 13 percussion players (1929-31) was described by one critic as "a sock in the jaw". It is based on rhythmic cells being expanded and permuted and is apparently inspired by the ionization of molecules. You have never heard anything like it (though it apparently owes something to Italian futurism), and it remains one of the most striking compositions ever created - Frank Zappa has claimed that Ionisation inspired him to pursue a career in music. Density 21.5 (named after the density of platinum) for solo flute is an exploration of space and time, and uses registral contrasts to effect polyphonic continuity (Sean Hickey) - it is another of Varse's works that sound like nothing else, and if you think unaccompanied flute primarily presents severe aural limitations, this work will surely make you think again. Dserts (1954) was something of a late breakthrough for the composer. It is an entirely novel take on "musique concrete" melding "everyday noises" into a remarkable sonic sculpture.

As bonuses we get two versions of the early song "Un grand sommeil noir", one with piano accompaniment, one with orchestral accompaniment. This is apparently the only one of Varse's early works to survive, and it is a beautiful, late-romantic work that, despite its different style, seems to embody much of Varse's musical philosophy. We also get Chou Wen-Chung's realization of the strangely delicate Dances for Burgess, a sort of impression of the echoes of a dance, though apparently with a touch of spiteful sarcasm thrown in.

Importantly, the performances are absolutely impeccable - revelatory, even. Not only does Chailly display deep understanding for and commitment to the music (and all of it, despite the stylistic development and diversity), but the Concertgebouw provides immaculate performances, full of wild, unbridled power (the performances exhibit more passion and fervor than any alternatives I have heard of any of the works) combined with utter attention to detail and textural subtleties and colors. The sound is wonderful as well. Indeed, this is a set that should be acquired, studied and savored by any music lover, regardless of the kind of music one's taste gravitates towards. Now, the extent to which Chou Wen-Chung's tinkerings and realizations fully capture every aspect of Varse's vision can of course be discussed, but as an aural experience this set is without peers. A must.

reviewText: I have been listening to this album for over 40 years; I remember my parents buying it for me when I was in kindergarten and it has been a regular holiday favorite ever since.  When I bought my first CD player, this was one of the first holiday recordings I purchased to replace my old vinyl collection.  Alvin and the gang are here in force - singing with glee.  But one thing that gets little mention are the fabulous orchestral arrangements, which are rich, intricate and worthy of any of the crooners which graced the recording industry at the time (Sinatra included).  The "White Christmas" arrangement is probably my favorite version - above and beyond even Crosby's iconic recording.  It is one of the most beautiful treatments of that song ever recorded.  The other songs are equally well presented and one can't forget that wonderful "Chipmunk Christmas Song" that has never gone out of fashion.  Now I treat my nieces and nephews to this album - and they like it as well.  I only wish some channel would re-run the old "Alvin Show" so that they can see the wonderful cartoons this was based on.
label: positive

reviewText:
Bottom-Line: Mind, Body & Soul is a beautiful, soul sophomoric release for Joss Stone.  R&B lives within this young lady from Devon England and I for one am glad it does.

One of my favorite genres of music Rhythm & Blues (R&B) is going through a revival of sorts.  When I was going through my teens in the 70's, groups like The Commodores, Ohio Players, and my beloved Earth, Wind & Fire--a group I still consider the greatest R&B group of their generation--graced the airwaves.  Their music was sane, it made sense, it spoke to the cultural and social upheavals of the day without being disrespectful; these men had talent, they could sing, they could actually play instruments, they embodied soul.  The artist that replaced them by-and-large lack and lacked the aura and talent these groups possessed; when Justin Timberlake is referred to as an R&B artist, you know the genre has lost it luster, and is wandering aimlessly in search of spirit.  Recording a true R&B album takes a special something, called, well soul, one has to feel the music, live the music, not merely got through the motions of lyrical recitation.  The lack of soul shines through in every song, fore soul is felt on both ends, artist and listener share a bond, without which a song no matter how well song, lacks emotive meaning.  Which brings me to Joss Stone.

It is for the above stated reasons that it is a rare occasion these days that I am actually inspired by any artist enough to actually pay real money for a whole CD.  But once and a while a true artist comes along who rocks my world, literally.  Such is the case with 17 year old blond haired British phonon Joss Stone. Looking like she just walked off a the pages of Teen Cosmos, Ms. Stone's outer wrapping suggest yet another spiritless (white) wannabe, but her soul tells a different story altogether.  As I mused in my review of Ms. Stones first release, The Souls Sessions, could Joss be Christina's (Christina Aguilera that is) sister in wholesome packaging?

I first heard Ms. Stone, or should I say heard of Joss Stone in Newsweek of all places.  And then on one of those rare occasions when I was actually listening to something other then NPR on my car radio, I heard to one her new releases from Mind, Body & Soul, Right to Be Wrong, and I was hooked.  So I went to the beginning and I placed an order with BMG.com for her debut CD The Soul Sessions--a collection or rare R&B classics--that very evening.  After listening to the CD continuously for about two weeks to and from work, I purchased her second release, Mind, Body & Soul.
Joss Stone's sophomore release Mind, Body & Soul is a collection of sweet soulful tunes (mostly ballads which are defiantly Joss's forte) that cement her position as one the new--authentic--voices of female R&B.  Mind, Body & Soul follows the same laidback formula that made The Soul Session such a sensational album; the old-fashion instrumentation; the attention to musical detail; the almost perfect harmony between lyric and music, between voice and instruments.
Thankfully there is no sweeping revision here, in Mind, Body & Soul Joss still works with many of the same musicians she did on The Soul Sessions; indeed the album was produced by the same team of Steve Greenberg and soul veteran Betty Wright.  Ms. Wright (background vocals) along with Willie "Little" Beaver (Drums), and Nile Rogers (Fender Rhodes) headline a whole roster of excellent musicians and vocalists who back Ms. Stone on this album.  And while Mind, Body & Soul's tenor emulates Ms. Stone's first album there are some subtle shifts in tone and feel sprinkled throughout the CD.  The CD isn't as quite and purposeful as The Soul Sessions, Joss's voice isn't always at center stage; it has been tones down for certain songs.  And this album is more commercial than The Soul Sessions; certain songs are a little brighter as of they were produced for radio play, there's a more pronounced hip-hop vibe to some beats.  The third cut on the album You Had Me, is a perfect example of this.  The lyrics are sharp and contemporary and the music, defiantly speaks hip-hop with its heavy bass riff and gyrating back beat.

You Had Me (Partial Lyrics)

You had me
You lost me
You're wasted
You cost me

Spitting in my eyes and I still see
Tried to keep me down
I'm breaking free
I don't want no part in your next fix
Someone needs to tell you this is it

Hey listen you'll be missin'
Out on all my love and my kissing
Make your mistakes on your own time
When you come down you're just no good to have around
Instead of making money you took mine

Chorus
You had me
You lost me
You're wasted
You cost me
I don't want you here messing with my mind
I've realized in time
that my eyes are not blind
I've seen it before
I'm taking back my life...

...Vodka and a packet of cigarettes
That's all it used to be but now
You're sniffing on snow when you're feeling low
Suffocating dreams that could have been
Maybe for a minute I was down with that
But it didn't take long for me to see the light
You swore you had control of it
But when I stepped back you slipped on your supply

And Joss sounds a little more like a diva this time around, her voice is a little more seasoned, more nuanced--not enough that fans of The Soul Session will feel alienated, but enough to win some new ones.  Speaking of Joss' voice, where did it come from, where does she get the depth and feeling that coats her young voice with so much emotional spirit?  How did she end up singing R&B; a white girl from England?  Or are these questions important?  I think not, what is important is that she speaks to me, to my soul, she does what a musical artist is supposed to do, speak to me soul, make love to my emotions and make my heart smile and cry all in the same span of time.

Mind, Body & Soul speaks to me; the album has a seductive, sultry, but not overtly sexy feel to it.  The production is smooth and glides by the ears like silk, but there is some genuine grit to the rhythms.  All of the songs, some co-written by Joss, are good, there is no filler here; indeed I enjoyed almost all of the songs.  The lyrics are solidly written and catchy, each building one the one that preceded it.  Joss has come into her own on this album, she owns every song, every line of lyric, though she does have a tendency to over-embellish ever so slightly, she is careful not to over do it, and in the end possesses a rich, resonant voice that's a sheer joy to hear and experience.

My favorite track in an album filled with favorites is track 6, Less is More.  The beat is irresistible, and has a reggae/calypso back beat that is immediately appealing.  And this song personifies the attention to detail the producers of this album paid on every track.  The occasional, almost whisper of trumpet in the background is for me intoxicating; I just love brass instruments in any song, the Joss's (do you think she'll forgive me for being so familiar) voice blends perfectly with the music.  The lyrics are again contemporary, with occasional inner-city lexicon to lend legitimacy to the track.  The overall effect is almost hypnotic.

From opening note to last, Mind, Body & Soul is intoxicating, smooth, soulful, fresh, and just plain fun to listen to.  Joss's voice is more subdued on this album, but it still takes center stage, as the instrumentation blends perfectly with her soulful renditions of this new R&B material.  Where again did Joss develop the emotional depth she displays in every song?  This is the question I keep asking myself as the satisfied smile stayed fixed to my lips, and my head swayed to and fro, track after delicious track.

Mind, Body & Soul is in the final analysis, a beautiful emotion laden sophomoric release for Joss Stone.  R&B lives within this young lady from Devon England and I for one am glad it does.  And like The Soul Sessions, even the CD cover art involves the funk, soulful vibe of the seventies.  Again, Joss Stone has a clear winner Mind, Body & Soul.  The CD, like The Soul Sessions before it, is well worth the cost of admission, and if you enjoy the sound of real music, real soulful inflection, real talent, then Mind, Body & Soul for you.
label: positive

This cd is truely an amazing piece of work!!  If you've liked any of Brad's work in the past, 5th Gear will not disappoint.  It has its share of ballads, it has humourous songs, and it has songs that make you want to crank the radio up and drive fast!!  There's a nice instrumental too!

My favorite track is definately "Online."  It will surely be released as a single with it's clever look at the way people's identity changes when they login on their computer.  A 5'3" man who is overweight and still lives at home with his mom, suddenly transforms into a 6'5" hunk when he goes online.  It's just plain hilarious!!

Another track worth mentioning is "Letter to Me."  This track is what the singer would say to himself at the age of 17.  The lyrics speak of life-lessons.  This is one of his more senitmental songs.  It really describes the thought process of a young man at 17.  It is somewhat inspirational in that it describes the mindset of a 17 year old and how things seem so tough at that age, but having aged a bit, he's learned that things will only get better from there!!  wow, what a song!

If you're into ballads, you will fall in love with "It Did."  It is obviously a slower song.  It describes several of life's little moments and how you think it can't possibly get better at the time, but guess what? It does!!! yay!

There are several fun songs on this album, besides "TICKS" and "Online".  "I'm still a guy" looks at the differences between a woman and a man.  It mentions all the things a woman will do to a man to make him more feminized, but in the end, he's still a guy.  There are some really great lyrics on this track, but I don't want to give it away so go get the album!!

Lastly, I'd just like to say that you don't have to be a Brad Paisley fan, or even a country fan to find something on this album that you will enjoy.  The spectrum of songs is so vast that there is something for everyone.  What are you waiting for?  Get this album, you will be amazed! "*****"
