reviewText:
Mark Lanegan is the type of artist who couldn't be dull if he tried. From his days in the great unheralded Screaming Trees whose masterpiece "Dust" should be force fed our children in public schools through to collaborations with Isobel Campbell, Josh Homme and Greg Dulli he positively oozes class and has charisma to spare. His most potent weapon however is that borderline death yowl of a baritone which has survived a heavy drug dependency over the years and can tackle blues, hard rock and folk and make it sound effortless. It is a tremendous asset and it is on full display in this scintillating new album in which "shock horror" Lanegan tackles disco head on and succeeds with arrogant aplomb. It is Lanegan of course and the album is about as dark as Kazumura Cave without a flashlight containing much of his best work since god knows when.

It all quicks off with verve on the pounding blues of "The Gravediggers Song" with almost an Adam Ant style drum back beat and a brooding vocal so nasty that social services should be called. Throughout there are a range of cracking songs and the classic blues motif spread over the six minutes plus of "Bleeding Muddy Waters" is one of those. "St Louis Elegy" is a beautifully dark beast with a feast of ferocious imagery while that is clearly a Visage style disco beat lurking inthe backdrop of the excellent "Grey goes black". As you can tell it really is difficult to single out any songs for special praise since there is strength in depth here and taken as a whole set Lanegan barely puts a foot wrong. "Riot in my house" for example echoes the best rocking preoccupations of the Screaming Trees and what higher recommendation do you need? One of the longest tracks here "Ode to a Sad Disco" could be profitably covered by Donna Summer and it would be equally great, it has that sort of pounding synth electronica combined with high melody which New Order once patented. At over six minutes it passes at great speed and shows an artist prepared to take risks and not so much rest on his laurels as burn them. By the time the standout long concluding track "Tiny grain of truth" ends the album in a mix of first class acoustic blues and concludes in a wave of synths you know you have been on one of the more interesting musical journeys on a "Deep Black Vanishing Train" in quite a long time and you have thankful that Lanegan picked you up at the station. Add to this that in songs like the "Quiver Syndrome" he displays a ear for melody which would take any other artist in the direction of the album chart top ten and squat there for age.

There is enough musical variety in "Blues Funeral" to stage the album in the Radio City Music Hall. It is gritty, exciting, threatening and shows this great singer on top of his game. This is an album that grabs you by the collars on your first listen and eyeballs you to ensure your full attention. It is time well spent for this album deserves tractor loads of praise and a generous potion of hyperbole. How many singers do you know who can can away with a line like "if tears were liquor/I'd have drunk myself sick" and yet you know that he sings this with the raw honesty of a man who has ridden the emotional and chemical roller coaster yet emerged the other side all the better a musician for it. The musical stakes are raised for 2012.

reviewText:
As a huge fan of EPMD, Erick and Parrish Making Dollars, for any old school hip hop novices out there, I was introduced to Redman on EPMD's "Business As Usual" CD on a track called "Hardcore".  He definitely delivered a nice verse and he also gave a nice performance on "Brothers On My Jock" which was featured on the same CD as well.  Redman's 1st solo CD, "Whut? The Album" was released in 1992 and I still remember the cassette maxisingle that I purchased when I was in high school that had 2 versions of his first single, "Blow Your Mind" and another track, "How To Roll A Blunt".  Once I purchased this CD it was definitely in heavy rotation as Erick Sermon produced a masterpiece and Redman kept your attention with his clever wordplay and his humorous stories.  My favorite songs ended up being "Time 4 Sum Aksion", "So Ruff", "Watch Yo Nuggets" w/Erick Sermon, "Tonight's Da Night" and "A Day Of Sooperman Lover".  'Til this day, "Whut? Thee Album is my favorite Redman CD of all time.  One of my favorite Redman collaborations of all time, "Head Banger" was featured on EPMD's next CD entitled "Business Never Personal".  "Head Banger" also featured K-Solo and that track may contain Redman's best verse of all time.  Redman's next solo disc, "Dare Iz A Darkside" was released in 1994.  The 1st single, "Rockafella" gave you an indication that this CD would be different from his first, but the CD still ended up being a classic.  "Journey Throo Da Darkside", "A Million And One Buddah Spots", "Cosmic Slop" w/Erick Sermon & Keith Murray, "Can't Wait", "Tonite's Da Nite (Remix) and the hilarious "Green Island" ended up being my favorite tracks.  However, just as "Whut Thee Album", "Dare Iz A Darkside" could be played in its entirety.  Redman's 3rd solo disc "Muddy Waters" was released in 1996.  The 1st single "It's Like That" (My Big Brother) featured K-Solo and the 2 MCs went back and forth over a track that was produced by Redman.  My favorite tracks ended up being "Pick It Up", "Creepin'" "Do What U Feel" w/Method Man, "Da Bump" and "Whateva Man" which featured Erick Sermon.  If you are a Redman fan these 3 CDs in any order should be your favorite Redman CDs.  After the singles ran it's course: "It's Like That", "Whateva Man" and "Pick It Up", Redman recorded one of my favorite tracks from him of all time in "Funkorama".  The track was released on a CD entitled "Insomnia" which was actually an Erick Sermon compilation CD.  The track sampled the Tribe Called Quest song "Midnight" from the "Midnight Marauders" CD that actually gave a shout out to Redman during the song.  Redman's 4th solo CD, "Doc's Da Name 2000" was released in 1998 and the first single ended up being the hilarious "I'll Be Dat".  My favorite tracks ended up being "Get It Live", "Da Goodness" w/Busta Rhymes, "Keep On '99", "I Don't Kare", and "Brick City Mashin'".  A year later Redman and Method Man released "Blackout" after the success of their collaboration "How High".  That CD also created  the infamous "Da Rockwilder". "Y.O.U.", "Cereal Killer", and "Run For Cover" which featured Ghostface Killah and Streetlife.  In 2001, Redman dropped his 5th solo CD, "Malpractice".  While I enjoyed the 2 singles, "Let's Get Dirty" and "Smash Sumthin'" there was something that was missing from this Redman album.  It didn't have the same appeal and playability as his first 4 solo CDs and "Blackout" did.

FINALLY and I mean FINALLY, Redman is back 6 years later with his 6th solo CD, "Red Gone Wild".  After several delays and hardly any promotion, Redman is back!!!!  His 1st single is "Put It Down" and it is produced by Timbaland.  Redman's energy level is where you expect it to be and you will definitely be bobbing your head as you are driving and listening to this track.  "Fire" serves as an intro and just as reviewer "ctrx" states its basically a song letting you know that Redman is back and hopefully here to stay and to not wait 6 years between another solo release.  Dr. Trevis makes a guest appearance to introduce intro #2 "Bak Inda Buildin".  Just as "Dare Iz A Darkside" did with "Bobyahed2dis" and "Journey Throo Da Darkside", "Fire" and "Bak Inda Buildin" really are just an extended intro.  Pete Rock shows up to produce "Gimme One" and Redman takes advantage of the Pete Rock track as Ghotsface did on "Fishscale" on the tracks "R.A.G.U." and "Be Easy", with his clever wordplay.  "Sumtn 4 Urrbody" allows some time for other members in the Gillahouse clique to get their shine.  Rockwilder shows up to produce the funky "How U Like Dat" which has an impressive verse from Gov Matic as well.  Scott Storch dumbs things down a tad bit on "Freestyle Freestyle" as the track doesn't sound like anything he has produced before.  However, Redman's lyrics will have you forgetting all about the beat by the time you get to the end of the track.  "Walk In Gutta" features Erick Sermon and Keith Murray and it is nice to hear the Def Squad altogether on a track in the year 2007.  Although, I am sure that this was recorded before this year.  You'll be hard pressed to find a Erick Sermon, Redman or Keith Murray aphilliated CD that doesn't have these artists on atleast one track on that CD.  Melanie Rutherford stops by to drop some smooth vocals on "Wutchoogonnado".  Redman continues with the clever word play and this track is definitely in my Top 5 for this CD.  Just as Erick Sermon did with Marvin Gaye's voice on "Music" he does the same favor for Redman and Al Green on "Rite Now".  The track is definitely my favorite track on "Red Gone Wild".  The track is edited however which was probably a provision made by Al Green so the sample could be cleared for this track.  On "Blow Treez", Redman employs Ready Roc and Method Man to help him talk about his favorite girl, "Mary Jane".  While the track is nice, you will definitely remember the other tracks where he covered this territory before like "How To Roll A Blunt", Muddy Waters' "Smoke Buddah" and the infamous "How High".  "Merry Jane" does the exact same thing to less results with Snoop Dogg and Nate Dogg also.  Rockwilder is back once again with "Hold Dis Blaow".  This track will definitely get your attention and you will definitely be hitting the repeat button after you hear this track for the 1st time.  "Pimp Nutz" will have you doing the same thing as Redman, also known as Reggie Noble, adds another alias to his collection.  I heard "Gillahouse Check" a few years back when I heard another track "Rush The Security".  I personally like the track but some people will be turned off buy the foreign guy talking junk at the beginning of the track.  The oddest beat on "Red Gone Wild" clearly goes to "Get 'Em" which features Saukarates and Icadon.  However, I feel that the track will grow on you after awhile and you will still want to check it out.

As you all definitely know by now, no Redman CD is complete without a tale of The Sooperman Lover.  While this may not be better than some of the earlier ones Redman, Melanie Rutherford and E3 definitely add flavor to the collection.  Redman even employs Hurricane G, who I haven't even heard since Dare Iz A Darkside's "We Run NY", to deliver some nice lyrics on here as well.

Overall, "Red Gone Wild" is my favorite CD that has been released in 2007 so far.  Is this CD better than his earlier CDs, Not quite, but the CD can be played in its entirety and will definitely remind you of why you became a Redman fan in the 1st place.  Redman has also stated that he will release "Muddy Waters 2" by the end of the year.  Hopefully, that is the case.

reviewText: This is another true classic album of the early 70s that is generally overlooked by today's so-called classic rock radio stations - blues-rock at it's best. "Street Corner Talking" cooks from beginning to end."Tell Mama" is a rockin' anthem for drifters and losers. Savoy Brown's version of "Can't Get Next To You" is deep and powerful. If you turn it up loud, the Hammond organ will hit you right in the chest. "Wang Dang Doodle" is rowdy and dangerous. Ever had your heart broken? Open a beer and sulk along to "All I Can Do Is Cry". The title track of this album is infectious, as well as "Let It Rock". "Time Does Tell" sets some rather inane lyrics to some cool guitar riffs. Altogether, this is a great album - perhaps Savoy's best - that sounds as good today as it did three decades ago. Buy this CD and get it autographed by Kim Simmonds (he always obliges) when Savoy Brown comes to your town.

reviewText:
This remix CD is awesome.  It brings new life to songs that were just "eh" (especially Touch of My Hand, Early Mornin') and rejuvenates the best.  Here's a track-by-track breakdown:

1. Toxic (Reconstruction Mix) 6/5: This is the best remix of Toxic I've ever heard.  A pounding bass line and great synth match up to Britney's vocals and make one of her best songs even better.  You won't find another one like this.

2. Me Against the Music 5/5: This remix gives the song a rock edge that wasn't found on the original.  It pounds its way through and everything seems to come together a bit more than the original version.  Madonna's vocals aren't as pronounced, which is a great thing as well.

3. Touch of My Hand (Hamel Remix) 6/5: One of In the Zone's weakest songs, Touch of My Hand strived to be something bigger than it was.  But it just wasn't catchy.  This remix speeds things up and changes the song completely.  Using many of the original elements, it sounds like it belongs on the original album.  The vocals are mixed up a bit as well.  An excellent mix.

4. Breathe on Me 4/5: This remix isn't anything too spectacular.  The other remix by the same guy was featured on the GH bonus disc, which was really LOOOOOOONG and boring.  This one's a bit faster, but isn't much different from the original version.  A good mix, but could have been much better.

5. I'm a Slave 4 U (Slavedriver Mix) 6/5: One of the other best remixes.  It's a total reworking of Slave, with a pounding bassline, great new instrumentals and slightly faster vocals.  A truly great mix.  At just 5 minutes, you'll wish it was longer.

6. And Then We Kiss (Junkie XL Mix) 5/5: While the only version of the song heard, this song is actually really good.  A much better one than Someday, this song plays out really well.  What the original sounded like is anyone's guess, but this one is definitely a good start.

7. Everytime (Valentin Mix) 4/5: Not one of my favorite Everytime mixes (see the better Hi-Bias mix) it just sounds harsh and it doesn't match up to the vocals like it should.  The instruments are a bit too loud and drown out her voice a bit.

9. Early Mornin' 6/5: This mix has totally changed the song.  What was once annoying and always skipped has become a must-hear.  The funky guitar always playing in the background really drives the song forward, making it catchy and something you can actually listen to.

10. Baby One More Time (Ospina Mix) 3/5: I've never found a good remix of this song, and this definitely isn't one.  It's quite disappointing actually.  I have gotten used to it but I wish that it wasn't trying to be so funky.  Just a straight remix would be better.

11. Don't Let Me Be the Last to Know 6/5: This remix gave this song new life.  While I found the original version slightly annoying and forced, this made it fun and enjoyable.  It's an 8-minute song but doesn't feel like it.  One of my favorites.

The album is great, but could have been better with the inclusion of some more remixes, such as Stronger, Oops!, Do Somethin', Sometimes, etc.  Overall it's a great CD and you won't be disappointed.  Get it!!!

reviewText: Peter Gabriel Genesis and Phil Collins Genesis...for the most part, they are two different animals...both GREAT STUFF! And honestly, both "leaders" also had some "duds". So, with that said, I'm giving 'We Can't Dance' 5 stars to try and offset the undeserved current rating. Likewise, I wouldn't give 5 stars to an album that did not deserve it. This is a very good Genesis album that rates 5 in my mind, and not for the "hits"...though they are worthy. The real treasure with this album lies with the unknown songs. Driving the Last Spike, Fading Lights, Dreaming While You Sleep, Living Forever, etc...some of which contain some very cool "proggy" passages. Many other reviewers have rated the individual songs quite well, so I will simply say this album means a great deal to me and provokes many emotions within me (probably due to a "tricky" relationship I was going through when I first heard this CD). This is one of my favorite releases of the past 20 years, so beware of every review you read...you may miss out on something that might have become a treasured part of your collection/Life!  Jeff

on this piece of art. Excellent overall is all I can say. may even be better than 'Deadwing', which I didn't think was possible. This band is really special. I will break this one down, which I don't do often. but each track has its own unique quality.

Blackest Eyes - Great opener! Heavy, melodic and just gets it going perfect. 5/5

reviewText:
Let me begin by saying that most of the previous reviews were negative because they simply failed to read the lable where it clearly states "Dialogue Highlights with Original Score." It's visible right there on the cover illustration.

The original LP was a relic of it's time, where Shakespearean films and faux-Shakespearean films (like Beckett) often spawned albums which showcased dramatic scenes and dialogue highlights, backed by the score.

The liner notes for this CD even say that it was a phenomenon when teenagers of the 60's would put aside their pop albums and devote 45 minutes in rapt attention listening to actors their own age performing Shakespeare (BTW: There was another pressing issued at the time -a deluxe four LP set with illustrated booklet in a box featuring the entire film's audio track, issued to schools and libraries).

My only gripe (and it's barely even that) is that the music used is often not that which accompanied the scene. There are moments where music from another scene has been repositioned to bridge the edited dialogue sequences. It makes for a better "flow" but I miss some of the familiar "hits" that Rota worked into his score to accompany certain lines (like the discordant squeal when Lady Capulet appears).

Summing up, this is an excellent CD and should actually be in every home library along with the DVD of the film. It is far superior in most respects to the Leo & Claire version under any circumstances. It may come across as 'Shakespeare Lite' to some purists, and it is not the MUSIC soundtrack album, but it stands very well on its own.

The sound is clear and "present" -marred only by the excessive dubbed-in sound of the original film's dialogue tracks. The stereo separation preserves the spread of the music as well as the 60's period left-right channel spread of sound effects, movement and dialogue.

For those who want the music only, there are two CDs out there you can look for (both of which I own).

The actual motion picture soundtrack in stereo is available on the Cloud Nine lable (deep red cover with a still of R&J touching palms at the feast).

A digital re-recording of the complete score was issued by Silva Screen and while it is very nice in that it presents every cue and in very clear sound, it fails to compare to the original in terms of performance (the vocals are awful) and lack of "feeling."

For the serious collector and R&J fan, you can also hunt down the deluxe 4 LP set [SWDR-289] Romeo & Juliet - The Complete Motion Picture Soundtrack Recording (which of course I also own). Transferred to CD it fits nicely on two CDs, so I don't know why some record company hasn't done so already.

reviewText:
SUPERUNKNOWN is one of the defining rock albums of the 1990's.  It is Soundgarden's 'magnum opus' if you will, and it foisted the band into the limelight like never before.  This album is menacing in sound and style.  The lyrics are generally depressing, although I would not put them on the same level as Alice In Chains 1992 release DIRT.  Never has depression sounded so good!  The band was able to craft some of its best songs, and arguably its best album here.  In fact, there isn't a single lousy track here.  Almost everything the band did here turned to gold.
The opener is acidic power/grunge rock at its best.  "My Wave" succeeds with a great guitar line and spiteful lyrics.  "Fell On Black Days" is a massive downer lyric wise; just when everything was starting to go well...etc, etc.  The guitar and bass lines in the song almost have a mourning sound to them as they weave in and out.  It's creepy.  The title track is one of the more -dare I say- 'poppy' tunes on the album, but it still carries the Soundgarden intensity ('...first they steal your mind and then they steal your...').  "Head Down" and "Black Hole Sun" are two of the albums standouts.  The latter contains one of those ultra-catchy choruses that you can't get out of your head and was turned into one of the more bizarre videos to ever air on MTV.  "Limo Wreck" explodes with anger and angst as Chris Cornell sings "I'm the wreck of you, I'm the death of you all!"  It's cathartic in a way.  "The Day I Tried to Live" begins with a singular bass line followed by Kim Thayil's ever-so-slight distortion and Cornell's voice.  The song grows into a monster of a tune with a great chorus.  "Fourth of July" and "Like Suicide" are probably the high points on the album.  The former contains a sludge-heavy guitar riff that pounds your eardrums.  The latter is surprisingly poignant and intriguing.  The guitar melodies after the chorus are beautiful.
SUPERUNKNOWN is pound-for-pound among the best hard rock albums of the last ten years.  I was not a fan of Soundgarden before this release, but I certainly followed them afterwards.  The band so surprised me with their ingenius song and lyric writing that I kept finding this album in my cd player years later.  A thoroughly amazing listening experience.
Essential.

reviewText:
"American Idol Season 3:  Greatest Soul Classics" showcases the talents of the 12 Finalists from Fox's American Idol's third season.  Each of the showcased 12 finalists performs a song individually and there is one group number.
What may surprise fans of the series is that even those performers deemed as the "weaker" of the group all turned in solid performances on the tracks making this a CD of definite keeper tracks.  Fans of American Idol and Motown will love the Idols and their takes on these old school classics.
Below are the 13 featured songs with my comments on the side:
THE TRACKS
1. "Chain of Fools" - Fantasia Barrino:  Outstanding rendition by the top rated Fantasia as she definitely puts the soul into it.
2. "Me and Mrs. Jones" - by George Huff:  The ever popular and outstanding Huff brings new life to this classic as his voice definitely puts the groove into Mrs. Jones.  One of MY favorites from this track.
3. "I Heard It Through the Grapevine" - by Diana DeGarmo:  Great rendition of this classic by Diana and her Southern twang.
4. "If You Don't Know Me By Now" - by LaToya London:  Good job by the top rated LaToya on this, smooth and subtle if not powerful.
5. "Neither One Of Us (Wants To Be The First To Say Goodbye)" - by Jennifer Hudson:  Not one of my favorites on the track and not really one of my favorites on the show but Jennifer definitely does a good job with the song.
6. "You Make Me Feel Brand New" - by Amy Adams:  Smooth version of this classic love song by the ooh to early departed Amy Adams, one of my personal favorite songs and one of my personal favorites from the track.
7. "(Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay" - by Matt Rogers.  Surprisingly well done track by Matt Rogers who does a fine job on the Otis Redding classic.
8. "Midnight Train to Georgia" - by Jasmine Trias:  Not really Jasmine's genre of music but she does a good job with it.
9. "My Girl" - by John Peter Lewis:  Again, another surprisingly well done performance by John Peter Lewis who does Motown proud with this rendition.
10. "Until You Come Back To Me (That's What I'm Gonna Do)" - by Camille Velasco:  Never heard this song before but Camille does a real catchy rendition with it as it's a perfect fit for her voice and style.
11. "Betcha By Golly, Wow" - by Leah Labelle:  Again, surprisingly a great rendition of this song as Leah's vocals and the background make it an infectious track.  One of my favorites.
12. "You Are Everything" - by John Stevens:  Not a bad track.  This isn't John's genre but his mellow laidback sound make this track a pretty decent serenade.
13. "Ain't No Mountain High Enough" - The Top 12 Finalists:  Motown never sounded better than the 12 Finalists kickin' it on this old school classic!!!
THE VERDICT:
Overall you get a SOLID bag of tracks.  What I found great about this track is that they arranged to songs to play to ALL of the Finalists strengths as even the "marginal" singers in the group still turned in solid performances in the track.  In my opinion there were no weak performances on the CD.  Here's my rundown:
Keepers:  George, Fantasia, Amy, Camille, "Ain't No Mountain High Enough"
Goods:  The rest
Bad:  None whatsoever
With no bad tracks on here and a truckload of classics and favorites this CD's a definite keeper.
If you were a fan of the show you'll definitely want to get this CD.  Even if you aren't an A.I. fan you'll definitely dig these new takes on some old classics.
Highly Recommended

Track list for this CD is as follows;
1. Your mind
2. Love hangover (Live @ BET 2007)

13. You got me (featuring The Roots)
14. Think Twice (featuring Roy Hargrove)
15. Ye-yo
16. Today
17. Never
18. Your precious love (featuring D'angelo)
(Note: tracks 17 and 18 are merged into one track)

I came across this CD while writing my review for Erykah Badu's new CD "New Amerykahn..." on Amazon and had never heard anything about it. It appears to be a bootleg released on some label called Think Differently Music, and it comprises some odds and ends from Erykah's career. Despite being a random collection, it is quite cohesive, much like any of her studio releases.

A few tracks have appeared on previous Badu albums; "Ye-yo" from 1997's "Live", "Didn't cha know" and "Bag lady" from "Mama's gun" ("Bag lady" here is the remix version that made Billboard's top 10 and not the album version), "I want you" (with the awesome electric guitar ending edited out), "Think twice", and  "Wu" (which is a snippet of "Woo") from "Worldwide underground".

A few others had also been previously released; The Grammy winning "You got me" from The Roots' 1999 album "Things fall apart", the Grammy winning "Love of my life" with Common from the "Brown sugar" soundtrack, "Fly away" from "The Hollywood recordings" by Sa-Ra Creative Partners, the breezy  "Hold on" with Pharaoh Monch (with lyrics about having pride in black beauty, it starts off with Erykah talking to her daughter about being teased at school) from his album "Desire", and "Your precious love" with D'angelo.

The others are "Your mind" (a swinging retro ballad which becomes a funky ditty towards the final 2 minutes and recorded live), "Love hangover" (her outstanding disco/neo soul tribute to Diana Ross recorded live at the BET awards 2007 with a few bars of her "I want you" thrown in), "Apple tree cafe" (lovely jazz song with muted sax and pianos), "Music is everything" (a sparse funky horn sprinkled song), "Live" (a brief jazz/funk number with a scratchy bassline), and  "Today" (a jazzy ballad with a groovy bassline and sprinklings of flute).

Chances are there are a few odds and ends here which you don't already own (like I also discovered). Essential to every Baduist!
label: positive

reviewText:
Beeyootiful music.

Evans is stellar as most always, and Hall steps up to the plate and plays as well as he ever did on record.

The version of Valentine that opens the disc swings hard, with some surprisingly funky comping from Jim during Bill's wonderfully over the top solo. Hall tries to ease him back into the head afterwards, but Evans just keeps on cruising, quietly pushing the beat while the guitar pulls back on it. The resultant sound is unusual and a cool end to a wild ride.

The rest of the (sadly) short album is five ballads, with nary a boring moment to be found. This is perfect bathtub music (just ask the gal on the cover), and will send your mind to some lovely places.

I have not yet heard the reissue with the extra tracks, and am looking forward to it. I have the Japanese remaster, and it sounds just fine, very clear and warm (got it from the used list here on amazon, and imagine my surprise when I got a 25 dollar import for four dollars, in perfect unplayed shape. It pays to look around...).

Undercurrent makes a perfect companion to Evans and Hall's other recording, Intermodulation; they both fit on one cd and create a lush ambience.
label: positive

reviewText:
As an adolescent growing up in the mean streets of Chicago I was turned on to Death by accident. Just getting into metal after hearing "One" by Metallica, I went to the local used CD outlet & saw "Spiritual Healing" by Death in a stack & bought it only because the cover attracted me & it was $5. The moment I got home I dropped it in the CD player only to have my jaw drop out of its socket. Being a composer myself I recognized a true genius at work.
Chuck Schuldiner is by far one of the greatest composers/  songwriters of all metal period!!! His brilliance at riff creation ranks up there with James Hetfield in his prime(1983-1988), Dave Mustaine(1985-1994) and Jeff Hanneman(1985-1990). These 3 are of course not death metal artists but are whom I consider incredible riff technicians.
After buying "Spiritual.." I purchased Human, Leprosy and IndividualThought Patterns. All are great but "Spiritual", "Human" and "ITP" are 3 cd's which really excel with both music artistry & song topics of social relevance. "ITP" is not monotonous either. Unlike many death metal bands which have little to no variation from track to track, Chuck and his sidekicks take you though twists & turns the likes of old Metallica throughout the album. It is impossible to describe the mood of each song because of this.
Just by the damn thing and prepare to be dazzled.
It is a travesty that a man we in the metal community held so dear was taken from us. I brushed back a tear after hearing of his demise. More than a musician, he was a pioneer, an innovator like no other in the genre. Chuck, we love you man. Our hearts & ears are with you. We will all make sure to "Let the metal flow (C. Schuldiner)"

reviewText:
Yes, I'm another longtime Kate Bush loyalist, and I'm feeling absolutely no shame. I was like a junkie who hadn't a fix for 12 years and I didn't even know it. But whatever you do, don't give up after you bond with your favorites, and mine were Sunset, The Architects Dream, and the snippet The Painters Link.  Just realize your favorites are preparation to understanding the purpose of this journey, and Kate is a unique tour guide. Pay attention to Prologue, a masterpiece in my opinion. How could I have possibly passed it over on first listen? Reverent and romantic, slowly building in rhythm, with piano, drum and bass and the Kate layered choruses we have come to appreciate.

There is so much more I could say because she has given us so much, and I'll leave that to others to share with you. As far as poetry and storytelling, she is at the top of her game in Aerial, covering uncharted territory in the world of popular music.  My favorite cd thus far is "A Sky of Honey," a relentless homage to the great beauty of this world we have taken for granted; the rising and setting of the sun, the song of the birds, the magic and mystery of the artists craft, the natural transformation of color ...and our children.  I can truly say, yes, I have been to the church of Kate Bush and I have been blessed - for I was blind but now I see.  I recognize and feel a sense of homage and appreciation to these forgotten wonders through her lens.  Aerial is classical Kate --- a glorious, shameless expression of adoration...from sunrise to Sunset and Somewhere in Between. Tesoro mio, bella...feel the joy.

reviewText:
Let me start by saying that Zakk at Black Label Society is musically distinct from him at Pride and Glory. There are two groups of his fans around; on the one had there is a fan who have followed him since the Ozzy days, hence since the birth of Pride & Glory; on the other hand there is a fan who starts following him from his Black Label Society outputs. The expectation toward his works should be definitely different between these two groups. The former tends to be reminiscent of his magnificent song-writings at this "Pride & Glory" album, which I believe was served as a solid foundation of his roots of music consisting everything from Rock N' Roll, Metal, to Country and Southern Rock.  This diversity in genre was what makes Zakk Wylde to be among world legendary songwriters.

What mostly differs "Pride & Glory" from his recent works is that this album offers a body of great melodies, which leave listeners no choice but humming along ("Shine On" "Lovin Women" and "Troubled Wine").

Also, I particularly like his style of singing at this album, which is bit different from "Book of Shadows" and Black Label Society. The way he expresses his words is extremely unique here in a very good way. What is good in this album is that he manages excellently well to manipulate his range of both high and low pitch at a same verse. Even at some aggressive tunes, one can clearly hear the vocal lines. Note that his high tone in this album is conceptually different from what I consider it be to high at the recent songs like "Say What You Will", in which I sometimes tend to parallel his with Ozzy's vox.

Some who recently question his singing abilities need to listen the following two songs; "Sweet Jesus" and "Found A Friend."
These songs are enough to demonstrate that he can not only sing very professionally, but also can write the greatest ballads as beautiful as "Home Sweet Home" or "Love Bites." (sorry for the poor comparisons, but cannot come up with good ballads)

For those who want tunes as hard as Black Label Society, "Toe'n the Line" is a good candidate. For those who want some Skynard, you can go no wrong with songs like "Lovin' Women" or "Cry Me a River."  In the end, "Pride and Glory" contains the most diversified approaches done by Zakk Wylde ,and I cannot ever be bored with this masterpiece for certain.

Again, depending crucially upon where you started being interested in Zakk's music, how you evaluate "Pride & Glory" is varied. If you are into him through Black Label Society, this album seems at first being a large mystery, but I promise that it will grow on you and eventually become among the heaviest rotation of your Itunes or CD players.

As other reviews state, "Pride and Glory" is one of the decent albums came out in the last decade, and with a bonus CD including 5 more songs, this CD keeps strong and never get old. Finally, I sincerely hope that Zakk would take times to write songs and release the sophomore CD for Pride and Glory as a band.

Saga started right here 1994!!!

reviewText: Five Finger Death Punch are back with their 3rd album, American Capitalist, and they are on the top of their game. Using the same producer as the band's previous release, 5FDP has perfected the sound they've created as their own. Ivan Moody's vocal range has never sounded better, flowing effortlessly from heavy edged verses into clean choruses on most tracks, without ever sounding forced or repetitive.  There is nothing overwhelmingly new here to change peoples' minds that already dislike this band, but new and previous fans will love this offering without a doubt. The pummeling drums and heavy, catchy riffs begin with the opening track and hardly ever let up.  The drums in particular sound as good as they ever have and the guitar solos sprinkled throughout are very enjoyable as well. By now I'm sure you've heard the lead single "Under And Over It", and that song is a great indicator for what the rest of the album sounds like. The few songs that slow it down a little bit include "Coming Down", "Wicked Ways", and "Remember Everything"... the latter of which has kind of an 80's ballad feel to it, with Five Finger's special touch, and they actually pull it off pretty well. The heaviest tracks of the bunch include "American Capitalist", "The Pride", "Menace", and the fantastic album closer "100 Ways To Hate" which might be the best 5FDP song of all, with its absolutley brutal verses and haunting pre-chorus/chorus. The heaviest songs are great as always, the "slower" songs are very well written, and everything in between that hasn't been mentioned is just as good. A perfect and logical follow-up album from 'Way Of The Fist' and 'War Is The Answer' from the kings of mainstream metal.  If you haven't bought it yet, do so....then sit back and enjoy the 11 track ride!

reviewText: ...and to paraphrase a later song, more fool him. You see, he was used to the "Trick Of the Tail" and "Wind & Wuthering" Genesis. While musically excellent, those albums lacked the "thinking man's punk" iconoclasm Peter Gabriel had taken away with him when he'd left just before. It's still at full strength here though. With the original wave of prog, when the rock'n'roll purists weren't calling prog by the apparent oxymoron "art rock", they were saying that all that was wrong about prog could be summed up in one word--"genesis". Like calling Rush "the headbangers' Genesis" and Kansas "the cornfed Genesis". But it was this period of Genesis that gave the lie to claims of pseudo-profundity and artsy-fartsy elitism. All you had to do was pay attention to the music. Like the song "Return Of the Giant Hogweed", a "Day Of the Triffids"-style descendant of the Coasters' "Poison Ivy" done up smartass in the finest Gabriel tradition. The giant hogweed is a particularly nasty weed that got imported into the West in the same way kudzu got imported into the American Southeast--some inquisitive idiot found it interesting. .... One interesting note from the song "Hogweed": "Strike by night, they are defenseless--they all need the sun to photosensitize their venom"--that's true, sunlight does strengthen the corrosive power of the plant's secretions. And you'll wind up with permanent scarring. You gonna try to tell me it ain't cool to write a driving rock boogie that's a mixture of a botany lesson and a monster movie scenario?

reviewText:
While I've always had an appreciation for all aspects of Steve Winwood's music (solo and non), I've never really gone nuts for any of it.  Until now...

Nine Lives is simply a fantastic album.  The instrumentation is sparse, made up of mostly Winwood on Hammond and guitar, a drummer, and a percussionist.  Occasionally, he's joined by a sax or flute player, and on one track Eric Clapton jumps in for a smokin' guitar solo.  The vocals consist of Steve, solo, without a doubled lead vocal track or any background vocals.  It's a fairly minimalist arrangement, but the sparseness just makes it that much more effective.

The groove is mostly laid back, and the songs are extended into mostly five to seven minute explorations of a musical idea.  The album isn't flashy, and Winwood doesn't seem to be trying to impress anyone with his skills.  He's just out to have a good time, and make some music that he enjoys.  It translates to a remarkable album.

Nine Lives is an unexpected joy.  I can't seem to listen to it enough, and I know I can't recommend it highly enough.  It takes a lot for an album to really blow me away.  Nine Lives blows me away...

reviewText:
When a veteran R&B performer is compelled to update her sound(s)to fit the style of their contemporaries at a time when the sound of music was changing more toward the New Jack/Jill Swing styles of the late 80's/early 90's, it's a daring and challenging move.

Such is the case with the opening cut (and first single,) "Here's Looking At You" (#12, R&B,) which boasts an absolutely contagious rap by the Lady herSELF.  "The Sugar Shack" and "Mr. Icecream"  are also solid and good and fall into similar territory (New Jill Swing.)  THEN, you dive into the second single, "If I Were A Bell" (#8 R&B) "Cupid Is A Real Straight Shooter" and "Miracles Need Wings to Fly," and you know EXACTLY where she's comin' from:  The HEART and SOUL of the human condition.  And those CHOPS!...This little lady can hit notes 4 DAYS!

Another special moment here is in the title cut/tone poem which has some of the most beautiful language goin' on and which attests to the fact that she truly IS a poetess and that her talent always HAS lied within the lyrics as well as within the music.

A couple more treats to note are the Jazzie B. (of Soul to Soul fame) -produced tracks, "Just Us Two" and "Since Day One," where she employs outside production (for the first time since Rick James) to serve up two sizzling slices of decent U.K.-ish R&B/Soul, in which she shows off her chops and impeccable Soul sensibility by executing "scatting" on the latter.

"The Red Zone," the album's last track, chugs along to a reggae-ish offbeat with a political metaphor and closes out the CD.

For her first album of the 90's, despite the changing trends in music, it was so impressive that a verteran performer could STILL secure a Top 20 and Top 10 R&B hit while writing, arranging, producing and performing her own music as she had been all along, save for her debut album which dates back to 1979 with production from the late, great Rick James. Beside Patrice Rushen and Angela Winbush, no other woman in R&B was doing this.  Teena Marie has always been a pioneer of the form and with brilliant execution and results.

Though "Ivory" was not the blockbuster one might have expected it to have been after 1988's brave comeback, "Naked To The World" with its #1 R&B hit single, "Ooo La La La," it served in further cementing the fact that the amazing talent of one little lady with a very big and soulful voice, would resurface fourteen years later with the Gold-selling, "La Dona" on Cash Money Classics.

Although never having won a Grammy, she was awarded a prestigious Pioneer Award that would trump any and ALL Grammy's and end up being the icing on the cake of her brilliant musical life/career and the way her brilliance AND music touched generations of fans of R&B around the world.

She might have been "Ivory," but no one cared.  To US, she was always "Wild & Peaceful, Lady Tee!"

reviewText:
Let me first say that I agree with some of the earlier reviews seen here that there are songs missing that should have been included in a collection such as this.  That being said, let's get real, this is The Mighty Elements we are talking about and any of their output from the 1970's in paticular is truly powerful and worthy of way more than the 5 stars we are allotted here to vote!  This box set gives the listener a very solid overview of Earth, Wind and Fire's career up to and including the mid 80's material which was no slouch either.

The title of this box set is very appropriate, this band did and still does with each listen take us on an "Eternal Dance" through life, love, mind, body, soul and spirit!  They truly had a tremendous output of truly great and genre changing songs that gave every band and artist after them the freedom to express themselves in their own unique way.  Earth, Wind and Fire dressed like no one else, sung like no one else, performed like no one else, recorded like no one else, wrote like no else and made no apologies for it either.  They were going to be trend setters and not fall in line with the status quo of the music industry of that day!

This is were their true genius comes from, you could never place them in a "box" and say they were just this type of band or that type of band.  Whenever you thought you had them figured out, they would "flip the script" on you and release something that you could never have imagined and that brilliance would lead them into multi platinium records sales and the adoration of millions of fans around the world while obtaining respect for their music from their contemporaries and peers across the genre spectrum.

The first cd includes songs from the bands inception with Warner Bros. with their first incarnation as a band, the reformation of the band from scratch (with the exeption of Maurice & Verdine White) and their move to Columbia records.  You can really hear their incredible growth as artist and writers here as they begin to lay the ground work for what they were soon to become.  This cd ends with the beginning of their "classic" period starting with the release of "That's The Way Of The World".  The second cd is a trip through the bands mightiest period between 1975 and 1979 were they released 6 albums that changed music forever!  You also get a taste of some of their incredible live performances which is truly what set them apart from anyone else both in terms of the music and the effects that came with each show.

The third cd is a collection of their 1980's output up to the time the original members called it quits, they never again after this time performed together again as a whole until their induction into the Rock and Roll Hall Of Fame in 2000.  As stated before, this is a great overview of the band and how they became the music Royality that they are.  I highly recommend this set for anyone wanting an overview of "The Elements Of The Universe"!

reviewText:
Pearl Jam's newest record, RIOT ACT, has been released today.  To understand RIOT ACT, it helps to understand what's happening with Pearl Jam's fellow bands of the grunge scene.  This review helps explain the context of what is going on these days, because those fans who keep waiting for another TEN or VS. to roll out just simply have no clue.  There will never be another TEN just like there will never be another NEVERMIND.  But there will be Pearl Jam, and, hopefully, for many years will be around to show us what a real rock and roll band can do.
The year's 2002.  Cobain's been dead eight years.  The compilation NIRVANA has been released, showing off the `long lost' Nirvana cut "You Know You're Right."  A Nirvana box set has been indefinitely postponed because of legal wranglings among bandmates Krist Novoselic and David Grohl and Cobain's widow, Courtney Love.  Layne Staley died this year because of drugs.  Jerry Cantrel has gone solo.  Cantrel's record, Degradation Trip, show us just how badly drugs ruined Alice in Chains, ruing their chance at a fully productive career. Soundgarden broke up five years ago (has it really been that long?).  The Smashing Pumpkins called it quits in 2000.  Scott Wieland has been in and out of drug treatments so many times he almost defines that old cliche of `sex, drugs, and rock and roll.  Bush is still going, but they were never innovators in the first place.  Who's left of the old crew?  Not many.  Of the major players, Pearl Jam alone has persevered, and even they have long ago left grunge.
Pearl Jam has traveled a long road since they broke out with their debut TEN, emerging as a seminal Seattle band along with the likes of Nirvana, Soundgarden, Mudhoney, and Alice in Chains.  Pearl Jam, of the major bands from that scene, has always been the most classic-rock oriented of the bunch.  While Nirvana was essentially an indie-rock band with some heavy undercurrents and Soundgarden was just heavy, Pearl Jam, from the very beginning, has tempered their sound with the sensibilities of the `classic rock' of the 1970s.  It's no surprise Eddie Vedder's favorite record as a teen was The Who's QUADROPHENIA.
While Nirvana blew apart the country musically with their seminal NEVERMIND, it is Pearl Jam that kept grunge going.  Nirvana was rooted much more in a punky, indie sound while Pearl Jam made 1970s rock informed by 1990s angst.  Pearl Jam stayed within in the grunge movement, though, and helped shape the genre for its short life, being one of it's major players.
Of course, the Seattle scene, one could argue, ended when Cobain was found dead from his own hand.  Grunge petered out.  It's my belief that, while maybe not in their personal lives, Pearl Jam was on the same downward spiral musically as Cobain was in real life.  Their first three records (TEN, VS., and VITALOGY) get progressively darker, bottoming out at "Immortality."  Everything Pearl Jam have done since then is very drastically different from the grunge sound they helped pioneer.
Since VITALOGY, Pearl Jam given the world four records (1996's NO CODE, 1998's YIELD, 2000's BINAURAL, and 2002's RIOT ACT).  None of these records sound like grunge but they all sound like Pearl Jam very naturally evolving.  Pearl Jam was on a crash course and I believe Cobain's death got them out of their own downward spiral.
These four records sound much like a classicist rock band than anything else.  NO CODE is very radical. NO CODE is very startling because just a mere two years ago these guys had released the very dark, angry, almost nihilistic VITALOGY and now they'd grown reflective and, well, rather subdued, like they've lost all their rage.  They loosened up; they've grown philosophical and reflective.  Refer to my review of NO CODE for more about my beliefs on how important this album is in the Pearl Jam story.  While NO CODE is the first album length work we had from the band since 1994, the "Merkinball" E.P. helps foreshadow this change in their career.
Since that record, Pearl Jam has been playing whatever music they want, sounding like a 1970s leftover.  As far as current musical trends, Pearl Jam hasn't been relevant since 1994 when grunge fell apart, and quite frankly the world is better for Pearl Jam pursuing their own path.  The late 1990s saw us in a wasteland of teeny-bob boy bands on one side and dark, entirely too serious angst `new metal' on the other.  Even Cobain made fun music, but not bands like Creed.  These are serious times and the world is just so terrible, so we must make serious music.
Pearl Jam, with RIOT ACT, hasn't changed the direction they are moving in, and have been their entire career.  Eddie Vedder and the boys are so far left of what's happening in the music today that, ironically, they show just how relevant they really are.  Pearl Jam shows us that when a band evolves and goes where it needs too to survive and prosper that, whatever's going on around them, they will be better for it.  For those awaiting another TEN, RIOT ACT will not soothe that taste.  Just like people, bands change and their identity evolves.  There will never be another TEN from these boys, and if there was it would be a regression.  People calling for another TEN or VS. haven't been with Pearl Jam since 1995.
For those looking for one of America's great rock and roll bands making great music, totally out of step with mainstream (Thank God) and showing how impressive they actually are. RIOT ACT hits home, and it hits hard.  Pearl Jam shows us that they can still write a melody, they are still growing musically, they can still maintain their political stance without becoming a parody of themselves, and most of all, Pearl Jam shows us with RIOT ACT how a great band makes great music.
label: positive

In my opinion, this is the greatest rendition of the Tchaikovsky Violin Concerto that I've ever heard.  Heifetz plays the first movement very fast, but every note is audible and clean.  There are literally moments where my jaw drops each time I listen to this recording.  It would be hard to imagine a more technically and musically superb version of this wonderful concerto, although there are many other good versions (Milstein's in particular is great as well).

The Mendelssohn is great, and like all of Heifetz's work, it's pretty much perfect.  While it is great, I wouldn't name this as my favorite version.  Hilary Hahn's Mendelssohn is equally good and the sound quality is considerably better (because Heifetz's was recorded a long time ago), so Hahn's is my preferred Mendelssohn.

This disc is a must have.  Because of the sound quality of the disc, I would not place this Mendelssohn as my top choice because they are other versions that are technically similar with better sound quality.  The sound quality on this CD isn't bad (it's actually pretty good), but it's not as good as modern recordings.  The Tchaikovsky is so spectacular, however, that even with better sound quality recordings out there, Heifetz still remains my top choice.  Enjoy!

reviewText:
Most often, singles collections tend to be rehashed hits designed to bring more cash to record labels.  "Like the Deserts..." is a welcome exception from one of my personal favorite bands, and does a great job of mixing previously unreleased or rare material, remixes, and older songs onto a compilation that fits into the collection of either the fan with several albums or one who's never heard a note of their music.
  Most apparent is Thorn's and Watt's center of songwriting: whether it's the acoustic ballads like "My Head is..." and "Rollercoater," or the drum and bass melee of "Missing" and "Walking Wounded," the lyrics are from the heart, cleverly writen, and underscored by great melodies.  Tracey Thorn has one of the most striking voices out there, and this CD allows you to track the evolution and refinement of her abilities; she's gained much control and technique without compromising a drop of emotion.
  Other highlights are "Corcovado," a bossa nova tune to beats (and Thorn in portuguese!), "Protection," a Massive Attack song I've heard in a thousand tv shows it seems (and now you don't have to buy that album, which isn't MA's best at all), and "Tracey in My Room," which is so cool it alone is worth the fifteen bucks!
  EBTG are just great, and this CD is an testament to their talent.  I usually always recommend an actual album (and yes, I still call them that!) to back up a "best-of," but you almost don't need one with the strength of the material; however, "Amplified Heart" (which marks the transition from their eighties work) is a good place to start.

reviewText:
This is Cinquecento's fourth disc since their formation in 2006, and in their short career so far I have become a big fan. Like the Brabant Ensemble, they are unearthing some little-known but very beautiful music from the 16th century, and this is another beauty.

Stephen Rice (director of the Brabant Ensemble) claims in his excellent notes that Vaet would undoubtedly have been among the best-known composers of the 16th century if he had not died young. Perhaps that's a slightly overblown claim, but he was a very fine composer and I thought his were the outstanding works on Cinquecento's disc of Music for the Court of Maximilian II Music for the Court of Maximilian II. The music here is beautiful, dramatic in places and extremely skilfully constructed, and there is no doubt that Vaet deserves to be heard much more widely.

Cinquecento bring their characteristic empathy and beauty of sound to the music. An all-male ensemble, they sing in the Flemish tradition of lower pitch and record in a resonant acoustic which produces a fabulous, rich sound but never obscures the individual lines. Intonation is impeccable, the balance and blend of the voices is perfect, and they show a fine understanding of the relationship between music and text. I found the whole disc a huge pleasure, just as I have with all their previous discs. (Their recording of Regnart is a particular favourite of mine.)

The recorded sound by Hyperion is excellent and the notes are interesting and informative. It's an excellent disc, recommended very warmly.

reviewText:
Distinguished performances and recordings by important C20 maestros. The Berlin Philharmonic is captured in fabulous sound and must here be regarded at its very best. Wow, what an orchestra under Karajan! They make other bands sound precisely that - bands!
Michel Glotz, the producer travelled with Karajan to DG to in the 1980s, and helped create the overblown, heavily spot miked /multi track mixed down digital recordings which I think are past Karajan's best..But here in 1977, in gorgeous analog, at EMI the balance between piano and orchestra is perfect while the recording has a lovely tone giving good stage effect in traditional stereo.

It is therefore somewhat disturbing for this old pair of ears to find such a classic recording sounding superior in detail and overall tone to a modern day digital dainty as the recent Lang Lang/Eschenbach release which appears to have been recorded to suit in-ear headphones and crude MP3 downloads.

So much for the audiophile sound. It is easy to dismiss Weissenberg as an unmusical virtuoso, a keyboard prodigy who lacks subtlety. But there is none of that here. I could not find a single instance where the soloist goes to "sleep" in these frankly testing concertos. Every opportunity for phrasing, interpretation and colour is eagerly exploited and Weissenberg who, for me, is the very incarnation of the fiery composer pianist when they were premiered. Beyond the musical intelligence - which Weissenberg has in abundance - is the feeling that imbues nearly all of his recordings - that he is playing on the very knife edge, pushing his technique to the limits. The result is electric - exciting like a Horowitz in an encore - and throughout with a power reminding one of Gilels.

These are beautifully produced recordings of performances that have withstood the test of time but continue to divide the critics. Sometimes top results where the musicians are keen to partner together in a solid interpretation does turn off some listeners.

As with Weissenberg's set of Chopin's concertos also for EMI (France) with the late and great conductor Stanislaw Skrowaczewski, I find these indispensable reference points (though certainly not the only ones) which are more and more pleasing every time I listen to them

reviewText:
Anthrax originally released STOMP 442 in 1995, and it couldn't have been at a worse time (this is a re-release); 1995 was a hard time for metal, if one wasn't Metallica: old school metal was passe and New Metal was in Kindergarten. All of the other established bands were finding it hard to find a place in the era of post-grunge inbred clones (or, rather, the record company marketing execs were looking for the next inbred offspring of Nirvana and ignored the metal bands in their roster). Corporate upheavals severed the relationships that led to the signings of metal bands to big labels in the early nineties. Hence the mid-90s abandonment of so many great bands, like Prong, Biohazard, and C.O.C., all of whom came up from the underground scene to the majors in the early 90s to be subsequently dropped by mid-decade.
Anthrax, of course, is on the very short list of ground-breaking and influential metal bands of the 1980s. In addition to being one of the fathers of "speed-metal", their tongue-in-cheek renditions of the Beastie Boys way back in 1987 and their collaboration with Public Enemy certainly planted the seed for the "rap-metal" style of young metallurgists a decade their junior. When these kids mockingly throw around the term "Addidas Rock", do they know what they're referencing (credit must also be given to RUN D.M.C.)?
By 1992 Anthrax had evolved to a such a point creatively that they parted ways with long-time vocalist Joey Belladonna. In Armored Saint singer John Bush they found a jolt of creative and energy and began, or so they had hoped, a new era for the band. They signed a lucrative three-record deal with Elektra, home of Metallica. 1993's SOUND OF WHITE NOISE was a creative, critical, and chart success.
Unfortunately, Anthrax was no exception to the above scenario. The people who signed them at Elektra had departed by the time 1995's STOMP 442 was released. The execs in suits didn't see them as viable in the musical climate of the time, and therefore ignored them. Consequently, STOMP 442 was neglected, not promoted at all, and criminally ignored by the buying public. Scott Ian, the rhythm guitarist, has said that "Random Acts of Senseless Violence" (STOMP 442's frontal assault) is "Heavy. Too bad no one heard it". Ian has also said that Anthrax's last three records (including 1998's VOLUME 8: THE THREAT IS REAL, another unseen masterpiece now out of print due to the label closing its doors! Hopefully to be reissued as well) have been the most satisfying creatively. Again, a crime they haven't reached many ears, ears that, in my view, would eat this stuff up.
Flash forward to 2001. In the April issue of Rolling Stone (Julia Stiles cover), STOMP 442 was NUMBER 20 on the Reader's Poll!! In the same list as the BEATLES!!! As a flabbergasted Ian said, "who knew?!?!" So there are people out there who know of STOMP 442, have heard it, and like it. Unfortunately it has been out of print. But now it and 1993's SOUND OF WHITE OF NOISE are back and better than ever, remastered with extra goodies!!
Probably as far back as 1996, with the launching of OZZ-FEST, metal has been back en vogue and harder than ever (had Anthrax been on the bill....). Iron Maiden makes a double-barrel comeback. New Metal with all its trappings has helped make metal relevant again. And now Anthrax is busy and ready to bust @#$! up. New label, tour (with Judas Priest), record in the works, collaboration with John Carpenter on the score to GHOSTS OF MARS (great stuff--check it out, if only for their contribution). The Elektra records are finally back, from their new label, Beyond Music, remastered with extra tracks and Ian-penned liner notes. What more could a metal fan ask for?! Content-wise, this stuff has aged better than fine wine. More like a strong small-batch barley wine. It packs a punch harder than ever. Case in point: it had taken me 5 years to get into this record.
This material is so relevant today, in this stale musical climate. STOMP 442 features tighter arrangements than ever before; tight, crunching musical statements in 5 minutes or less. Emphasis on songwriting: Simple yet whiplash-enducing riffs, melodies and hooks that leave a bootprint on your brain. And John Bush's vocals: he had fully integrated himself into Anthrax's sound. Hopefully now that time has given us some perspective, STOMP 442 will finally get the attention it deserves. reviewText:
On December 13, 2013, while engaged in a world tour, and without any pre-release announcement, Beyonce released her self-titled 5th solo studio album exclusively via the iTunes store. Developed as a simultaneous audio-visual medium, the album's songs were accompanied by short films that illustrate the musical concepts conceived during production. In just 3 days, "Beyonce" sold 828,000 copies; records were broken, music history was made, new industry rules were set. 14 songs, 17 videos, switching from uninhibited female empowerment to kitchen sink drama, it was not just merely a record by a megastar, but a statement, as everything about this dark and complex record suggested that, despite the eponymous title, Beyonce was demanding more of herself than just being Beyonce.

Co-written and co-produced by herself and A-listers such as Pharell, and Timbaland, among others, and with references to her competitive showbiz upbringing and acknowledgments of her beloved hometown, Beyonce continued the game of role-playing she is so good at: pop diva, fashion icon, wife, mother, herself, Sasha Fierce, revolutionary, provocateur etc. Explaining her motivation, she said she would often connect images, childhood memories, emotions and fantasies to songs she was in the midst of composing, and that she wanted people to hear the songs with the story that was in her head. The result was a grown-up pop album that is mature without being boring, bold without being forced, and entertaining without being a drag. Not a small feat in pop music where rarely something exciting happens.

3 months later, "Beyonce" is considered by critics and fans alike as B's creative and commercial peak. The enormous enthusiasm of overwhelmed fans for this bold, expansive body of work is making sales growing steadily. In an obvious attempt to boost sales furthemore, this career highlight from one of showbiz's most hard-working superstars is now available in a CD+blu-ray set. Those who purchase the new edition, will find nothing new included on here. This edition is simply an alternative to the original set, featuring identical tracklist, artwork and packaging, all housed in a slipcase cover. The attraction is just the format itself which improves the videos in particular, now visually enhanced. One can marvel at the astonishing details in picture, the crisp sound, and pristine production.

Sonically brilliant, visually magnificent, entertaining and substantive in every respect, "Beyonce" is easily B's most accomplished project to date, and undoubtedly one of the best albums of 2013-2014. And, since the other big pop title of 2013 was released just a month earlier than this, I can claim that, where Lady Gaga failed with "Artpop", Beyonce triumphed with this (I am a Gaga fan, but "Artpop" was admittedly a disappointment).

It should be how it connects with you - PERIOD.  I don't think you should like a certain band because it makes you look cool or helps you fit in with some sort of crowd.  It should be because the music is well-written.

That being said, American Idiot is an amazing album.  Do I like bands like Blink-182, Sum Whatever, Simple whatever and most of those other pop-punk bands?  No.  But Green Day is the real deal.  Just like I listen to Tool and not all the other Tool-clones, I listen to Green Day because they write the best songs by far while those clones get nowhere close.  American Idiot is a testament to what a great band Green Day really is.  They write great songs, period.

Punks that call them sell-outs miss the point.  They can keep their crappy, one-dimensional bands - I'd rather listen to bands that progress and aren't afraid to sound unpunk.  I'd rather just listen to bands that write good music, period.

Every song on American Idiot is amazing.  It is a very well-written album and the energy and message Green Day seems to have wanted to portray comes out clearly.  Simply put, the whole album is solid.  It seems like they couldn't have written any of those songs better.

I also love the message of this album and how it can connect with a new generation on how not to be brainwashed by the Republican agenda.  It pulls this off in a very powerful way and yet doesn't seem to be forced like some political bands can seem.  It all just flows.

American Idiot is a classic album by a classic band and I'm not afraid to say that.  Indie kids can continue limiting their judgement to indie bands so they can hang out in the "cool crowd" with their indie clones and punks can do the same.  I'll just continue listening to great, original artists that write amazing music whether they have indie haircuts, punk haircuts, or not or sell millions of albums or just hundreds.

Great music is great music and American Idiot is full of some of the best music I have heard in awhile.  Nice going Green Day.  This Bay Arean is proud of you.

reviewText: Sometimes a great band fizzles out just at,or just before the point where they begin to really get some momentum going. Incognito were something of a one off project in the beginning with their debut Jazz Funk. Since Jean Paul "Bluey" Maunick returned with the band in 1991,they've spent the last 21 releasing a steady stream of albums that celebrate 70's jazz funk as a full fledged musical movement as opposed to a passing musical fashion trend. Never seems to matter if few seem to be listening. If Amazon.com is any indication there are lots of people who appreciate Bluey and his commitment to musical and creative vision over mass popularity. Musically it's always been a bit of an open house. But generally the band gets it's distinction from two sources: Bluey and the wonderful vocals of Maysa. As usual other singers,in this case Natalie Williams,longtime member Vanessa Haynes and male singer Mo Brandis join in on lead...Maysa is almost the bands lead singer especially considering Incognito is almost by nature a revolving musical collective rather than a steady band. Even so nothing is lost on the quality of the music overall. "The Less You Know","Ain't It Time" and the dripping "Capricorn Sun" are all wonderfully uptempo danceable 70's style jazz-funk numbers,full of that elaborately chorded sense of melodic exploration they are so great with explorting. "Above The Night" and "To Be With You" are beautifully crafted ballads that explore the same territory only with the tempo a bit mellower. "Restless As We Are" takes the music to a more stripped down place,with the horns and arrangements playing more of a punctuation role as the song is built on an elaborate bass/guitar interaction that takes presidents. As the album goes on into numbers such as "Rivers On The Run","The Way You Love" and "Thoughtful Fantasies" they stretch out,even on the non vocal parts into areas that are jazzier. The rhythm remains locked right down while the horns,keyboards and harmony vocals improvise in,over and around the funk and create it's own little grooving instrumental universe. Again it's the band hot and cold style of melodic development that makes these songs really stand out. "Don't Want To Know" is all about melody,with the horns locked into a pattern not dissimilar to another band: Chicago. Most people I hear,on both sides of the pond in this day and age,who are looking to make funk music tend to do so through the filter of hip-hop. Whether it be via samples of old songs or a guest rapper/producer it seems that funk is supposed to be somehow indebted to a genre that has become,frankly a somewhat uneven and often lyrically juvenile mainstream style of music. But I am not criticizing hip-hop. A lot of good has come out of it too. And many funkateers utilizing it as a filter make creative music doing so. However Incognito have kept up their strength as one of the few self contained bands (along with Mint Condition) who devote themselves to funk music. For a collective with such an anonymous name who are known for so many collaborations primarily,they've maintained a very consistent and stable musical identity all the while. To hear unified funk bands such as this,you still often would have to look in the jazz sections of your record stores to find it as I did with this. Or maybe electronica in some cases As stated before,most modern funk acts you'll find in the R&B section are almost all linked in some way with hip-hop. So the present and the future of studiocentric live band jazz/funk will likely lay with groups like Incognito.

reviewText:
Regardless of what anyone says, The Devil You Know is the fourth Black Sabbath album featuring Ronnie James Dio on vocals despite the change in the band's name. The only reason they are going by the moniker Heaven and Hell is because they do not want to be bothered by Ozzy-obsessed fans when playing live.

Just like its predecessor, Dehumanizer, the album was recorded at Rockfield Studios in Wales in only three months, which has given the band the chance to capture a rather live feel which is both intense and powerful. The band did take a longer time to write the album though, partly in England and partly in the USA.

The Devil You Know expands on the classic Sabbath sound, chock full of thunderous riff work, stomping drum intensity, growling bass lines, and godly vocals. This album once again solidifies the fact that Dio is and always will be the voice of Heavy Metal. He is in fine form here, slightly straying from his style on his recent solo material, and revisiting his glorious past where he exerts a doomy vibe on some of the tunes that fits the compositions like a glove.

It all begins with the sonic punch that is "Atom & Evil" (Adam & Eve) whose rolling drum intro suggests the production on this disc is huge and powerful. Everything sounds crisp; the range of dynamics is great and the instrumentation very vivid. As Iommi lays down his unique riffs, a dark, menacing atmosphere is achieved and perfected with the arrival of Dio singing lyrics of abstract symbolism. Note the use of discreet synths in the background, proceeding through a terrain of rhythmic power. Also pay attention to the mini-riff that is planted beneath Dio's vocals on the chorus. That riff doesn't let go till the end -- it is absolutely fantastic.

Being a fan of Sabbath's darkest and heaviest material, tracks like "Follow the Tears," (what a great, great song!) "Bible Black," and "Breaking into Heaven" are the album's most shining moments. The heavy, almost sludge-infested opening riff of "Breaking into Heaven," once again complete with metaphorical lyrics about fallen angels trying to break into paradise, is a modern take on doom metal while the intro of "Follow the Tears" is so heavy that it would crush just about anything that gets into its path. Iommi will always be the god of riffs, as his writing has been unparalleled for over thirty years. He unleashes riffs, rhythms, and solos unlike any other guitarist in the world. His acoustic guitar playing on "Bible Black" is stunningly dark, as is his volatile, chugging lead solo that follows it. The way the song builds from a pain-ridden dirge to a monstrous finale induces goose bumps every time. Add to this Dio's vocals that recall his stuff from his most underrated album Strange Highways and Iommi's schizophrenic solo and you have a masterpiece of composition.

Geezer Butler mostly stands out on the bass-centric "Double the Pain," again with vocals reminiscent of Strange Highways, where he lays down a sick, stomping bass solo. Likewise, it is the bass that permeats "The Turn of the Screw" which boasts a shred-intensive guitar solo that erupts like a volcano following the patient build-up. This would make for a perfect live performance given the energy between the drums, bass, and guitars.

About the other songs, "Eating the Cannibals," the shortest song on the album, is the loud, in-your-face number, retaining its heavy drive from start to finish while "Fear" sees Dio's most theatrical singing highlighted with awesome drum fills by Vinny Appice (whose work on the earlier albums is much, much better -- perhaps the best drumming in Heavy Metal).

Admittedly, "Rock & Roll Angel" and "Neverwhere" lack the same intensity and songwriting bliss of the other tunes, but the lead solo on the former is arguably Iommi's finest on this album as it recalls his blues-inflected playing on Mob Rules quite a bit, and the latter is a hook-laden, catchy rock anthem into which scalding riffs and slamming drums are tucked.

A great entry into the mostly brilliant Sabbath catalogue. Though at this point, I rank it below the other three albums with Dio, this is still one of the best Heavy Metal albums of the year.

Their music is rock-- it's like a more pop version of Dream Theater and a man's version of Evanescence, energetic with a darkish flavour. Their style is very consistant in all their songs, and if I didn't know, I would have thought they were from New Jersey, not Finland. It would be an overstatement to say they are the Bon Jovis of Finland, but you get my point. I was also surprised at their English accent, no hint of Europe here, either.

reviewText:
There are three musical genres in which the Mormon Tabernacle Choir excels: sacred music, patriotic music, and folk songs.  "Come Thou Fount Of Every Blessing" is filled with stunning examples of the third category, and it is one of their strongest albums ever.  A huge reason for the album's success lies in the striking arrangements of their current musical director, Mack Wilberg.  Long recognized as a premiere arranger of folk songs, his musical stamp is all over this recording, with thirteen of the seventeen songs being his own arrangements.  "Saints Bound For Heaven" opens the disc, and a more joyous, powerful reading could not be hoped for - from there, the disc alternates between gorgeous, lyrical melodies (like "Death Shall Not Destroy My Comfort" and "His Voice as the Sound") and joyous declarations of faith, such as "Bound For The Promised Land," "How Bright Is The Day," "Down To The River To Pray," and the title track.

Most surprising of all is the soulful gospel revealed in songs like "I Want Jesus To Walk With Me" and "Rock-A-My-Soul In The Bosom Of Abraham" (both featuring soloist and choir member Alex Boy).  The size of the choir, coupled with their diligent perfectionism result in some of the most moving, inspiring music making of their entire oeuvre.  Other favorites of mine on the disc include "The Battle Of Jericho" "Deep River" and the seminal "Amazing Grace" (also in a new arrangement by Mack Wilberg, which is stunning.)  But I cannot recommend this disc highly enough - in these difficult times, this is music to lift you up.

reviewText:
Anatoly Liadov (1855-1914) didn't write a lot of music (famously because of his laziness). He was nevertheless a skilled composer of miniatures; his orchestral works are well known, of course, but there are quite a few piano pieces, and the selection offered by Stephen Coombs for Hyperion here can only make you wish that there was much more of it. Some of the music verges on the salonesque, but it is always delectably crafted and quite memorable; other works show traces of something far deeper and more serious, despite the miniature format (the op. 64 set perhaps in particular). Among the lighter music, The Musical Snuffbox is well known in its orchestral guise and is a charming and brief bagatelle in its piano version; the Little Waltz is similarly brief and delightful, whereas Marionettes is inventive and imaginative. I guess the op. 11 pieces would count as belonging not too far away from the salon as well, though they show that Liadov could emulate Chopin in a way that was almost as successful as what Chopin himself wrote.

The op. 24 pieces are somewhat more substantial, with traces of more adventurous harmonic ideas; these are thoroughly engaging and enjoyable works and would deserve to be better known. Chronologically, the op. 36 preludes followed next, but they are lighter and more conventional (but very enjoyable); the Barcarolle op. 44 is relatively conventional as well, but thoroughly beautiful. With the op. 57 pieces we have what must be considered miniature masterpieces, and even more so the op. 64 are wonderful, even captivating, works of imaginative, atmospheric late romanticism.

The two sets of variations here are apparently the largest works Liadov wrote. The op. 35 set (on a theme by Glinka) does perhaps not really say anything new; it is inventive enough and contains enough twists and fine ideas to make it worth its time. It pales, however, in comparison to the op. 51 set (on a Polish folk theme), which - with its glittering colors and wonderful atmospheres, especially in the faster material - is a real gem. Stephen Coombs clearly enjoys the music, and it really isn't much wonder why. He seems to have thought long about every one of these miniatures, and I can hardly imagine anyone making a much better case for them. Recommended with some enthusiasm.

If you want to know America, watch its cartoons. There is so much more reality in any episode of "The Simpsons" than in any episode of any daytime soap opera. (And most Americans look more like the Simpsons. . .big-roundish plumb and funny-haired.)
So it is with "Fritz The Cat". I think I chose to watch it seeking a naughty thrill. What I got instead was a startling, nostalgic, real picture of the America of 1972. Yes, yes, you do see a horse-woman's rump, and Aunt Jamima's boobies, and a policeman's peenie. What you see more, though, is the American-teenage-world-view of the 1970's: the cool cats wanting to understand the black birds, the pretension of higher education, the thrill of drugs, and the need to jump into the nearest sack or tub or trash-can for, well, you know. . .
