reviewText:
Since the very beginning of Murs' career, he has always had a different outlook on the game than his fellow peers from the west coast power-house collective, the Living Legends crew. Since 1995, Murs has been one of the hardest working rappers in the game. Officially, this is his 7th full-length album, which barely speaks of his entire career. He's a part of the collective known as 3 Melancholy Gypsy's, who've released 2 full-length albums. He's also part of the duo Felt, with Slug from Atmosphere, who are currently working on their 3rd album. And besides appearing on 7 full-length Living Legends releases, he's appeared on approximately 50 records within and outside the crew.

One of the things I've always noticed about Murs is that he's never been tied down to a certain type of sound or producer. From Eligh, to Bicasso, to El-P, to 9th Wonder, to Terrace Martin; Murs stays inspired like a true artist from the golden age. Whether he's dropping material on an independent label, Definitive Jux, Rhymesayers, or Warner Brothers; Murs has never compromised the quality of his art or craft.

Plain and simple, mainstream hip-hop needs a record like this. Murs brings back that golden age aesthetic to a time when hip-hop albums are vastly disposable in the commercial and underground scene. Murs has always spoke on tales of the common man, and has always brought a conscious, personal, and thought provoking message of real life events to the table. Being a long time fan, I feel Murs has really stepped up his game up lyrically, and is flexing his muscles to their tightest for his major label debut. Now more than ever, it's apparent Murs is trying to change the game with an eye-opening record of positivity and realness - and now he has the tools and the distribution to make that happen on a global scale.

Having heard Murs' entire catalog, the production was the thing I was most interested in. Producers include Wild Animals, 9th Wonder, Keith Harris, Scoop DeVille, LT Moe, Khalil, Josef Leimberg, Terrace Martin, & Knotch. One of the most notable additions to the production is DJ Quik. If you are unfamiliar with the west coast legend & audiophile, just know that his mixing and engineering skills have given this production a mainstream glossiness that Murs has never had before, which demands more presence from Murs than ever before.

01. Intro (produced by Wild Animals): The album kicks off with "Hail to the Chief" - a press conference style introduction. Although unnecessary, it exemplifies the magnitude of the project nicely.

02. I'm Innocent (produced by 9th Wonder): An excellent opener featuring a nice sample from Honey Cone's "Innocent 'Til Proven Guilty". Murs introduces himself to the mainstream with some very nice skill. Dope quote - "I'm anti-thug, and anti-drugs, brought peace to the party and got anti-love".

03. Lookin' Fly (produced by Keith Harris, co-produced & featuring Will. I.Am): This is probably the most commercial sounding track here, and Murs handles it nicely. Diehard fans of his older Living Legends material may find cuts like this a little out of the norm, yet he tackles a different sound and does it well. Features a sample of Al Hirt's "The Green Hornet Theme"

04. The Science (produced by Scoop DeVille & DJ Quik): Taking a cue from revolutionary artists like KRS-One & Chuck D, Murs literally drops some "Science" on us. He speaks intelligently on new and old hip-hop, slavery, genocide, freedom, and race through the facts of cocaine and crack, and how the public and government view it. An excellent message track with live flute and bass-lines.

05. Can It Be (Half A Million Dollars And 18 Months Later) (produced by Scoop DeVille):  This is the lead single from the album. And it exemplifies what Murs is bringing to the game excellently. The beat is a favorite of mine, as it utilizes samples of "I Wanna Be Where You Are" by Jackson 5. Great message & great hook.

06. Everything (produced by LT Moe): Nice piano-filled production with James Blunt  on the hook. Definitely a different sound for Murs. And he delivers excellent lyrics and flows with an inspirational theme.

07. Road Is My Religion (produced by Khalil): Nice production which includes a nice guitar and synth line. Murs speaks on the struggles of touring, missing his girl, money issues, and self-doubt. Not the most original concept, but dope nonetheless.

08. Sooo Comfortable (produced Josef Leimberg, featuring vocals by Kokane): This one changes up the rhythm nicely with a smooth west coast flavored banger that features soulful hooks & production.

09. Time Is Now (produced by Terrace Martin, featuring Snoop Dogg & Latoiya Williams): This is probably my favorite cut on the album. Unlike the Will. I.Am guest spot, Snoop actually drops a smooth 16 bars. The soul-clap production is straight up ear candy. Nice to see Murs getting some solid validation from one of today's most popular and recognizable rappers.

10. Think You Know Me (produced by Nottz): Excellent cut here. Murs brings a little gangsta flavor here, only to eliminate any connotation that he's actually a gansgta. He's just a common man, and speaks on it in a very interesting way. Features nice samples from "Moment Of Truth" by The Originals.

11. Me And This Jawn (produced by Nottz): Mainstream rap has some major problems respecting women nowadays. Murs is one of the few rappers in the game today that flips a love song in interesting ways. He describes everything about his one and only love in his life. Features samples from "For The Love Of You" by The Isley Brothers

12. Love And Appreciate II (produced 9th Wonder): When Murs gets together with 9th, they make some extremely personal, and soulful cuts. This is my favorite song here. Murs is once again dropping knowledge on relationships, and he may have reached his apex here. Once again, in an age where mainstream rappers fill the air waves with misogynistic lyrics, Murs is truly a breath of fresh air. Features samples of "Now It's Time To Say Goodbye" by Freda Payne.

13. A Part Of Me (produced by Terrace Martin): Here, Murs speaks about making mistakes in a relationship, his struggles with his decisions, and how much he misses his girl even though they weren't meant for each other. I honestly never thought I'd hear production like this under Murs. It brings out his emotional side as Murs let's lose heart-wrenching lyrics.

14. Break Up (The OJ Song) (produced by Knotch): Murs continues with his stretch of love songs, and this one is about the painful ventures of a break-up, and how he wished she would just call him up and apologize. He would take her back at the drop of a hate; but his pride is in the way. It features a very alluring sample of "Charlene" by Anthony Hamilton. Another favorite of mine.

15. Breakthrough (produced by 9th Wonder): The album closes with an excellent banger about his dreams to make changes in the game of hip-hop. By this point, nobody should have any doubt that Murs has what it takes to bring a quality change to the game. As the common man, he proclaims if the album fails and doesn't sell he'll be getting a job at McDonald's, Burger King, or maybe Target or Best Buy (at least he gets a discount). It's hard to imagine a more humble rapper than Murs.

If you picked up the "Special Edition", you got the bonus DVD. The DVD is only 25 minutes long, but has an excellent production value. Basically, it's one long sketch about the 2008 Hip-Hop Presidential election. It all takes place on "3:16 News", which is a format which pokes fun at Fox News. There are 3 candidates; one is an ignorant, new-school Souljah Boy-type rapper who's only been rapping for a few months. He pretty much represents everything wack about hip-hop today. Then there's a 60-something white man who is completely out of touch with the culture and just wants to exploit it's commercialism. Then of course, we have Murs as candidate #3, who embodies all that is hip-hop - the well-educated veteran who came to take the Obama approach and change the game for the better. Not only is the program funny, it has a wealth of very interesting things to say about hip-hop. So if you're debating over which version to get, I'd highly recommend the "Special Edition".
label: positive

reviewText: I actually went to one of those 17 performances before the show folded on Broadway. I went because I'd been a Georgia Brown fan since "Oliver!."  I quickly realized as I watched the show that I was watching a musicalized version of "Buona Sera, Mrs. Campbell." Despite the lovely songs, the show lacked the joie de vivre and much of the humor of the popular movie version.  First off, there was far too much time spent on Carmelina's relationship to Vittorio, which was not too comedic, although Paul Sorvino gave a wonderful performance, as expected of him, The movie version stresses Carla's juggling of the three American "fathers" of her daughter, Gia, as well as their American wives. The show version gave short-shift to these relationships, even though the three American men get to sing the most beautiful song, "One More Walk Around the Garden." The story deserved better, and when it was again adapted into "Mamma Mia," it finally succeeded (but with songs from ABBA). Still, the songs by Burton Lane and Alan Jay Lerner are delightful in their own right, as this CD proves.

reviewText:
Should a Definitive Collection include EVERY single video? Maybe not.  But in Def Leppard's case, the ratio of videos made to worldwide hits was more than 1 out of 2, so a collection with 20 videos out of 39 made will definitely miss some important videos.
Of course you can find ALL their videos in the previous DVD compilations: Visualize/ Video Archive and Hystoria/ In The Round In Your Face (both themselves compilations of previously released VHS).
What no other Def Leppard DVD includes that this one does is the new video for No Matter What and the band's audio commentary for each of the tracks released here.  The video for Now is included in the recent British DVD release called The Best of, which also includes Long Long Way To Go, the second video from their X album which would have been a great addition to this DVD.

So, in the plus side, you get a choice of their best videos plus one brand new video (No Matter What) and another never released in the US (Now).  Also, you get the band's commentary.  Owning the aforementioned DVDs the band's commentary was the MAIN reason in getting this, and it's worth it.  You'll hear both serious comments about the locations, the shoot, the directors, the schedule for each video.  Also, some funny tidbits of the Leps acknowledging their own infamous anecdotes, and mostly, watching in amazement the long way of the videoclip as a medium in the 20 plus years they have taken full advantage of it.  The show they are serious about having fun, even if it means making fun of themselves.

On the downside, there are some key videos missing, like the UK version of "Sugar" or the masterful epic version of "When Love and Hate Collide".  However, you can find them on other Lepps DVDs, and at a price of less than $15, this is a great DVDeal!

On Through The Night: 0 videos on this DVD out of 1 available form this album (missing Hello America)
High N' Dry: 1/5 Bringin' On The Heartbreak (three live videos, plus Me and My Wine)
Pyromania: 3/5  Photograph, Rock Of Ages, Foolin' (Rock, Rock Till You Drop; Too Late For Love)
Hysteria: 7/8 Animal, Women, Rocket, Pour Some Sugar On Me, Armageddon It, Love Bites, Hysteria (alternate version of "Sugar")
Adrenalize: 2/7 Let's Get Rocked, Have You Ever Needed Someone So Bad
Retroactive: 1/3 Two Steps Behind (Action, Miss You in a Heartbeat)
Vault: 1/2 When Love And Hate Collide (Epic 8 minute version of this same song)
Slang: 2/3 Slang, Work It Out (All I Want Is Everything)
Euphoria: 1/2 Promises (Goodbye)
X: 1/2 Now (Long Long Way To Go)
Plus No Matter What (which is labeled as "studio rehearsal" but it's actually a neat little videoclip).

Still, this DVD is the perfect companion to their recent double CD: Rock of Ages.  If you love Lep and have their other DVDs buy this for the band commentary and the two new videos.  If you like Lep and don't have any DVD, well then you are in luck, purchase this one, it's amazing!

reviewText:
This is not only one of the most memorable pairings of a "popular" singer with a jazz giant--ranking with the first Sinatra-Basie album and the Coltrane-Hartman session--but one of the most productive as well. What's remarkable about the album is that the association is as much a timely showcase for the Ellington band's unique musicality as for Rosemary's credentials as an artist transcending her pop-star status in the 1950s.
Ellington was the first orchestrator to appreciate the potential of the human voice as one more sound in the orchestral mix. In fact, one of his earliest recordings, "Creole Love Call," uses the soprano voice as a wordless instrument. But perhaps because Duke's musicians themselves came to have such identifiable, personal voices on their instruments, the Maestro subsequently paid little notice to the stream of vocalists who appeared with his band over the course of a 50-year career. With only a few exceptions (Ivy Anderson, Betty Roche), the singers were mediocre musicians and glitzy performers--"throwaways" to please the eyes and ears of the less educated ticket payers. Duke gave them free rein to sing whatever inferior material they chose, providing undistinguished, indifferent support--much like the disappointing Sinatra-Ellington recording session of the 1960s.
Even more to the point, Duke's biggest-selling recording--the "Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue" from the Newport 1956 album --was no more representative of his artistry than "Come On A My House" was of Rosemary's.  As a result, "Blue Rose" was a rare opportunity for the public to catch a glimpse of both performers in full bloom.  In the wordless vocals of the title song and the vocal harmonies of  "Mood Indigo" as well as the rich woodwind choirs complementing the voice on "Sophisticated Lady" and "I've Got It Bad," Clooney and Ellington achieve a balance that practically erases any distinction between solo and accompaniment let alone the two "star" performers.
Which is not to say that each doesn't shine in their own light--but it's more a reflected luminescence picked up from an inspiring companionable source.  Even Johnny Hodges' jaw-dropping, virtuoso playing on Strayhorn's "Passion Flower" (easily worth the price of the album all by itself) becomes an organic element in a programmatic whole. As for Rosemary, she's never sounded better--nor, for that matter, has Ellington.

The 70's numbers are both the best and worst tracks on the album. I was at a music store as they previewed this recording. Thank God for small miracles. A beautiful combination of great songs, a powerful voice, good arrangments and musicianship.

My personal favorites are "Ghost Train", "Silver Thunderbird", "True Companion", "Walking in Memphis". Sincere truthful readings. No stance or affectations. Pop music at it's best.

Marc Cohn strikes many familiar chords with this album clearly with his own style.  He tells stories of people we know, people we forgot, of the guy up the block or down a ways. Of women we lost, women that matter most. Of midnights on hot summer nights. That wistful memory that comes upon us all, of earlier days.  Never heavy handed, or sappy.

None are throwaway and while Marc may be best known for "Walking in Memphis", many of these song are it's equal or better and that's saying something.

Marc is a compelling story teller, he has a real gift, a unique, strong voice and a soulful delivery.

The band and arrangements are first rate.  All done with a mind to convey imagery, yet supportive of the vocalist.

These songs, still resonate years later.  You can pull this one out and play it anytime.

This kind of pop music/song writing has been gone for quite a while and is missed.  I found that 10 years after it's release these songs have aged quite well.

reviewText: If you grew up in the 1980s, you got the wrong idea about a lot of great 1970s artists. Three letters say why: MTV. Maybe when Steely Dan broke, 1980, they knew a day was around the corner when a great songwriter would have to get filmed on a jet ski to sell records. If you had any music cred whatsoever, you hated Hall and Oates, you know, the guys in the "Private Eye's" video, back when that M was for music. Kind of. But there were some inconvenient truths. One was that underground prince, Robert Fripp, had produced Daryl Hall's Sacred Songs after an invite to appear on Fripp's Exposure. I have listened to both and neither come near a jet ski. Neither does Abandoned Luncheonette. This is simply how pop should sound. Hall and Oats existed at that sweet spot where pop and soul meet. Listen to their cover of "She's Gone," done by Tavaras. Hall and Oats smooth the texture, but make this work as pop, soul, and both. "Las Vagas Turnaround," could be the Spinners singing a Brian Wilson song. Hear the orchestrated funk hooks of "Laughing Boy." Funk with a pop heart. Everything on Abandoned Luncheonette is just immaculately written and arranged. Pop as craft, pop as shine, pop as perfection. If you could blame Hall and Oates for anything, it is letting their music get rolled into 1980s big hair, and if all you remember is the videos, who can blame you, But forget all that and hear what these guys were truly capable of. Get Abandoned Luncheonette. There are no jet skis here, either.

reviewText:
I have been a fan of Taylor Swift approximately since 2007, after I heard her debut LP that was released in the year 2006. Since then, I have listened to all of her records and I was able to witness her changes throughout the years. I always wanted to write a review about Taylor Swifts 1989 album, but I thought it would be best to do it after that era was over. Now, after almost a year and a half after its release, I decided to write a track-by-track review.

First of all, 1989 is Taylor Swifts first documented pop album.  She always flirted with the concept of pop songs but she never went full-out with it. When you listen to 1989, you notice that it is a pop album, but it is far from bubblegum-pop meaningless songs that make no sense at all. As the album title suggests, she was inspired by the music and ideas that were flowing in the decade she was born in, and you can notice that in some songs. Every song on the album is perfectly crafted, they all have her signature heart-on-her-sleeve-open-diary songwriting but you can notice that she has grown as a person by reading the lyrics, something I highly recommend.

This album includes the following songs:

-Welcome To New York: it is the perfect song to start the album with. Right from the start you can tell that it is a pop song and it sets the tone of 1989. Taylor sings about how moving to the magical and eclectic city of New York changed her and her perspective.

-Blank Space: it is one of the best lyrically-written songs on the album. This song is about the man-eating image the media has created of her. Instead of sitting in a corner and cry, she decides to take on that idea and create a catchy song about that fictional character that was created of her.

-Style: if there is one song in 1989 that definitely sounds like the 80s, this is it. In this one she sings about that kind of relationship that always comes back around (they never go out of style) and you can hear a Miami Vice vibe hear that is perfect for this song.

-Out Of The Woods: this is one of the many highlights of the album. It has a chorus that really makes you feel what she was feeling (are we out of the woods yet?) and it is written so perfectly it will be hard to get it out of your head.

-All You Had To Do Was Stay: in this song, Taylor does something she has never done before: she incorporated a high-pitched Stay in the chorus. The song tells the story of how her lover broke all of his promises and she tells him that the only thing he had to do was stay, but it is too late for him to return.

-Shake It Off: probably the most up-beat song on the album, Shake It Off is an ode to her independence from everybody else's opinion. In this instant hit, Taylor declares that she is aware of all the things that she is criticized for, but she is not going to change who she is in order to be more liked, she is just going to shake off the haters.

-I Wish You Would: this is a very innovative song from the point of view of the narrative: it constantly goes between the point of view of two people that were in a relationship and how they wish the other one knew how they really feel.

-Bad Blood: This song is about betrayal, and how Taylor was affected by the other persons actions. It has some strong beats that really makes this song stand out. It would be great if the album also had the version with Kendrick Lamar.

-Wildest Dreams: a slow-paced song in which she sings about a relationship that she knows she is going to end sometime soon, so she wishes that her partner remembers her in the best way possible (standing in a nice dress, staring at the sunset). It is a great song that starts with a minimalistic sound then develops into a larger-than-life song and then goes back again to that intimate sound.

-How You Get The Girl: a funny, upbeat song about how a man has to win her heart back. It almost feels like a step-by-step guide met a fairytale, and that is awesome. It is one of the most full-out pop songs and she nails it perfectly.

-This Love: this slow song feels like it could be sung by millions of people in a stadium while still feeling intimate. It paints the situation of how she felt her lover had gone but he reappeared out of the blue.

-I Know Places: when you listen to this song for the first time, you might say that it is different from what she has done before: and it is exactly that. You can feel that this song is almost like a movie (it even has the sound of a movie starting and stopping at the beginning and at the end of the song, respectively). It is a great song about the fragility of a relationship at the beginning and how she wishes to keep the media away from them given how publicly known she is.

-Clean: the song that closes the standard edition of the album, Clean is a masterpiece. In this song, Taylor refers to her relationship as something not healthy for her. She has grown out of it and she wishes to get clean, just like an addiction. It really makes you stand in her shoes and it is beautifully written.

All in all, 1989 is an amazing album that rightfully won Album Of The Year at the Grammy's. I completely recommend it because it shows that Taylor Swift knows who she is and you can see it reflect on her music. Now, all there is left to do is to eagerly wait for her new music and smashing hits.

reviewText: This has been one of my favorite CDs of 2004. Anyone looking for a Theatre of Tragedy sound here will be disappointed, though. This isn't GOTHIC so much as it is NORDIC. If "Lord of the Rings" had a heavy-metal soundtrack, this would be it, with lots of that "galloping" metal style pioneered by the likes of Iron Maiden. And Liv Kristine's voice, as always, is beautiful and angelic above all the pummeling. If you like the style of Within Temptation's "Mother Earth" album, then this is for you!

Two things about this album that longtime fans of Duran Duran should know. First, it is in many ways the most diverse album they have ever recorded, and second, their trademark sound is still present throughout. In recent years, Duran albums have had some very strong singles, but the albums as a whole were very inconsistent ("Medazzaland," "Pop Trash," "Wedding Album," and "Liberty" fall into this category.) The exception, of course, being 2010's excellent "All You Need is Now," which had some potential singles, but it was an album with not a single bad song, which hinted of a resurgence from the band.

"Paper Gods" is a resurgence in the singles department, as there are several tracks that are right up there with their best work. The hit single "Pressure Off" is reminiscent of their 1986 smash hit "Notorious," while "You Kill me with Silence" begins with an intro that is a direct homage to their underrated song "The Chauffeur," before soaring into a beautiful chorus that shows that Simon LeBon's vocals are stronger than ever. The presence of some memorable guests enhance the effort, as the appearance of John Frusciante on "What are the Chances" and "Universe Alone" put those two songs over the top.

Duran Duran has accomplished several things with this album. They have stayed current while paying homage to their past, which galvanizes them as a band who were ahead of their time. They have embraced the changing of the times and discovered the art of making great pop singles again. While not all the experiments work, most of them do, and a few of them REALLY do. This is an excellent effort from a band who has been around for more than 3 decades now. The fact that they're still giving us music at all is an accomplishment in itself; the fact that they're still doing it this well is something rare and noteworthy. While not their best ever release, it's one of their most important. This is certainly worth a purchase. 4.5 stars.

As a crossover fan of nearly every genre and a range of artists from B.B. King to Mozart to Royal Trux to My Life with the Thrill Kill Cult, I've noticed one very interesting thing: fans get mad when an artist changes production styles.
This is a much more smoothly, shinily-produced PJ Harvey than we've all known in the past. You know what? It works for me. The music is beautiful. It's mature. It's stirring. Only now, it's also easy-to-swallow pop music.
If you're very genre-absorbed and can't possibly like a good pop record, then this isn't the record for you because the production in these songs is decidedly pop. I personally love older, more raw PJ works and I also love the melodic sounds of "Stories." I find that while her older discs are cathartic in a kind of tense, clawing way that I very much like, "Stories" is both soothing and beautiful enough to at times raise a few goosebumps, especially on windswept, U2-esque tracks like "A Place Called Home" or the (aptly described by other reviewers) second coming of Patti Smith (and perhaps even Chrissie Hynde) of "Good Fortune."
Naturally, if you hate U2, Patti Smith, or the Pretenders, this may not be the record for you. But if you like these artists and you've been a PJ Harvey fan as well, you'll definitely find something to get excited about here.

reviewText:
Hard To Find 45's is a collector's dream from the Eric Label. Those of us who are completists, working on musical projects or just fans find out very quickly that most Cd collections have the same songs, more or less, the big hits of whatever decade. How many times did I buy a collection that had one song I wanted and fourteen I already had. Another trick was to buy a one hit wonder's Greatest Hits CD, and though some are interesting, others had little to offer besides that one hit. And even in these days of buying MP3 versions of individual songs, there are still many songs unavailable that way, especially when you go back to the Fifties and Early Sixties, which is the general territory of Eric. A British label, Ace, is similar but they rarely venture post British Invasion whereas Eric has even done some 70's and 80's material.

You can be confident with this label. It's the kind of label where the people involved love the music, know their stuff and are dedicated to getting it right. You'll find only original masters here, engineered by people who know how it should sound, and highly informative booklets that discuss every track. The licensing of the songs only lasts so long so get them now. Once before most fell out of print and were selling for around $100.00

With Volume 11 Eric goes into the territory formerly covered by Rhino's Super Hits of the Seventies series, but with CDs able to hold 19 songs instead of 10 and constraint of having only the Seventies to choose from. In 1968 the pop-rock-R&B scene began to split apart with the new heavier rock migrating to "Underground" FM stations who were willing to play heavier rock tracks, long songs and album cuts. This left the AM Top 40 stations mostly to the pop and R&B people though '68 would still see major Top 40 hits by Jimi Hendrix, Cream, Big Brother & the Holding Company and Iron Butterfly. Contrary to the dogma of rock critics, this was a very creative time for pop when many rock elements were incorporated into pop tunes and producers were able to use many of the new developments in studio technology, especially multi-tracking.

By this point pop could sound like practically anything and even though this disc sticks to a "Sugar Pop" aesthetic, a style sometimes only one step away from Bubblegum, there is a great variety of styles here. This was an era when many pop songs were the concoctions of songwriters and especially producers with the named artist or band mostly providing a vocal and occasionally being created after the fact of the recording as a touring and promotional entity.

Eric has done its usual fine job here not only selecting interesting songs but arranging them in a way that leads you from straight on pop to some really odd novelty numbers to an almost easy listening segment and finally some semi-operatic pop. They start off well with the ubiquitous Tony Burrows, this time as White Plains with his second biggest hit, My Baby Loves Lovin' (his biggest was Love Goes where My Rosemary Goes, as Edison Lighthouse). Gallery, with its nice country rock steel guitar bridge in Nice To Be With You was a band practically formed in the studio with various Detroit band members and was surprisingly produced by the usually more funky Dennis Coffey (Scorpio). Vanity Faire's Early In the Morning boasts a prominent electric harpsichord and a vaguely Eastern European folk melody. The Peppermint Rainbow are one of the last examples of pure sunshine pop and are much influenced by Spanky & Our Gang. The oldest song in the collection, Lou Christie's take on Tchaikovsky, Rhapsody In the Rain actually had to have its lyrics changed because of censorship in early 1966 (Eric gives us the uncensored version).

There's every other type of song here imaginable from Chirpy Chirpy Cheep Cheep whose Europop melody seems to almost turn into Little Eva's Locomotion periodically; Daddy Dewdrop's surrealistic Chick-A-Boom, a kind of musical R.Crumb cartoon; to a real oddity like 1900 Yesterday by a group of hotel lounge-playing Hawaiian models led by Liz Damon doing a song so easy listening that it could have easily been featured on the Lawrence Welk Show. There's the light, breezy pop of Mr Diengly Sad by the Critters from the Fall of '66, the Claudine Longet style whisper-singing of Stay Awhile, and songs that are in styles of earlier musical traditions like Indian Lake, How Do You Do and Look What They've Done To My Song. It all ends with the proto-Queen operetta, Sugar Baby love and the bravura vocal of Baby take Me In Your Arms. If you have any taste for this kind of thing, Sugar Pop Classics is about the best disc out there.

EXTRA NOTE: I just have to plug one of my favorite "Sugar Pop"songs of all time, the mostly forgotten You Are the One by the Sugar Bears, which made it to # 51 in early 1972. It would have done better if most of the copies had not been given away free on the back of the popular General foods cereal boxes. It's pure, melodic pop with a driving rhythm that most resembles Love Is In the Air. The song's style and the great tenor voice singing it do not at all sound like a band of cartoon bears, though that it what it was supposed to be (much like The Archies). Oddly, the singer was Mike Settle, previously a folksinger who had songs recorded on Judy Collins' early albums and was later a member of The New Christie Minstrels. The song was also written by Kim Carnes and she sings background vocals on it. truly a pop-oddity, I've never found a Cd recording of it and had to settle for a version posted on You Tube. I hope Eric puts it on a CD someday.

reviewText:
I'm probably one of the few people around who thought Pulp's '98 album This Is Hardcore was Jarvis Cocker's crowning achievement.  Yes, Different Class is a masterpiece in it's own right, however, the brooding, intense Hardcore had an emotional pull that still haunts me whenever I hear it.  I remember buying Hardcore upon its release and being so overwhelmed by the maturity of the material.  I honestly thought it would be an even bigger hit than Class.  Sadly, this did not happen.  It would go down as a critical darling but didn't have the Pop appeal to snag the casual fans who purchased Class in droves (in England and Europe at least).  Their subsequent album We Love Life ended up being a bit of a reactionary album to regain momentum they had lost with the public at large.  Although a great album it lacked the hunger of Class and the realism of Hardcore.  It didn't suprise me one bit that they went on (possibly permanent) haitus after its release.  All this is my opinion of course, only the band members themselves know what their motivations were.

Which brings us to Jarvis.  Mr. Cocker's first full album of material since the days of Pulp.  I wasn't hesitant to buy it as soon as it became available domestically in the States simply because of the amount of time I was sure he had put into it.  My only wish was that he would be an artist of 43 and put out an album that reflects his age and songcraft up to this point yet not try to recapture the the mood or tempo of Class in some sad attempt to please a mass market.  I wasn't disappointed at all.  Quite simply put, this is a disc that any artist could release one day then get hit by a train the next with the knowledge that his or her vision and talents had been fully realized.  Not only does Jarvis have the intelligence, wit and playful sarcasm of Class but it also has the emotional depth that made Hardcore so great.  I was in no way prepared for how brilliantly he has been able to pour his entire career in music into one cd.

It's hard to pick one or two favorite tracks because they all have a feel of their own.  Not every song will grab you on first take but once you let the album simmer a bit you'll be hard pressed to pass any up.  Cocker has always been a brilliant lyricist and in many cases the lyrics drive the melody of the song.  Whether its lamenting the plight of a teenage girl in Big Julie [She's by herself again\in the quiet secret night\Below the neighbour's window\Hands in pockets\head on one side] or pondering society's fate in From Auschwitz To Ipswich [Evil comes\I know from not where\But if you look inside yourself\maybe you'll find some in there] Cocker has a way of being totally descriptive while still leaving a bit of interpretation up to the listener.  This record may be his best effort yet with regards to lyrics.

Sonically the album sounds amazing.  It was recorded at multiple studios and was produced by Graham Sutton, Sam Lockwood, John Watson and Jarvis himself.  With so many hands in the pot and recording locations one might assume the album to be inconsistent with regards to sound, however, this is not the case.  The album feels organic and direct with instrumentation that is never out of place.  Let's hope this is only the start of Cocker's musical output in the coming years because though c**ts are still running the world, with Jarvis around to kick them in the rear it makes everything a little more bearable.

Note:  If you buy the pre-packaged album instead of downloading you will find that Running The World is a hidden track that pops up after Quantum Theory with a 28 minute gap in between.  It's a bit irritating so be prepared.

I took a bit of a gamble with this purchase, because after listening to Hamelin I was not sure that anyone else could  play Alkan as well as he does.  But Gibbons more than holds his own; I am very happy with him.

This 2-disc set covers about 2-1/2 hours of mostly wonderful music, and is important because Gibbons includes Studies 1,2,3 and 11 of Opus 39, which Hamelin has not covered.  These remaining studies are amazing:  No. 1 is called Like the Wind, and it is exactly that - a study in just how fast fingers can move on a keyboard, non-stop.  This is clearly a study in the traditional sense, but it is musical nonetheless.  I also like Nos 2 and 3, and No. 11, called the Overture, is terrific.

I generally like Hamelin a bit better for the Symphony (4-7) and the Concerto (8-10), with the exception of the Presto, number 7.  Gibbons to me makes it sound more like the ride in hell that it is supposed to be.

What makes this set even more fun, though, are the other pieces that are included.  I just love the nearly impossible Allegro Barbaro, Op 35, No. 5, which Gibbons plays brilliantly, and right after that there is a piece called, simply, "Very Lively", though it's actually moderate in tempo.  This is one of the catchiest tunes I have ever heard - you can't get it out of your head once you have heard it.  But wait till you hear the one called "Song of the Mad Woman by the Seashore".  This has to be one of the creepiest, spookiest pieces of all time.  This piece also comes after another one called "Bad Weather", which is almost as spooky.  This is what I love about Alkan - his ability to tell a story, or create a vivid tone picture on the piano.

Overall this set is a very good deal for the price, and will provide a lot of enjoyment for Alkan fans.

reviewText: "Et exspecto. . . " was meant to be performed out-of-doors. It was a DeGaulle Commission for the dead of the Second World War. The obvious subject matter is directly reflected in the immense physicalness of the  music,the large recurring brass statements. Like the recurrence we  experience in cathedrals, we feel the weight, the severity here. Messiaen  sets up a spiral-like structure and ultimately this is what you feel as a  listener. Boulez as always brings a punctuated clarity to this hommage with  metal percussion sounds,glockenspiel,almglocken helping to pinpoint these  brass laments. Hearing the work live you will experience this separation of  these sonorities more than this recording. Also with a large array of  tam-tams spread over the stage area there is a sonic-like symbolism, as if  Messiaen is constructing a piece of sonic sculpture. Huge surging like  tam-tam tremoli as well, overwhelming makes you "feel" and sense  the dead. "Chronochromie" as well was the first to exhibit what  now is known as Momente form. This is where you have large creative  configurations of materials, timbres,chords,linear ideas. To help organize  and project these ideas you align them in terms of similarities, so for  instance several screens of music can contain one to ten of these musical  ideas in gradations. And certain moments become defined by what musical idea  is most prevalent. So in certain moments, one can say are saturated by the  woodwind sound, or the presence of a chord.  What Messiaen does here is  reduce his musical ideas from simple woodwind, fast-filigreed ideas to  large orchestral tutti complete with as-fast-as-possible scales and  arpeggios. This is now a classic work and has stood the test of time, so  much so that many subsequent works of Messiaen have been dwarfed by it.  Boulez and Cleveland as always brings a refinement of means.

reviewText:
As a food lover and an admirer of Paris, to have the two come together in one film is a dream come true. And what better genre of movie for this to happen than an animation, helmed by the old wisdom of Disney and the new talent of Pixar. I will definitely watch the film when it gets released here in Australia, but I got my hands on the score as soon as it was released.

I recall first getting to know Michael Giacchino through the score of THE INCREDIBLES, another Disney/Pixar masterpiece. I thought his music was quirky, light-hearted and expressive, but nonetheless did not impress me much. This time around, Giacchino has a brilliant story/medium on which to write his score, and he took every advantage of it. Frenchy, exciting, appetizing and at its heart - touching - Giacchino ought to be very proud of his achievement for RATATOUILLE. Indeed, I am a proud owner of it and I dare say this would finally get Giacchino a nod for Best Original Score come Oscar time next year.

"Le Festin", performed by Camille, is a fantastic opener and mood-setter. Camille's a great French chanteusse, and this song is entertaining and uplifting. I wouldn't be surprised if this song got nominated for an Oscar (Best Original Song). The theme found within "Le Festin" populates the entire score in different variations - tango-ed, slowed down/accelerated, jazzed up - it's all there.

As for the music, I find it difficult to impart to you anything more about it, other than it has your usual rich orchestration and interesting choice of instrumentation. Perhaps let me try telling you what it reminds me of: I always wanted a CD with that Parisian sidewalk cafe feeling; one that would give me a unique, indescribable feeling. Accordians on a breezy night, chattering that gives you the sense of company but never intrusively loud, soft ember glows emitted by Federation-style lamps, waiters bustling about in the most prim and proper of manners and gastronomically enticing food. RATAOUILLE conjures all these. Above all, it gives me such great pleasure listening to this CD - I'm sure you'd enjoy it just as much as I.

If you were lucky enough, such as I, to have experienced the magic of Disney's BEAUTY AND THE BEAST, and happen to recall a particular scene in which Lumierre, Cogsworth, Mrs Potts and Chip presented Belle with her dinner and the genius "Be Our Guest", and loved that - then you HAVE to get RATATOUILLE.

Three words from moi: "C'est tres bon!".

reviewText: Whenever an album (or any piece of media, for that matter) reaches a certain level of cultural and critical fame, there's a risk of backlash from the listening public. Expectations have been set very high coming in, and new listeners are not likely to be forgiving if the album falls short, no matter how unattainable what was promised might be. It seems being overrated is a far worse crime than being merely of poor quality. This is the challenge that Master of Puppets finds itself in. Metallica's third album has been widely hailed not only as a brilliant achievement, but a clear contender for the title of greatest metal album ever composed. That's no small claim, and whether or not it holds up in the end, expectations are still going to be incredibly high. And I have a hard time believing that it doesn't meet them. Giving this record a listen for what may be the hundredth time, it's a testament to Metallica's compositional prowess how fresh it still sounds. There's a bit of magic in the performance; the band is angry, unforgiving, and inspired, and it shows throughout the fifty-some minute running time. Hetfield gives his definitive performance here, with his melodic snarl melding perfectly with Kirk Hammet's harsh, oft-chugging guitar work. Cliff Burton bass is as good as the band has ever been, and Lars... well... he can hit drums somewhat competently, I suppose. Every song is given the treatment it deserves here, from the colossal "Battery" to the proggy instrumental "Orion". The typical Metallica album layout is here, and refined to perfection. "Battery" is an up-tempo thrasher hard enough to break your teeth on, but still catchy enough to follow from the first listen. "Master of Puppets" and "Disposable Heroes" are both epics, with some of the best solos of Kirk Hammet's career. "Welcome Home (Sanitarium)" is a great improvement on the similarly-styled "Fade to Black" from Ride the Lightning, with a light, melodic first half, and a heavy, instrumental second half. "The Thing That Should Not Be" is another Lovecraft-inspired bit of horror; it may have a plodding pace, but it fits the subject matter perfectly. "Orion" is the instrumental; Metallica seemed to be going with a progressive feel for this one - it strikes me as vaguely Opeth-ian, which is a very good thing. With light, atmospheric work blending with the heavier riffs and organic solos, this one is a real winner. Some songs, such as "Leper Messiah" are admittedly weaker than the rest, but that just means the bar is set to "high" rather than "very high". Master of Puppets is undoubtedly required listening, and I would recommend getting any non-metal friends around to listen as well. You may not win any converts, but it is textbook metal, and will give them a better idea than anything of what the genre is about. Best metal album ever? Maybe. One you'll still be listening to years from now? Definitely.

reviewText:
As you no-doubt can tell I LOVE The Beatles.  I also love Miles and Brubeck and 50's/60's music, having grown up with all of it.  I was NOT a Fiona Apple fan, however, and when watching this movie for the first time, I had my socks blown off by her incredibly sad rendition of my favorite Lennon composition.  I do collect covers of Beatles music, especially love the jazz interpretations, and have a library of albums like the soundtrack to I Am Sam, Across The Universe, and interpreters like Chet Atkins, Al Di Meola, George Benson, etc.  So... Fiona made me a fan, at least temporarily and I even tried out one of her own albums (not bad).

This movie of course is not about The Beatles but is one of those messagy stories which John would have approved of I am sure, and the basis of plot uses music (with a wonderful aural spectrum provided by Randy Newman and not included here except at the end with the main theme) to coincide with the personal "growth" of the characters, so that by the time you arrive at Miles Davis' So What, all hell is breaking loose in the pleasant little town of Pleasantville!  Break it on down folks!

(If you are interested in the Randy Newman original score for the movie that is sold separately as Pleasantville Original Motion Picture Score; this album is the " Music From The Motion Picture" so be aware of which one you want)

Music is not lightly picked in most film scores and while Randy Newman composed an awesome and sweeping (as usual) original score for the movie, the motion picture soundtrack also heavily relies on the non-original music tracks which further enhance the total cinematic experience.  Coy little 50's ditties like Dream Girl, Be-Bop-A-Lula, Elvis' Teddy Bear and (wink wink nod nod) Larry Williams' Lawdy Miss Clawdy are strategically placed where they provide the witty lyricism needed to amplify the story.  Two songs on this soundtrack did not appear in the film and one only wonders where Fiona's cover of Please Send Me Someone To Love and also Billy Ward's not-so-subtle 60 Minute Man were slotted to show up!  Brubeck's Take Five, Etta's At Last, Buddy Holly's Rave On, and especially Davis' So What show up when big splashes of color are about to make major transformative shifts in the Black & White Leave It To Beaver World of Pleasantville.

The script and music in this movie provide a wonderful allegory in the realm of individualism over homogeny, "nothing's gonna change my world" (Lennon), and so it is only natural that Fiona's somewhat evenly drab but provocatively breathy voice was used to deliver the overarching message of the medium: "Words are flowing out like endless rain into a paper cup they slither while they pass they slip away across the universe pools of sorrow waves of joy are drifting through my open mind possessing and caressing me"; and when the process of transformation begins to undulate and the individualism creates friction against the immovable force of static, the momentum is slow but sure, "Images of broken light which dance before me like a million eyes they call me on and on across the universe thoughts meander like a restless wind inside a letter box they tumble blindly as they make their way across the universe."  Like the Beatles song, Pleasantville is a unique and beautiful film made with wit and empathy, and the soundtrack is a stream of consciousness slice of life journey through the disturbing of the quiet sameness.

So if your world is too blandly black and white, and you need a splash of color traumatization, jimmy and jive your way through the bends and curves, let Miles beg the question So What?  You'll feel better in no time.

Sorry for the corny title but it's all I can think of. This is the most dark and depressing Katatonia CD. I realize a lot of people might not like it very much. The songs are not very appealing or catchy, they seem dry and bland, the production and the vocals are bad compared to newer Katatonia efforts, and there doesn't seem like there's much creativity in the songwriting. The song structures are mostly verse-chorus-verse, which I don't usually enjoy too much, but Katatonia knows how to make it good. What makes this CD good is essentially the guitar riffs and vocal melodies, there isn't much creativity or originality otherwise. I just like this CD for it's genuine deep, dark, chilling feeling that very few CDs give me.
The Vocals are just so relaxed, he is not trying to sing to impress you at all, he is singing for the mood of the music. The guitars make it pretty heavy at times but there is no growling whatsoever on this CD - Katatonia has abandoned it starting with this album. There are also very quiet, dark guitar melodies between parts of songs. The most noticeable one is in "Deadhouse" when the song suddenly breaks down into a gloomy sad part with unusual, unsettling little howls.
"Saw you Drown" is probably my favorite song. It is just so dark and dreary. As Jonas sings "In the water, I saw you drown / Down the water, Saw you drown" I just picture him very depressed, standing by a pool of murky water in a sewer type area, and a girl is drowning helplessly in it, and he really wants to save her and he can save her without any trouble, but he just doesn't for some reason because he just needs to tell her that he saw her drown, and not save her.
Another one of my favorites is "Instrumental" which is a very creative name for an instrumental song. It is amazing how they create such a dark atmosphere with just guitars. "I Break" is also one of the best songs, which does the same thing. There's nothing else much to say, all the songs sound similar but don't get boring. "Distrust" abruptly ends the CD with a sudden unexpected cut, which I think is metaphoric and could mean life sometimes suddenly ends, or this review suddenly ends

These two musicians are a force of nature.  Having just seen their second Minneapolis concert, it is clear that their musicianship far exceeds the press they have received, and in their latest album their virtuosity is jaw-dropping and the breadth of their material has evolved in a very striking way.

Dedicated by the duo to 11 of their mentors -- among them Carlos Santana ("Hanuman"), Jimi Hendrix ("Buster Voodoo"),  Astor Piazzola ("Hora Zero") and Israeli Oud (Triveni")-- the album seizes the listener by the throat with its opening track and never lets up until the final chords of "11:11," dedicated to Pink Floyd.

Residents of Ireland, Rodrigo Snchez - lead guitar, and Gabriela Quintero= - rhythm guitar have created a style so uncanny and original, it is impossible to call it flamenco nuevo nor rock.  In a word, it is "release." Ms. Quintero's mind-boggling percussive work on her guitar must be seen to be believed. Happily the duo's last few releases include DVD's to make it possible.

In this particular album, the fact that they're able to fuse their style seamlessly to their colleagues says much about their love of music and their place in the line of splendid artists on this instrument. A wordy sentence, but no better way to say it.

Mr. Snchez produced 11:11, and has completed the task with splendid audio, both warm and balanced. While I would have appreciated a few more cuts, I hardly feel shortchanged. These two musicians, on record or onstage, are among the most generous with talent of any I've seen or heard.

reviewText:
If you've seen Kylie's live DVDs before, you know just how much she puts into these performances. This is very much along the same lines as previous DVDs: outstanding entertainment from beginning to end. From the acrobatics to the dancing to the costumes and sets, everything fits Kylie's music perfectly. It's imprtant to me to note that Kylie actually performs her songs, and a band actually plays the music. Given the amount of work she has to do to perform a 2+ hour show, she naturally has background singers (and I belive some pre-recorded vocals in place) to support her, but she really sings at her concerts and never lip-syncs, unlike some other pop singers out there.

I was fortunate enough to be at the Ft. Lauderdale performance of Kylie's Aphrodite: Les Folies tour, so this DVD stands out for me because it helps to conjure memories of that show. I can honestly say it was the best show I've ever seen. I love Kylie's music, and there was so much to hold my attention throughout, but mainly it was for the joyous frenzy Kylie whipped the crowd into. Everyone was on their feet, dancing, often singing along. Sometimes we were mesmerized by the spectacle; sometimes we felt one with the spectacle. I've been to plenty of shows over the years, but this one was the most full of wonder. I can be as cynical as they come, but, for the duration of the concert, the stresses and problems of the world really slipped away, and Kylie became the focal point of positivity for an arena full of people. I think that's a wonderful thing that pop music can do, and I think Kylie's the best in the world at it.

This CD/DVD collection captures Kylie's London performance and takes its place in a long line of great Kylie concerts. As always, it helps that the Aphrodite album is so good, as many of those songs are mixed in with her established classics. It's great to hear the new stuff, as well as the new arrangements on the older songs, the almost hard rock version of "Can't Get You Out of My Head" being just one example.

Kylie fans: you already know how great she can be. I definitely think this is as good as or better than her previous live albums and DVDs. For the rest of you, who may be curious after hearing so many positive reviews: This wouldn't be a bad place to start if you're looking for an overview of Kylie's best songs, as well as her ability to entertain live.

To coincide with Dolly's European tour of 2007, there were several CD releases including yet another best of compilation and three twofers (of which this is one) featuring six albums, five of which had never been released on CD while the other had only briefly been available in the early days of CD. Three of Dolly's older albums were also released with bonus tracks (of which this is one) although only the bonus tracks were new to CD, the main albums having already been made available on earlier releases.

The basic Jolene album as originally released had ten tracks, all of a high quality.  Two of them became number one country hits for Dolly before eventually becoming internationally famous. The first was the title track, which became a British top ten hit in 1976. Dolly's music has been popular in Britain ever since, and may now be more so than in her homeland, although her popularity isn't reflected in raw chart statistics. Many singers have covered Jolene over the years since, the first major cover being by Olivia Newton-John, who included it on her 1976 album, Come on over.

The other famous song on Dolly's Jolene album is, of course, I will always love you, though it took much longer to achieve international acclaim.  Linda Ronstadt was the first major artist to cover it when she included it on her 1975 album, Prisoner in disguise. Dolly re-recorded the song for her 1982 movie, Best little chicken house in Texas (yes, I know it wasn't a chicken house), whereupon the new version repeated the success of the original by becoming a number one country hit. International success eluded the song until Whitney Houston made it into a worldwide pop hit. Then Dolly had another country hit with the song, this time as a duet with Vince Gill, though it didn't make the top ten. As a footnote, it's worth noting that multi-artist pop compilations featuring the song often include one of Dolly's solo recordings rather than Whitney's version, presumably because of royalty issues.

There was always much more to the original album than the two classics. Eight other great songs include When someone wants to leave (a sad song about a one-sided love), River of happiness (I always loved this upbeat, happy song, though I cannot listen to it now without thinking of Amazon), Highlight of my life, It must be you and Living on memories of you. There are also two outstanding songs that weren't new to Dolly's existing fans, though they were new to me at the time because I was just starting my record collection when I bought this album in 1978; more about those later.

None of the four bonus tracks have ever been released before although one of the songs (Barbara on your mind) should be familiar to Dolly's fans. Dolly later re-recorded the song for her 1982 album Heartbreak express, along with three other songs that she had previously recorded (Release me, Do I ever cross your mind, My blue ridge mountain boy). As originally recorded in 1973 in a style similar to the other album tracks, Barbara on your mind sounds somewhat different from its 1982 re-incarnation. Brilliant as that track is, my favorite among the four bonus tracks is Cracker Jack, a story song about a dog that supposedly had fun with as a child, having discovered him as a homeless stray. I don't know if the story is true or a figment of Dolly's fertile imagination, but it's brilliant either way. The other two songs (Another woman's man, Last night's lovin') are also excellent.

With four tracks of such high quality that could have been included in the original album, one is left to wonder at the decision to leave them out, especially as two of the chosen songs were not new. Lonely coming down first appeared on My favorite songwriter Porter Wagoner, an album released in 1972, less than two years before the song re-appeared on Jolene. Early morning breeze is a little older, having first appeared on the 1971 album Coat of many colors, although Dolly re-recorded it (only slightly differently) for the Jolene album. Well, it doesn't matter now that the expanded album is available. The curious thing is that the liner notes only comment on the original album although the recording details cover the bonus tracks as well.

If you've already got the original album on CD, you may be reluctant to buy the expanded version. If you're a committed Dolly fan as I am, you'll easily by the inclusion of three previously unheard songs and a fourth that is very different (and more countrified) than the hitherto familiar version. Compare that with the re-releases of Coat of many colors (also four bonus tracks but only two previously unheard songs) and My Tennessee mountain home (only one bonus track, Secred memories, available elsewhere on CD, it first appeared on the album Love is like a butterfly, which album still awaits a CD release). If you have all three albums on CD already, the bonus tracks here offer better value than the other two.

reviewText:
At the turn of Sixties and intensely through the first half of the Seventies, German Rock and Electronica influenced music all over the Western World. CAN, or Kraftwerk or even Ash Ra Tempel-- Gottsching's group--influenced different but important artists here, from Talking Heads to Anthony Kiedis, David Bowie or even Johnny Rotten.

Gottsching's second solo album--"E2-E4"--leaves behind the brand of Space Rock he helped invent for a crisp but extremely poetic dialogue between his guitar and Electronica. More human than Kraftwerk, Gottsching travels similar but less paved landscapes than the classic Autobhan.

Along with Michael Strother and CAN's Michael Karoli, one of the best guitar players of Rock and Electronica to ever come out from Germany. This album is a classic, a classic that remains adventurous even after almost thirty years.

reviewText:
Beethoven was actually pretty much completely deaf when his late period music was composed, so this quip is not entirely true. But Sir John Gardiner and his Orchestre Rvolutionnaire et Romantique use period instruments, musicians who are supremely skilled in playing these instruments, and a method of conducting that harks back to the late Classical period and not the full-bore Romantic, big dynamics, rubato and liberal interpretation we usually associate with most 18th and 19th century interpretation in modern symphonic style.

A week ago, I wanted to listen to The Eroica, and I realized I didn't have a set of the complete Beethoven. I was debating if I wanted Bruno Walter (my go-to guy for Beethoven symphonies), George Szell or Toscanini (who was my choral teacher's professor, and whose recordings were the earliest ones I owned as a kid.) I started searching on Amazon. After some frustration and rejection of a few conductors (like Kurt Masur, no way) and not finding hardly anyone vintage except for Szell for the 20th Century conductors I admire, I stopped looking.  I messaged my best friend from college who was and still is (thanks to Facebook) my guru on all things classical recordings, and he immediately replied "Gardiner! The way Beethoven ought to sound."

When these arrived, I put on the Eroica (Symphony #3) and not only was I thrilled, but a guest who was listening with me, was equally impressed.

Not all the symphonies are equally good--I was slightly disappointed with the 7th, especially the insanely beautiful 2nd movement (the Allegretto) which sounded to me, downplayed and dare I say, fobbed off. The fourth movement, the Allegro con brio almost sounded as if it belonged to a different performance.

The Fifth is VERY good--not quite the same as listening to superstar Gustavo Dudamel's celebrated recording with the Venezuela Youth Orchestra, the recording that really launched him to stardom, but still, quite amazing. For one thing, this is a FAST version (Toscanini-fast. We used to joke in choral class about C, common time, C with the slash, cut time, and T Toscanini time. Which was twice as fast as cut time.) This is T, Toscanini Tempo. But what really appealed to me were the brass instruments, which are of the type from Beethoven's day. These horns are less brassy, more rounded and mellow and have more odd harmonic overtones, making for a very "real" or "live" sound. And they don't overpower the rest of the ensemble, though they certainly stand out. (Serge Koussevitsky, famed conductor of the BSO was reported to say about conducting, "I glare at the brass section from time to time. They aren't doing anything wrong, but it keeps them in line.") These horns are well-balanced, not muted artificially but standing out as they ought.

If you are serious about Beethoven, you probably should own a set of Gardiner's "revolutionary" (or reactionary) recording of the symphonies. Over all, it sounded wonderful to me.

reviewText:
With many considering 1980's Emotional Rescue as warmed-up leftovers from Some Girls, though I'm not one of them, perhaps that is why listeners embraced Tattoo You, generally considered the Stones' best and probably only great album of the 1980's.  If anything this shows them going back to their roots, albeit updating it for the decade, particularly with some guitar work showing they still have teeth.

Perhaps it was due to the Stones coming up with another classic song, with those three recognizable beginning guitar riffs.  The hard-edged stomp of "Start Me Up" proved the Stones still had it in them.  This song seemed poised to take the top spot on the singles chart, only to have Hall & Oates' "Private Eyes" leapfrog over it.  Three weeks at #2-oh well!  Of course, it got restarted up when Microsoft was busy flogging Windows 95 to the general public.  Thank goodness it has had time to rest so we can all enjoy it once again.

Next comes the rollicking doo wop meets rockabilly of "Hang Fire," complete with falsetto harmonies, the third single from the album that barely scratched the Top 20.

The leisurely mid-paced romp of "Slave" has the same harmonies of "Hang Fire" intercut with a sax solo, a lingering guitar solo, and snatches of piano throughout.

"She's my little rock 'n' roll/my t-ts and a-- with soul baby," sings Keith Richards in the updated 50's rock of "Little T&A," showing that they haven't abandoned any of their trademark naughtiness behind.  Another 50's-influenced track is the racing rocker "Neighbours," where Jagger tells his neighbors to stay away from his woman and quit eating his food while he's working hard, along with the Confucian ethic of "do unto strangers, do unto your neighbours what you do to yourself, yourself, yourself."

Classic blues time, harmonica included, with "Black Limousine" on how rock stars look back at their glory days riding in said cars with girls in tow, and seeing how they look  now.  This song, along with the ballad "No Use In Crying," are the two where Ron Wood contributed to songwriting along with Jagger and Richards.

After the rockers, it's time to relax with the softer stuff, and Mick's soul-like falsetto carries "Worried About You," on the sadness one feels when one realizes the girl turns out not to be the girl of one's dreams, and how the quest must begin anew, but until then...

"Tops" exhorts one who has enough natural born talent to reach for the top, but not to listen to the sleazy promoters who'll come and give those familiar lines, such as "stick with me, kid, I'll make you a star" and all that guff.

The moody "Heaven" scores with its watery guitar and Jagger falsettos, and is one of my favourites here.  Finally, the album ends with the second single, the reflective #13 "Waiting On A Friend," with some philosophy of women, the love game, and real needs and "don't needs" of a man mixed in for good measure:  "A smile relieves a heart that grieves."  This song also benefits from a sax delivery by Sonny Rollins.

Tattoo You shows a lot of polish, and although there is a few filler tracks, the whole album is consistent and strong in delivery.  Not as good as Some Girls, but it's one of their better albums.  Wish I could say the same for Undercover, but that's another review away.

reviewText:
With this CD, Little Feat proves they are not just a nostalgia act.  Surviving the loss of the world's funkiest drummer (Richie, you ain't gone) and contracting to a 6-piece after the departure of Shaun Murphy, they have refocused their songwriting and arranging prowess, with a few assists from Robert Hunter and the late Stephen Bruton. They originally intended to put out a collection of blues covers, but with new material this strong the covers were limited to the opening lascivious romp through Mississipi John Hurt's Candy Man Blues and Sam Clayton's playful growl on the closer, Little Walter's Mellow Down Easy, both fully Featified. In between you get the full scope of this band's diverse influences: the title track's echoes of The Band (Bill Payne's vocal resembling Rick Danko more than Levon Helm), spooky swamp funk and jazz from Fred Tackett (who has evolved into an effective singer in his own right) on Church Falling Down and Tatooed Girl, to another patented Feat driving anthem in Rag Top Down, some Texas swagger in Just a Fever, great Sonny Landreth-style zydeco in Salome, a second line beat propelling the driving guitars and wry vocal interplay in One Breath at a Time, a bit of Bruce Hornsby-style jazz rock in Bill Payne's Way Down Under, and some clever jams in Tackett's Jamaica Will Break Your Heart and the Bill Payne/Gabe Ford composition The Blues Keep Coming.

This CD harkens back to the rootsy first two Feat albums, and the prevalence of Bill Payne's vocals recalls the mid-70s period where he shared the spotlight with founder Lowell George. The later evolution of the band and it's jazz and funk explorations are well represented as well. Gabe Ford channels his former boss Richie Hayward, Kenny and Sam deliver the rhythm, Fred plays the hell out of everything he gets his hands on, Billy has rediscovered the B3 (best keyboard sounds on a Feat album since the 70s), Paul keeps the slide greasy, and Hunter's four lyrical contributions fit perfectly into the slightly warped Feat sensibility. Plus they have Rounder's distribution and promotional weight behind them giving them more exposure then they've had in years. If this CD doesn't re-energize and expand Feat's audience, there's no justice.

reviewText:
This is a masterpiece that rewards listening after listening.  "Deloused" was also a masterpiece of this order, but "Frances" offers other riches for the sonically adventurous besides.  My personal favorite is the free-jazz flute and saxophone on "Cassandra Gemini" (when the saxophone starts screaming and honking with digital delay on it, I find myself wishing that Pharoah Sanders or someone like him would have established this as the norm in jazz years ago or, vice versa, that punk/heavy music would have used free-form sax years ago: the horizon for music to come).

The first time I listened to it I was not sure if it was as good as "Deloused," though I certainly loved what I heard.  On the second through fifth listens, I began to hear that it was different from "Deloused," but at least equal.  Now I find it is almost completely irrelevant to say which one is better.  They are both completely realized.  These pieces demand analysis and re-evaluation like great pieces of literature and more serious music, like Beethoven or Schoenberg.  Something that Cedric said about listening to "Deloused" with a dictionary handy to decode all of his portmanteau words made me think about a work I am studying in my studies for my Ph. D. in English literature: "Finnegans Wake" by James Joyce.

That work, too, makes little sense in any conventional fashion.  You can read its six-hundred pages over and over again and never rope in any single meaning to its stream of words, but it is always intensely moving.  When Cedric intones "I think I've become one of the others" at the beginning of "Cassandra Gemini," I still am not sure what he is getting at on my thirtieth listen or so, but I am sure that it rouses me more than any other spoon-fed lyrics I am supposed to adore from those alternative flavors of the month that flash and fade.  These guys will burn brightly when other more instantly-rewarding artists flicker, much like James Joyce is still firmly on the literary radar unlike those who criticized him for his difficulty back in the day.

Trying to figure out whether "Frances" is better than "Deloused" is like trying to figure out whether Joyce's "Wake" is better than his masterpiece "Ulysses."  You will have great conversations about it and talk yourself in circles, but you will come to the conclusion that both works are simply those that you will never stop returning to because they speak to something beyond conventional experience and native to conventional experience at the same time.  The French call this uncanny pleasure "jouissance," a sensation so intense and unexplainable that it exists on the border between pleasure and pain.  Joyce had this and Mars Volta have this.

Both demand that you continually come back for more.

reviewText: Julie Andrews was the definitive Eliza Doolittle (and should have played her in the movie version of "My Fair Lady"), but the role of Maria in "The Sound of Music" belongs to the Queen of the  Broadway Musical, Mary Martin. Not only is this because  of the stellar performances by Mary Martin and Theodore Bikel, but because  for some strange reason, the producers of the movie removed some fine songs  (e.g., "There's No Way To Stop It") and substituted cheesy and  unmemorable ones in their place.  Why?  The movie was a highly entertaining  presentation of the *story* of the von Trapp family, but if you want a cd  that presents the best version of the *music* from this terrific show, get  the Broadway version!

Imagine the pressure of having to complete an album without your group's leader- the one who held it all together, the linchpin of all of the sessions. 99.9 percent of all groups would falter, fade away and never be heard from again if what happened to the ABB on 29 October 1971 (and sadly again on 11 November 1972) happened to them.
No. Not the Brothers. Had Duane lived, I'm sure that the album would have been without the "Fillmore, Pt. II" material, but to have it there is having a great piece of live music.
"Blue Sky", "Stand Back, "Little Martha", especially "Little Martha" are all 5-star tracks by a group that didn't see what was just around the corner. "Ain't Wastin' Time No More", "Les Brers In A Minor" and "Melissa" are all loving tributes to the spirit one young man from the South had.
Some might say, most might say that "Eat A Peach" has its problems, its weak points and so on, but not me. "Eat A Peach" is the greatest album ever recorded. Any CD collection without it is incomplete.

Where Everything Everything is the essential live release by any techno artist, Dubnobasswithmyheadman is easily the most essential techno studio release. This was my first full exposure to any techno artist and after hearing many others after, I can say many cannot compete on this level. Simply put: Dubnobasswithmyheadman is a classic.
Where alot of their later albums began to incorperate more melody and ambience into their releases, this won is straight up release for the dance floor. Its propelled by pulsating beats, clever samples and the almost sensous voice of Hyde(Dark and Long anyone?). While there is a lack of variety in songs, the quality of them never dips. Each song is as good if not better than the last. What's even better is how seemless the record plays out. Thanks to stellar production, the CD almost plays out like a movie(complete with rising action[Mmmm Skyscraper I Love You], climax[Cowgirl], and finally fadding away with M.E.). Songs are of the usual Underworld length, ranging some where between 7 and 12 minutes in length. However, with songs of this quality, it doesn't really matter.
Those even remotely curious about the techno genre should immediately plunk down the cash for this release. You can't go wrong with this release(or any other Underworld release for that matter). To me, Underworld will always be the kings of techno. Dubnobasswithmyheadman is just a testiment to that arguement.

reviewText:
I've been listening to this box set all week, and it is a pretty comprehensive collection of classic metal. The focus of the box set is really from the 70's & 80's, though there are some songs from the 60's and 90's tacked on as well. If you don't see a particular band represented, the liner notes explain that some bands did not want to contribute to the box. The booklet included in the set is pretty cool, including a History of Heavy Metal by journalist Mick Wall. You also get a track by track summary which is pretty cool, as well as some interviews with Lita Ford and Ronnie James Dio. Here is the breakdown of what is on each of the four disks:

That is the kind of effect Delerium has. If you are reading this review in hopes of finding ethereal, ambient, mood, eclectic style music with a little dance thrown in, look no further. Karma will make your life better, simple as that.

reviewText: For all intents and purposes, this soundtrack to the hit movie "Waiting to Exhale" is a Babyface record all the way.  Here, Kenny Edmonds is in top form as a songwriter and producer, coming up with stellar tracks featuring a handful of the most respected female singers in r&b.  "Why Does it Hurt So Bad" is Whitney's best, and most crushing, breakup song ever; the legendary Chaka shows off her pipes in her reworking of "My Funny Valentine," and Brandy gives her best single yet in the cutesy "Sittin' Up In My Room."  Mary J. Blige brings the house down in "Not Gon' Cry," based on the movie's character, the troubled Bernadine.  SWV shine in "All Night Long," and I absolutely love Chante Moore's seductively mellow "Wey You." This would be Babyface's last great project before he would experience a slow and steady decline, but you can always turn to this soundtrack, which was one of the best albums of the 1990s.
